context: Any person found to be engaging in the manufacture, import, sale, or distribution of any misbranded food product, subject to appeal under this Act, shall be liable to pay a monetary penalty not exceeding two lakh rupees for the first offence and one lakh rupees for subsequent offences. The appointed authority may, upon receiving credible information regarding such violations, conduct inspections at premises suspected of harbouring these activities without prior notice, provided that reasonable cause is demonstrated in writing. Failure to comply with directions issued by the appointed authority concerning corrective actions or production recalls shall attract additional penalties as determined under this Act. Repeat offenders may be subject to suspension of licenses and prosecution before a court of law.

Where a dispute arises regarding the appointment or conduct of an appointed authority established under this Act, either party may apply to the designated judicial forum as specified in Schedule I. The application shall detail the grounds upon which the challenge is based, including but not limited to allegations of bias, conflict of interest, or failure to adhere to procedural requirements prescribed herein. Subject to just cause and fair opportunity being afforded to all concerned, the judicial forum may, after hearing both parties, issue directions modifying or setting aside the appointment or any action taken by the appointed authority. Any order passed under this provision shall be binding on the appointed authority and all other relevant stakeholders. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek appropriate costs in relation to such proceedings. Provided that no challenge to an appointed authority’s decision may be entertained if it is made after a period of ninety days from the date of communication of that decision.

Where any immovable property is vested in an appointed authority pursuant to an order under this Act, and dispute arises regarding the validity or interpretation of that vesting order, either party may appeal to the District Judge having jurisdiction over the property. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of service of notice of the vesting order, provided that the Court may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of such period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are demonstrated. The appointed authority shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the vesting to the District Judge upon request. Any decision rendered by the District Judge in respect of such appeal shall be final, subject to a further appeal to the High Court on grounds of law alone.

Every food business operator shall maintain records relating to the procurement of raw materials, production processes, quality control measures, packaging, storage, distribution and sale of food products manufactured or handled by them. These records shall be preserved for a minimum period of six months from the date of expiry of the respective food product or batch, whichever is later, and made available for inspection by authorised officers upon request. The format and content of such records shall conform to guidelines issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, as amended from time to time. Failure to maintain adequate records, or providing false or misleading information during inspection, shall be deemed an offence under this Act. Any officer inspecting a food business premises may require submission of these maintenance of records electronically where feasible.

Where a claim for compensation arises under this Act relating to injury to or damage sustained by reason of an accident involving a motor vehicle, any person dissatisfied with the award made by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal may prefer an appeal to the Transport Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such award. The appellate tribunal shall consider all relevant materials placed before the Tribunal and may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. It shall also direct that the costs of the appeal be paid by either party as it deems just. Provided that the appellate tribunal may entertain an appeal if the appellant satisfies it with sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within the stipulated period. The Transport Appellate Tribunal shall pass a reasoned order and furnish copies to all parties concerned, outlining its findings and directions regarding remedies available under this Act.

Registration of agreements relating to immovable property shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the existence of a contractual obligation subject to the provisions herein regarding fraud or misrepresentation. Where an agreement for the sale, mortgage, or lease of agricultural land is executed but not registered within three months from the date of its execution, such agreement shall be voidable at the option of the party who was not privy to the delay. The period of limitation for suits relating to contracts affecting immovable property shall be twelve years commencing from the date the contract becomes operative, provided that a suit may be brought within six years where the non-registration resulted from demonstrable clerical error by an official registrar. Any document presented for registration must clearly indicate the agreed timeframe for performance under this Act.

The amount payable towards gratuity, as determined by the Assessing Officer under this Act, shall be subject to the schedule of fees prescribed in the First Schedule hereto. The said schedule details charges applicable for verification of documents, assessment proceedings, and subsequent revisions undertaken pursuant to appeals filed before the Grievance Redressal Committee. Any dispute concerning the applicability or calculation of these fees may be raised by either the employer or the employee during the initial assessment process. Provided that, in instances where the Assessing Officer’s determination is contested, the Grievance Redressal Committee shall review the matter and determine whether the schedule of fees was correctly applied, considering prevailing guidelines and established precedents. The decision of the Grievance Redressal Committee shall be final, subject to appeal before the Labour Court as provided herein.

Registration of Goods and Services with Designated Standards Every entity intending to register goods or services under this Act shall submit a detailed application specifying the nature of the product or service offered, its intended consumer base, and the manufacturing process employed, where applicable. The application must include precise descriptions conforming to designated standards as may be notified by the Central Authority from time to time. Failure to provide such prescribed particulars will render the application liable for rejection. Further, any alteration to the registered goods or services necessitating a change in the description shall require a fresh registration and updated submission of all relevant information. The Central Authority may request additional documentation verifying compliance with applicable quality benchmarks at any stage during processing.

Every vehicle registered under this Act shall undergo a mandatory periodic inspection at intervals prescribed by the Central Government, notification of which will be published in the Official Gazette. The inspection shall be conducted by an authorized inspector appointed by the State government, possessing qualifications as specified in Schedule B appended to these regulations. Following each inspection, the authorized inspector shall prepare and submit an inspection report detailing the vehicle’s condition with respect to roadworthiness, safety standards, and emissions compliance. This inspection report shall contain a unique identification number and be maintained electronically within the designated transport department database. Any deficiencies noted in the inspection report must be rectified by the owner of the vehicle within thirty days. Failure to address these deficiencies may result in restrictions under this Act. The inspection report is conclusive evidence regarding the vehicle’s compliance status, subject to appeal before a designated appellate authority as provided herein.

Every undertaking engaged in inter-state commerce involving the supply of goods or services exceeding a turnover of ten crore rupees shall maintain a register of undertakings detailing all contracts entered into, including those sub-contracted, and shall make it available for inspection by authorized officers upon reasonable notice. Failure to comply with this provision shall attract a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees and may extend to two lakh rupees for the first offence. Subsequent offences will incur penalties doubled under this Act. The register of undertakings must be updated within thirty days of execution of any contract, provided that discrepancies discovered after this period are rectified immediately and reported alongside an explanation. Any attempt to conceal or falsify entries in the register shall render the responsible person liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year.

For the purposes of this Act, a statutory declaration is defined as a written statement verifying certain facts or assertions made therein, executed before an authorized officer as specified under the First Schedule. Such declaration shall contain a clear and unambiguous affirmation regarding the truthfulness of the matters stated, and may be required by public authorities for verification of information provided under this Act. A statutory declaration presented in compliance with prescribed procedures is deemed sufficient evidence of the facts declared, subject to challenge through due process as provided herein. The officer administering the oath or affirmation shall attest to its validity.

Every applicant seeking a learner's permit or a driving licence shall satisfy the licensing authority that they possess the physical fitness required for safe operation of a motor vehicle, subject to medical examination as may be prescribed. A provisional driving licence shall be granted only if the applicant has successfully completed the practical training specified under this Act and produced satisfactory evidence thereof. The conditions of licence include adherence to traffic regulations and responsible driving practices; any violation demonstrated through documented incidents or complaints may result in suspension or revocation. Where a licence is suspended, the holder shall remain ineligible for renewal until the period of suspension expires and they demonstrate compliance with remedial measures as determined by the authority. Any person aggrieved by an order suspending or revoking their licence may appeal to the appellate authority within thirty days of such order.

Where any person has failed to comply with a direction issued under this Act relating to environmental protection or remediation measures, the Central Government shall determine the amount due from that person representing costs incurred by the Government in taking action pursuant to the said direction. The determination of such amount shall be made after affording the concerned person an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in their defence. Recovery of dues determined under this Act shall be effected as if they were arrears of land revenue, and shall be recoverable from such person or their property, either movable or immovable. Provided that, before initiating recovery proceedings, a notice specifying the amount due and the grounds for its determination shall be served upon the concerned person by registered post with acknowledgement due. The Central Government may also direct any bank or financial institution to freeze accounts of the defaulting party to secure recovery of dues.

Where a dispute arises concerning the enforceability of an agreement for the sale of goods, or relating to breach of contract involving performance obligations exceeding ten thousand rupees, either party aggrieved shall first seek resolution through mediation facilitated by a panel appointed under this Act. Should mediation fail within ninety days from the date of appointment of the mediator, or if either party refuses to participate in good faith, the dispute may be referred to an appellate tribunal established for such purposes. The tribunal shall hear evidence presented by both parties and make findings based solely on documents submitted and oral testimony recorded before it. Decisions of the appellate tribunal are final subject to judicial review only on grounds of legal error demonstrable from the record.

Registration of Agreements Concerning Land Use Rights shall proceed according to established protocols, ensuring clarity regarding all material facts influencing consent. Where an agreement relates to the transfer or granting of land use rights, including but not limited to leasehold interests, easements, and licenses for specific purposes such as mining or cultivation, a duty of disclosure arises on the part of the grantor. This duty extends to any encumbrances, restrictions, or prior agreements affecting the land’s usability that are known to the grantor at the time of registration. Failure to disclose such information shall render the agreement voidable at the option of the grantee, subject to remedies available under this Act for misrepresentation and breach of contract. The Registrar may require affidavits confirming full disclosure before proceeding with registration.

Where a commercial vehicle is registered with an Assessing Authority, the owner shall furnish a security deposit equivalent to two months’ road tax liability at the time of initial registration. This security deposit serves as assurance against non-payment of applicable taxes and penalties under this Act. Failure to remit road tax within the stipulated period will trigger forfeiture of such security deposit in whole or in part, as determined by the Assessing Authority. The owner may apply for a refund of the unutilized portion of the security deposit upon transfer of ownership of the vehicle or cessation of operations, subject to verification and clearance of outstanding dues. Any claim for refund shall be processed within thirty days of receipt of application. The Assessing Authority may recover any unpaid road tax from the forfeited security deposit, provided that notice is given to the owner prior to such recovery.

Claims arising from accidents involving motor vehicles shall be preferred before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal constituted under this Act within a period of three years from the date the cause of action arose. Provided that the Tribunal may entertain claims filed after the expiry of said period if it is satisfied, from the record or evidence adduced before it, that the claimant was prevented by sufficient cause from making the claim within the prescribed time. Such cause shall include, but not be limited to, physical incapacitation preventing the filing of a claim, or demonstrable ignorance regarding the accident and potential right to compensation. The Tribunal shall afford an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned before determining whether sufficient cause exists to condone the delay. This period of limitation is jurisdictional in nature, and any deviation therefrom may render subsequent proceedings untenable under this Act.

Where food is served in a ready-to-eat form, the manner of service shall be deemed relevant for determining compliance with hygiene standards under this Act. Any licensed establishment providing food services may adopt methods including but not limited to plate presentation, disposable containers, or self-service counters; provided that such adoption does not compromise the safety and nutritional value as prescribed by regulations. Disputes regarding whether a particular manner of service constitutes a violation of these provisions shall be first addressed through conciliation under sub-section (2) of section 47. Failure to resolve the dispute through conciliation may result in an appeal to the Food Safety Appellate Authority, subject to the timelines and procedures outlined herein. The authority’s decision shall be final, barring appeals on grounds of legal error.

Every electricity distribution licensee shall ensure that all infrastructure installed for supply of electricity conforms to standards notified under this Act and guidelines issued by the Central Electricity Authority from time to time. The conditions of licence granted to a distribution licensee are subject to compliance with load forecasting procedures, which must be submitted annually and approved by the State Commission. Failure to adhere to these forecasts may result in penalties as determined by the Commission. A licensee shall also maintain adequate records pertaining to power outages and implement corrective measures within thirty days of identification of systemic failures. The State Government may, after due consultation with stakeholders, impose additional conditions relating to consumer protection and grievance redressal mechanisms.

Where a party has communicated his intention to revoke a contract offer, the revocation is deemed effective from the time that communication is received by the offeree, subject to any express terms agreed upon between the parties regarding notice periods. However, where such communication is ambiguous or incomplete, and reasonable doubt arises as to the genuineness of the intent to revoke, the party claiming revocation shall bear the burden of proving, to the satisfaction of a civil court, that the offeree reasonably understood the intention to terminate the offer. Disputes concerning grounds of revocation may be brought before a jurisdictional magistrate, whose decision is appealable to a district judge within thirty days from the date of such determination.

Where a consumer dispute is amenable to resolution through negotiation or mediation, the District Commission shall facilitate discussions between the parties involved with a view towards reaching a mutually acceptable settlement. Such facilitation shall include providing access to appropriate resources and guidance regarding consumer rights and remedies under this Act. The Commission may appoint conciliators as it deems fit for this purpose. Any agreement reached by the parties through such negotiation or mediation, documented in writing and signed by both parties and the conciliator, shall constitute a terms of settlement. This terms of settlement shall have the force of an order passed by the District Commission and be binding on all parties involved. Failure to adhere to the terms of settlement may render a party liable for penalties as provided herein. The Commission shall maintain a record of all such settlements.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a motor vehicle based on allegations of forged documents or misrepresentation concerning the vehicle's history, the burden of proof shall lie upon the objector to establish, with reasonable certainty, the falsity of the information presented during the registration process. This requirement applies particularly where claims involve alterations to the chassis number, engine identification number, or any other permanently affixed identifier as recorded in the Registering Authority’s records. The Registering Authority may demand supporting documentation and conduct inquiries deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the submitted details. Provided that the objector fails to discharge this burden of proof satisfactorily, the registration shall proceed as originally proposed under this Act.

Every authorized officer conducting an inspection of premises under this Act shall prepare a detailed inspection report documenting observed deficiencies related to product safety or service delivery. Such inspection report shall include particulars of any non-compliance with standards, regulations, or representations made by the business operator. The report must specify corrective actions required and timelines for their implementation, provided that such timelines are reasonable considering the nature of the deficiency. A copy of the inspection report shall be served upon the business operator within seven days of completion, allowing for a response within fourteen days as provided herein. Failure to rectify deficiencies within the stipulated timeframe may result in penalties under this Act. The authorized officer shall ensure accuracy and impartiality in the preparation of each inspection report.

Where a consumer has suffered loss or injury due to deficiency in service or unfair trade practice, they may file a complaint with the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission or higher appellate forum as provided herein. The complainant shall be entitled to seek compensation including damages for loss of property, services not rendered, and consequential losses arising from such deficiency. Upon receiving a complaint, the concerned authority shall provide notice to the service provider or manufacturer, affording them an opportunity to submit their response within thirty days. If the appointed authority finds merit in the consumer's claim, they may direct the business entity to rectify the deficient service, replace faulty goods, and pay compensation as deemed appropriate. Further, costs of proceedings including legal representation shall be awarded at the discretion of the appointed authority.

Every Regional Transport Authority shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all registrations of motor vehicles, including but not limited to details of ownership, insurance coverage, fitness certificates, and emission compliance reports. These records are deemed vital for the effective administration under this Act and for facilitating investigations into accidents or violations. Any alteration or deletion from such records must be accompanied by a duly authenticated reason and approved by an officer designated by the State Government. Failure to maintain accurate and accessible records shall constitute an offence punishable with a fine, as determined by the competent authority. An aggrieved party may appeal against any decision regarding access to or rectification of these maintenance of records within thirty days from the date of such decision, subject to judicial review.

Where a party to a contract has failed to perform his obligation in accordance with its terms, and the other party serves upon him a written notice of demand requiring performance within a specified period, failure to comply with such notice shall constitute a breach entitling the serving party to immediate recourse under this Act. The notice of demand must clearly state the nature of the default and the specific action required for remediation. Any attempt at partial or delayed compliance after expiry of the stipulated period in the notice shall be deemed insufficient. Where the defaulting party fails to satisfy the requirements of the notice, the aggrieved party may pursue remedies including but not limited to recovery of damages and enforcement of specific performance, subject to judicial discretion regarding penalties assessed.

Every license issued for the manufacture, processing, packing, sale, distribution, import or export of any article of food shall specify the prescribed particulars relating to the nature of the activity authorized, the location of the premises where such activity will be conducted and a detailed list of food categories permitted for handling. Such licenses may be assigned by the licensee to another entity subject to prior written approval from the competent authority, provided that the assigning party demonstrates continued compliance with all applicable regulations under this Act. The proposed assignee shall submit an application detailing their qualifications and facilities, which will be assessed against equivalent standards as those applied to original applicants. Any alteration to the prescribed particulars of a licensed operation requires notification and subsequent verification by the licensing officer.

An employer seeking to obtain a certificate of registration under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Controlling Authority specifying details regarding the establishment, including its registered address, nature of business conducted, number of employees employed, and annual turnover. The application must be accompanied by attested copies of relevant documents such as incorporation certificates or partnership deeds, as may be required by the Controlling Authority. An employer shall not be eligible for a certificate of registration if it is found to have defaulted in payment of gratuity to any employee under this Act. Any alteration in the particulars furnished in the application requires prior intimation to the Controlling Authority and approval thereof.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice of demand” with respect to information held by a public authority shall be deemed to have been duly served when it is delivered in person or sent by registered post acknowledgement due to the designated Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer, as applicable. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the information sought, including but not limited to the period covered and any specific documents requested. The public authority shall be deemed to have received a notice of demand on the date of its receipt by the said officer, provided that if no acknowledgement of delivery is received within fifteen working days from the date of dispatch, the notice shall be deemed received seven days after the expiry of that period.

Registration of Gratuity Claims and Resolution of Disputes Where a gratuity claim is submitted for registration under this Act, the registering officer shall verify the details provided by the employee or nominee against records maintained by the employer relating to employment history, salary drawn, and length of service. Any discrepancy identified during verification may necessitate further documentation from either party. The registering officer shall maintain a register detailing all claims registered, including dates of submission, acknowledgement numbers, and status updates regarding processing. Disputes arising concerning eligibility for gratuity or calculation thereof may be referred to a Grievance Redressal Committee constituted by the appropriate government. Such Committees shall endeavor to facilitate amicable settlement; however, where resolution is not achieved through conciliation, the matter may proceed towards compounding of offences as provided herein.

Where an inspection report pertaining to the roadworthiness of a motor vehicle is prepared by an authorized inspecting officer under this Act, any party disputing the findings contained therein may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of a copy of said report, file a written objection with the Regional Transport Authority. Such objection shall specifically detail the grounds upon which the inspection report is challenged and must be supported by documentary evidence where applicable. The Regional Transport Authority shall afford both the inspecting officer and the objector an opportunity for hearing, subject to principles of natural justice. A decision rendered by the Regional Transport Authority regarding the validity of the inspection report shall be final, provided that a further appeal lies to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

The rights granted to a concessionaire under this Act relating to the extraction of mineral resources from designated areas may be assigned or sub-licensed to any other entity with prior written consent of the Central Government, provided that such assignment or sub-licence shall not alter the obligations imposed upon the original concessionaire regarding environmental remediation and community benefit sharing. The manner of service of notices pertaining to proposed assignments shall conform precisely to those prescribed for service on arbitral tribunals under this Act, including requirements relating to registered post and certified mail. Any party seeking to assign or sub-license rights must disclose all material terms of the proposed transaction to the Central Government within thirty days prior to execution. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the government.

Any person desiring to execute a contract requiring verification under this Act may, in lieu of appearing before a Magistrate or other officer authorized to administer oaths, submit a statutory declaration affirming the truth and accuracy of the contents thereof. Such declaration shall be made before any Notary Public or Advocate practicing in India, who shall certify its execution. Failure to comply with the formalities prescribed herein for the preparation of a statutory declaration renders the contract voidable at the option of any party aggrieved. Any person making a false statement within a statutory declaration shall be liable to prosecution under relevant provisions concerning perjury and face penalties as determined by the Courts. The Notary Public or Advocate attesting such declarations shall be subject to disciplinary action if found negligent in verifying identity.

Where a party seeks to establish the existence or non-existence of a fact relevant to a contract, they may submit a statutory declaration affirming or denying said fact, provided that such declaration is made before an officer authorized by law to administer oaths. The declarant shall be deemed to have affirmed the truthfulness of the contents of the declaration under penalty of perjury as defined herein. Any party challenging the veracity of a statutory declaration may apply to the appropriate court for its scrutiny and determination; the court’s decision on such challenge shall be final and binding. Failure to comply with the prescribed form or manner of execution renders the declaration inadmissible as evidence, subject to judicial discretion considering mitigating circumstances. The liability for damages arising from false statements within a statutory declaration remains unaffected by this provision under this Act.

An application for a certificate of registration shall be made to the Controlling Authority in Form A, accompanied by copies of documents evidencing establishment, financial standing, and employee details as prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall declare, in the form, that the particulars furnished are true and correct to the best of their knowledge and belief. Upon receipt of an application, the Controlling Authority may require further information or clarification from the employer. Any such request must be communicated in writing within thirty days of receiving the initial application. Failure to respond adequately within fifteen days thereafter shall render the application liable for rejection. The Controlling Authority shall issue a certificate of registration if satisfied with the veracity and completeness of the submitted documentation, recording its reasons for satisfaction. A copy of the certificate shall be served upon the applicant by registered post.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act involving a dispute relating to a contractual obligation or relationship, the parties involved may, by written agreement executed before a judicial magistrate of the first class or a notary public, agree to compound the offence. Such agreement shall specify the terms and conditions for the compounding, including but not limited to the amount of compensation payable to the injured party and any remedial actions required. The judicial magistrate or notary public shall satisfy themselves that the injured party has freely consented to the proposed compounding and receives adequate consideration. Provided that no compounding shall be permissible where the offence involves fraud or moral turpitude as determined by the investigating officer, subject to confirmation by a designated authority. Any agreement for compounding of offences made in violation of these provisions shall be void.

Every establishment required to maintain a register of undertakings under this Act shall ensure that entries relating to each undertaking are made within thirty days of its commencement or substantial change in circumstances affecting gratuity liability. Failure to accurately record details such as employee names, dates of joining, and rates of wages will render the employer liable for penalties as determined by the Grievance Redressal Officer. An aggrieved employee whose particulars have been omitted or incorrectly recorded may file a written complaint with the designated authority, accompanied by supporting documentation. The authority shall investigate the matter expeditiously and direct the employer to rectify the register within fifteen days. Any delay in rectification attributable to the employer’s negligence will attract further penalties and potential recovery of gratuity dues from the employer.

In cases where a claimant seeks compensation arising from injury or loss sustained due to an accident involving a motor vehicle, and lacks documentary evidence establishing ownership or contractual relationship with the driver or owner, such claimant may submit a statutory declaration affirming their claim and detailing the circumstances of the incident. This declaration shall be sworn before an authorized Magistrate or Notary Public and must include particulars of the claimant, the vehicle involved, and the nature of the loss suffered. The Regional Transport Authority may require further verification as it deems fit to assess the veracity of the declaration. Provided that a fraudulent statutory declaration submitted with intent to deceive shall render the declarant liable for penalties under this Act, including but not limited to fines and potential criminal prosecution. Any award granted based on a statutory declaration is subject to review if evidence contradicting its contents emerges later.

An arbitration agreement registered under this Act shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent amendment or modification of the law under which it was made. Any person seeking to ascertain the status of a registration shall be entitled to inspect the Register of Arbitrators and Arbitration Agreements maintained by the designated registering authority, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed in that behalf as provided herein. The application for a certificate of registration must include certified copies of the arbitration agreement and any related documents deemed relevant by the registering authority. Failure to submit complete documentation may result in rejection of the application. An aggrieved party may appeal against the refusal or delay in issuing a certificate of registration to a higher appellate forum, as specified under this Act.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a record of all arbitration agreements registered under this Act, including details pertaining to the parties involved, the subject matter of the dispute, and the governing law applicable to the agreement. Upon registration, the Authority shall issue a certificate of registration, which shall be deemed prima facie evidence of the existence and validity of the arbitration agreement. Any party seeking to amend or supplement an existing registered arbitration agreement must submit a request in writing, accompanied by an updated copy reflecting the proposed changes. The Registering Authority may require further documentation substantiating the consent of all parties involved before approving such amendments. A material failure to disclose relevant information during the registration process constitutes grounds for subsequent review and potential invalidation, particularly concerning any duty of disclosure owed to other contracting parties.

Every contracting party engaged in commercial transactions involving the exchange of goods or services shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all agreements entered into, including but not limited to details of parties involved, description of goods or services rendered, agreed consideration, timelines for performance, and any modifications made to the original terms. These records must be preserved in a durable medium accessible for inspection by designated officers authorized under this Act. The preservation period shall be ten years from the date of completion of the contractual obligations, or such longer period as may be prescribed by regulations framed thereunder. Failure to maintain adequate records will constitute an offence and render the defaulting party liable to penalties as provided herein. Any officer conducting inspections relating to maintenance of records shall produce valid identification and provide written notice prior to access, subject to exigencies requiring immediate investigation.

Registration of Public Information Officers shall proceed according to established protocols detailed within Schedule A, ensuring adherence to principles of transparency and accountability. Any officer so registered undertakes a continuing obligation to maintain accurate records pertaining to information requests received and processed under this Act. The Central Information Commission may, upon receiving credible complaints, initiate inquiries into the conduct of registered officers. Following such inquiry, if it is determined that an officer has demonstrably failed to uphold their duties or engaged in practices detrimental to the intent of this legislation, grounds of revocation of registration shall arise. Such revocation requires a formal order published on the Commission’s website and communicated directly to the affected individual, subject to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

The Central Information Commission may, subject to the provisions of this Act, authorize a Public Authority to establish a scheme for the compounding of offences relatable to non-compliance with directions issued under this Act, provided that such scheme specifies the categories of offences eligible for compounding and the corresponding monetary amounts. Any Public Authority operating under such an authorized scheme shall obtain prior written consent from the Commission before assigning or subcontracting any portion of its responsibilities pertaining to offence investigation or compounding procedures. Such assignment shall not relieve the Public Authority of ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with this Act. Further, a third party acquiring rights through transfer of assets from a defaulting Public Authority may be held liable under this Act for outstanding compounded offences, proportionate to the value of assets acquired, as determined by the Commission.

For the purposes of this Act, “revocation” with regard to contracts for supply of goods or services means the unilateral termination of such contract by either party where conditions specified herein are met. Grounds of revocation shall include, but not be limited to, a material failure by the service provider to render services as originally agreed; demonstrable misrepresentation regarding the quality or nature of goods offered; and significant deviation from advertised specifications which substantially impacts usability or functionality. Revocation is permissible subject to providing written notice to the other party at least thirty days prior to the intended termination date. Provided that, revocation does not absolve a party from obligations accrued under this Act relating to refunds or compensation.

The Central Information Commission may, upon application, grant a certificate of registration to any entity engaged in the collection, processing, or dissemination of data relating to public services, subject to verification of their adherence to established protocols for data security and privacy. Such certificates shall be transferable upon assignment by the registered entity to another qualifying body, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the Commission and a formal notification of the transfer is submitted detailing the rationale and proposed operational framework of the successor entity. The Commission may impose conditions on any such registration, including limitations regarding the scope of data handled or the duration of validity. Any attempt to assign a certificate without fulfilling these requirements shall render the assignment void ab initio. Further, under this Act, the registered entity remains liable for compliance with all applicable provisions even after transfer.

For the purposes of this Act, a certificate of registration granted under this Act shall confer upon the registered entity the legal right to generate or supply electricity within the designated area specified in the certificate. The application for a certificate of registration shall include detailed information regarding the proposed generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, and distribution network. A certificate of registration may be revoked if the registered entity fails to comply with the technical standards prescribed under this Act or engages in practices detrimental to consumer interests. Any alteration to the scope of operations outlined within a certificate of registration requires prior approval from the appropriate regulatory authority as provided herein.

Where a creditor seeks recovery of dues from a debtor through presentation of documentary evidence, the onus shall lie upon the creditor to establish the existence of the debt and the amount due. The Court shall consider all documents produced by the creditor, including but not limited to ledgers, invoices, receipts, and bank statements, in determining the validity of the claim. Provided that, if the debtor raises a reasonable doubt regarding the authenticity or accuracy of any document presented, the creditor may be required to produce further evidence corroborating its contents. The Court may also call upon witnesses to testify concerning the transactions recorded in such documents. Failure by the creditor to satisfy the Court on these points shall render the claim unsustainable under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers or functions under this Act to any officer of the government or any authority empowered to exercise such powers or perform such functions, provided that no power relating to adjudication of offences shall be delegated. Such delegation shall specify the extent and duration of the delegated authority. Any order delegating powers may also include conditions governing the exercise of those powers. The Central Government retains the right to revoke any delegation at any time. This provision regarding delegation of powers is without prejudice to any other power conferred upon the Central Government under this Act.

Where a dispute arises between an employer and an employee regarding the eligibility or amount of gratuity payable under this Act, either party may apply to the Controlling Authority for resolution. The application shall specify the nature of the dispute and provide supporting documentation including appointment letters, salary slips, and any relevant correspondence. Upon receipt of such an application, the Controlling Authority shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity to present their case and submit evidence. Any agreement reached between the employer and employee through conciliation or negotiation, constituting a terms of settlement, shall be recorded by the Controlling Authority in writing and signed by both parties. Such terms of settlement shall have the force of an order passed under this Act and be binding on both parties. Failure to comply with the terms of settlement may render either party liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where any food business operator contests a decision issued by an appointed authority regarding the seizure of unsafe food or misbranding, they may file an objection within thirty days from the date of communication of the order. Such objections shall be submitted in writing to the appellate authority, clearly stating the grounds upon which the challenge is based and supported by relevant documentation. The appellate authority shall consider these objections de novo, affording both the objecting party and the appointed authority a fair opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence. Provided that the appellate authority may dismiss an objection if it finds the same to be frivolous or vexatious, without requiring further hearing. Any order passed by the appellate authority is final subject to further appeal under this Act.

Where any food business operator applies for a licence under this Act, the licensing officer shall grant such licence only if the applicant complies with all conditions of licence prescribed herein, including but not limited to adherence to hygiene protocols and proper storage facilities. Any decision regarding refusal or revocation of a licence may be appealed to the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The appellate authority shall consider any objections raised by the food business operator and may uphold, modify, or reverse the original order. Provided that the licensing officer shall provide written reasons for any adverse decision; failing which, the appeal is deemed to be without merit.

The authorization to undertake environmental remediation activities on land designated as a ‘Critical Ecological Zone’ under this Act may be granted by the Central Government to qualified entities possessing demonstrable expertise in ecological restoration techniques. Such authorizations shall specify the precise scope of work, including but not limited to soil stabilization, water purification, and reforestation initiatives. The holder of an authorization is permitted to assign or sub-license such rights to a subsidiary company or affiliated entity, provided that prior written consent from the Central Government is obtained. Any assignment shall include a detailed inventory of assets and liabilities associated with the remediation project. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated in the authorization may result in its revocation. A notice of demand for rectification of environmental damage must be served upon the authorized party before any legal proceedings are initiated.

For the purposes of this Act, “notice of demand” with respect to food intended for sale shall mean a written communication issued by an authorized officer to a food vendor or manufacturer requiring the production, submission, or furnishing of specified records, documents, samples, or information relating to the safety and standards of such food. Such notice shall clearly state the reasons for the demand, the specific items required, and the deadline for compliance as provided herein. The notice of demand may be served by registered post with acknowledgement due or delivered personally to the addressee. Failure to comply with a notice of demand without reasonable cause constitutes an offence under this Act.

Every employer who fails to furnish within thirty days of the death of an employee a statutory declaration verifying entitlement to gratuity, or furnishes a declaration containing false particulars, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Such penalty may be recovered as if it were an arrear of land revenue due from such employer to the Government. Further, where any officer is satisfied that an employer has wilfully suppressed information relevant to determining gratuity eligibility, or attempted to obstruct investigation under this Act, he may impose a further penalty up to five thousand rupees. The adjudicating authority shall provide opportunity for hearing before imposing any penalty as provided herein and its order shall be final subject to appeal to the appellate authority.

Where any consumer disputes the findings of an adjudicating officer relating to deficiency in service or unfair trade practice, they may file an application for review within thirty days from the date of communication of the order. Such application shall clearly specify the errors apparent on the face of the record and grounds upon which the original decision is challenged. The adjudicating officer may entertain such applications if satisfied that a substantial question of fact or law arises therein. Any party dissatisfied with the outcome of the review, if entertained, shall have the right to appeal under this Act to the State Commission within sixty days from the date of the reviewed order; provided that the appellate authority may dismiss frivolous appeals without hearing.

Where an employee claims gratuity under this Act based upon alleged continuous service, the onus of establishing that period of employment satisfies the requirements for eligibility, including compliance with attendance norms as defined by the employer’s standing orders, shall rest entirely upon the claimant. Provided that, if the employer fails to produce adequate records pertaining to the employee's service history, or such records are demonstrably incomplete or ambiguous, the benefit of any doubt regarding the extent and regularity of the employment shall be afforded to the claimant. Furthermore, where an employer disputes a gratuity claim on grounds of alleged forfeiture under this Act, the burden of proof demonstrating the existence of circumstances justifying forfeiture shall lie with the employer.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to provide information within the time specified under this Act, or provides inaccurate or incomplete information, an aggrieved person may file an appeal before the appellate tribunal established as provided herein. The tribunal shall consider such appeals and issue orders directing the Public Information Officer to rectify the deficiencies identified in the complaint. Any order issued by the appellate tribunal shall be binding on the Public Information Officer and the concerned public authority. Failure to comply with an order of the appellate tribunal may result in penalties, including fines as determined under this Act. The aggrieved person shall have the right to approach the appellate tribunal within thirty days from the date of receipt of the unsatisfactory response or denial of information. Further, the tribunal’s decisions are subject to judicial review.

Where any party disputes the findings of an adjudicating officer concerning the admissibility of documentary evidence presented before them, they may file an objection within thirty days from the date of the adjudication’s pronouncement. Such objections shall be submitted to a designated appellate tribunal established under this Act. The appellate tribunal shall review the record of proceedings and determine whether the adjudicating officer acted in accordance with principles of natural justice and relevant legal precedent. Provided that, if the appellate tribunal finds the evidence improperly admitted or excluded, it may order its re-examination by the original adjudicating officer, subject to such directions as the tribunal deems necessary. Decisions of the appellate tribunal are final, but may be challenged further under provisions relating to judicial review.

Where a dispute arising out of or relating to a construction contract is resolved through arbitration proceedings under this Act, the parties are bound by the terms of settlement agreed upon during those proceedings. Such terms shall constitute a legally binding agreement and may include provisions regarding payment schedules, rectification work, and adjustments to contractual obligations. Failure to adhere to the terms of settlement shall render the defaulting party liable for damages as determined by the arbitral tribunal or, in cases of further dispute, by a civil court exercising jurisdiction. The tribunal shall have the power to enforce compliance with the terms of settlement through appropriate orders, including specific performance and monetary compensation. Any application seeking enforcement of the terms of settlement must be made within three years from the date thereof, subject to just cause shown for delay.

Every public authority obligated under this Act to maintain a register of undertakings shall ensure that said register accurately reflects all contracts entered into by the authority exceeding a value of five hundred thousand rupees. The register must include, but is not limited to, details regarding the contractor’s name and address, the description of works or services undertaken, the commencement and anticipated completion dates, and the total contract value as initially agreed upon. Updates to any undertaking reflected in the register shall be recorded promptly, within seven working days of their occurrence. Failure to maintain an accurate and up-to-date register constitutes a violation under this Act. Information pertaining to ongoing disputes concerning undertakings is not required to be included, provided that such exclusion does not impede transparency as provided herein.

Where an arbitration agreement contains provisions concerning the place of arbitration, the arbitral tribunal shall sit at such place as is agreed upon by the parties or, failing such agreement, at such place as the court referred to in section 43 determines. The Court may, subject to appeal under Chapter X, direct the arbitral tribunal to conduct proceedings at a different location if it considers that circumstances render it necessary for the proper administration of justice. An officer authorised by the Court and acting under its direction shall have power of entry into any premises required for such purpose, accompanied by such assistants as may be deemed necessary. Such entry shall only occur during daylight hours and after due notice is given to the occupier, provided that this requirement may be dispensed with if the urgency of the matter demands otherwise, recorded in writing. The officer shall submit a report detailing the exercise of power of entry to the Court within seven days thereafter.

A statutory declaration made under this Act relating to any intellectual property rights arising from a contract for services rendered shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding concerning the assignment or licensing of those rights, provided that the declarant affirms, within the declaration itself, that they are duly authorized by their employer or principal to make such affirmation. The declaration must clearly state the scope and nature of the intellectual property interest being assigned or licensed, including a detailed description sufficient for identification under relevant industry standards. Any party seeking to rely on a statutory declaration shall be responsible for demonstrating its authenticity and compliance with these provisions. Further, any assignment facilitated by a statutory declaration may be sub-licensed subject to terms explicitly stated within the original declaration itself, without requiring further consent from the assignor unless otherwise specified in the underlying contract.

In cases involving claims arising from motor vehicle accidents, parties involved, including claimants, insurers, and respondents, may agree upon terms of settlement to resolve disputes without further adjudication. Such terms shall be recorded in writing and signed by all parties or their authorized representatives. The Motor Accidents Settlement Tribunal established under this Act shall have the power to facilitate such settlements and ensure fairness in the process. Provided that any term agreed upon must not contravene the principles of natural justice or public policy, and cannot prejudice the rights of third parties who are not a party to the settlement. Where a claimant accepts terms of settlement, they shall be deemed to have relinquished their right to pursue further claims related to the accident, subject to fraud or misrepresentation. The Tribunal may, at its discretion, review any such terms if it deems them manifestly unjust.

Where a Food Safety Officer has reasonable grounds to believe that any food is adulterated, misbranded, or otherwise unsafe as per the standards laid down under this Act, such officer shall have power of entry into any premises wherein such food is manufactured, processed, stored, sold, or distributed. This power of entry shall be exercised only during business hours, provided that in cases where the Food Safety Officer has reason to believe that evidence may be concealed or destroyed after business hours, entry may be permitted at any time with a written order from the designated State Food Authority. Any person obstructing a Food Safety Officer exercising such power shall be liable for penalties as prescribed herein. The officer shall provide clear notice of their identity and purpose before entering, except in circumstances where immediate action is necessary to prevent spoilage or contamination.

Any food business operator who fails to obtain a certificate of registration prior to commencing operations shall be liable to pay a monetary penalty as determined by the Food Safety Officer, which may extend up to ten thousand rupees for the first offence and twenty-five thousand rupees for subsequent offences. An application for a certificate of registration shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, and any applicant found to have knowingly provided false information in their application is subject to cancellation of the certificate and further penalties as deemed appropriate under this Act. A food business operator aggrieved by the refusal or suspension of their certificate of registration may appeal to the appellate authority within thirty days of the order. The appellate authority shall consider all relevant evidence and pass an order, which shall be final.

Every application submitted under this Act seeking authorization for the establishment or operation of an industrial unit generating effluent shall include prescribed particulars relating to the proposed site, including detailed topographical maps at a scale not less than one inch to two hundred feet, indicating existing land use and proximity to water bodies. The application must also specify the nature and quantity of effluents anticipated to be discharged, along with a comprehensive plan for treatment and disposal, conforming to standards as may be prescribed by the Central Pollution Control Board. Further, plans submitted shall demonstrate compliance with relevant setback distances from human habitation and ecologically sensitive areas. Any alteration to the proposed project following approval requires prior intimation to the State Pollution Control Board and may necessitate re-evaluation of environmental impact assessments. The Board may require submission of additional data or conduct site inspections as deemed necessary to ascertain adherence to prescribed particulars.

For the purposes of this Act, an Appellate Tribunal is defined as a body established for adjudicating disputes arising from orders passed under this Act concerning claims for compensation or other matters relating to motor vehicles accidents. The jurisdiction of the Appellate Tribunal shall extend to reviewing any order that has been made by a Motor Accidents Claims Settlement Authority or similar authority designated under this Act. An appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal subject to prescribed limitations regarding time and maintainability, as provided herein. The composition and procedure of the Appellate Tribunal shall be determined in accordance with rules framed under this Act.

Where a party seeks to establish a fact which is not admitted, the burden of proof lies upon that party to prove the existence of that fact. This obligation shall extend to demonstrating all essential elements necessary for establishing the truth of the asserted matter. The Court may require such party to produce documentary evidence, witness testimony, or any other admissible form of proof as deemed appropriate under this Act. Provided that, where a rebuttable presumption exists regarding a particular fact, the burden shifts to the opposing party to provide satisfactory evidence disproving the presumed circumstance. Failure to discharge this burden shall be construed against the party asserting the fact. The Court is not bound by any specific method of proof and may consider circumstantial evidence in determining whether the requisite standard has been met, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “record” includes any document, file, email, memorandum, dispatch or other communication in whatever form, whether physical or electronic, created, received, held, used or processed by a public authority; and the term "maintenance of records" shall mean the systematic organization, indexing, preservation, retrieval, security, storage, and disposal of such records as provided herein. A record shall be deemed to be maintained if it is accessible to an information officer under this Act, irrespective of its physical location or medium. The obligation to maintain records extends to all records relating to any action taken by a public authority affecting the rights or obligations of citizens; provided that exemptions permissible under Chapter IIA shall apply.

The onus of establishing the truth of any fact in issue lies upon the party who asserts it; that is to say, the burden of proof rests with the individual or entity alleging the existence of said fact. This obligation shall extend to proving all essential elements necessary for the factual assertion to be legally established. Provided that, where a statute expressly provides for a presumption regarding any particular fact, such presumption shall relieve the party from discharging the burden of proof relating thereto; however, this relief is subject to conditions as may be prescribed under this Act concerning rebuttal of said presumption. The standard required to discharge the burden of proof shall be that of preponderance of probabilities.

Applications for registration of societies seeking exemption from payment of fees under Section 27 shall be submitted in Form ‘A’ appended to these regulations, duly completed and signed by the authorised representative of the society. The prescribed fee for initial registration, as detailed in the schedule of fees annexed hereto, is payable at the time of submission. Provided that societies registered prior to the commencement of this Act may apply for re-registration within a period of one year from such date, subject to fulfilling all conditions stipulated herein. Any alteration in the society’s objectives or bye-laws after registration shall require notification to the Registrar and payment of a revised fee as determined by the schedule of fees. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

Where a party seeks redressal for loss or damage arising from breach of contract, fraud, or negligence, an action may be brought subject to the provisions concerning limitation as provided herein. The right to initiate such legal proceedings shall not accrue beyond three years from the date the cause of action arose; however, where the facts constituting the cause of action were concealed by fraudulent misrepresentation, the period of limitation shall extend to six years from the discovery of such concealment. Provided that in cases involving claims against government entities or public authorities acting through their agents, the prescribed periods may be extended as determined by the competent court based on demonstrable circumstances hindering timely awareness. Any claim brought after the expiry of the applicable period of limitation shall be deemed inadmissible, and the Court shall dismiss the same without further consideration.

The distribution licensee shall have the power to assign, pledge, or otherwise create a security interest over any receivable arising from electricity supplied under this Act, subject to prior approval of the State Commission. Such assignment or security interest may include all rights and obligations pertaining to the recovery of dues owed by consumers, including but not limited to late payment surcharges and disconnection protocols. The licensee shall provide notice of such assignment to the affected consumer at least thirty days prior to its effective date, detailing the identity of the assignee and any changes in billing procedures. Provided that, no assignment shall prejudice the right of the State Government or a municipal authority to recover outstanding dues from the distribution licensee under this Act. Further, the Commission may prescribe conditions relating to the terms and pricing of such assignments to ensure fairness and transparency in the recovery of dues.

Registration of Agreements Relating to Agricultural Produce Transactions Where an agreement for the sale or exchange of agricultural produce is sought to be registered under this Act, the Registrar shall require that the instrument specifies the nature and quantity of the produce involved, the agreed price per unit, and the date upon which possession and payment are intended to transfer. Furthermore, it shall be incumbent on the parties entering into such agreements to declare any existing liens or encumbrances affecting the produce in question. Failure to disclose such information constitutes a material omission. The prescribed particulars relating to the identity of the vendor and purchaser must also be clearly stated within the document presented for registration. Any alteration made subsequent to initial presentation renders the instrument voidable unless countersigned by both parties, as provided herein.

Where any officer authorised under this Act reasonably suspects that evidence relating to an offence punishable thereunder is concealed within any premises, such officer may exercise the power of entry into and search of those premises. Provided that before exercising such power, the officer shall, if practicable, give written notice to the owner or occupier specifying the premises intended to be searched and the reasons for the proposed entry. The reasonableness of the suspicion shall be a material fact for determination in any subsequent challenge under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing permission for such entry may appeal to the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, whose decision shall be final.

Where a consumer disputes the validity of an agreement entered into with a service provider or manufacturer, and seeks revocation under this Act based on grounds of unfair contract terms, the adjudicating officer shall first determine whether the term in question falls within the definition of “unfair” as provided herein. The aggrieved party bears the onus of demonstrating that the term caused significant imbalance in rights and obligations between them and the service provider or manufacturer. Should the adjudicating officer find a term to be unfair, revocation may be ordered subject to an assessment of compensation payable to the other party for any detriment suffered due to such revocation. Any order made by the adjudicating officer is appealable to the State Commission within thirty days, and the appellate authority shall consider whether the findings regarding grounds of revocation were supported by substantial evidence.

Where any contractual obligation requires the creation and maintenance of records pertaining to goods or services rendered, the party obligated to maintain such records shall be deemed to have undertaken a responsibility to preserve those records in a manner accessible for inspection by the other contracting party. Failure to do so, without reasonable cause attributable solely to circumstances beyond the control of the defaulting party, shall constitute a material breach under this Act. Any dispute arising from alleged inadequate maintenance of records may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. The arbitrator shall have the power to award damages reflecting loss suffered due to unavailability or inaccessibility of said records, subject to limitations prescribed by rules of equity and good conscience. An appeal against an arbitral award concerning record-keeping obligations lies only on grounds specified under this Act.

Any authorized officer conducting an inspection under this Act may, upon observing deficiencies in adherence to prescribed standards or practices relating to goods or services, prepare an inspection report detailing such observations. The inspection report shall specify the nature of the deficiency, relevant dates and times, and any corrective actions recommended to the business operator. Failure by a business operator to rectify deficiencies within the timeframe stipulated in the inspection report may result in penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to suspension of licenses or imposition of monetary fines. An appeal against findings contained within an inspection report may be made to the Central Authority within thirty days from the date of receipt thereof; however, such appeal shall not preclude enforcement action pending its resolution.

Every Public Information Officer failing to provide information within the time specified under this Act, without adequate cause recorded in writing, shall be liable to pay a compensatory amount as determined by the Central Information Commission, not exceeding twenty-five rupees per day of delay, subject to a maximum penalty of two thousand and fifty rupees. The First Appellate Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding such failure, issue directions for compliance and impose penalties under this provision. Any officer obstructing or misleading a Public Information Officer in the performance of his duties shall also be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to similar penalties. For the purposes of enforcement actions under this Act, the Central Information Commission shall designate a competent officer who will investigate complaints and recommend appropriate remedial measures.

Where an employer contravenes any provision of this Act or fails to comply with any notice served upon him under this Act, the Controlling Authority shall issue a show cause notice requiring him to explain, within thirty days from the date of receipt thereof, why he should not be prosecuted for such default. The notice shall specify the nature of the alleged contravention and the penalty proposed to be imposed. Upon consideration of the explanation, if any, submitted by the employer within the stipulated period, or failing such submission, the Controlling Authority may determine that an offence has been committed. Further, subject to appeal under this Act, the Controlling Authority may direct the compounding of offences punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, in accordance with prescribed procedures and conditions.

Every person intending to operate a food processing unit involving manufacture, processing, packing, storage, distribution or sale of any article of food shall apply for registration under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the licensing officer may require submission of detailed plans demonstrating adherence to hygiene standards and operational procedures. The applicant shall furnish a comprehensive register of undertakings involved in the supply chain, including primary producers, transporters, and packaging material suppliers. This register must be maintained accurately and made available for inspection by authorized officers at all times. Assignment of responsibility within the undertaking supplying food articles requires prior notification to the licensing officer; such assignment is subject to approval based on demonstrated competence. Failure to maintain a current register or provide accurate information constitutes an offence, punishable as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive index of all documents received pertaining to registrations undertaken under this Act, detailing the nature of the registration request, the date of receipt, and the assigned reference number for tracking purposes. Such index shall be accessible for public inspection during prescribed office hours, subject to restrictions as may be notified by the Central Information Officer regarding sensitive personal data. The maintenance of records relating to these registrations is paramount to ensuring transparency and accountability within the registration process. Any officer entrusted with maintaining such records shall adhere strictly to established protocols concerning their preservation and security, provided that digital copies are deemed equivalent to original documents for all purposes under this Act.

An undertaking seeking registration under this Act shall submit a detailed declaration outlining its principal activities, including but not limited to construction, manufacturing, or service provision, along with a list of all directors and key managerial personnel. The declaration must be verified by a practicing solicitor and accompanied by certified copies of incorporation documents and relevant licenses. Upon receipt of the application, the registering authority shall publish a notice inviting objections from any interested party within thirty days. Any objection received shall be duly considered before proceeding with registration. A register of undertakings maintained under this Act shall be accessible for public inspection during office hours, subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed. The registrar may refuse registration if information provided is false or misleading.

Where a suit is proposed to be brought under this Act for recovery of damages or compensation arising from a tortious act, it shall not be admissible unless such suit is instituted within three years from the date when the cause of action arose; provided that in cases where the defendant’s liability depends on proof of a material fact which could have been ascertained by him but was not, owing to fraud or concealment, the period of limitation may be extended at the discretion of the Court. Further, if the injured party was under disability, as defined herein, at the time the tortious act occurred, the period of limitation shall run from the date when the disability ceases; subject to the condition that such suit is instituted within three years thereafter.

Where a party to an agreement fails to perform his obligation as agreed, and such failure constitutes a breach of contract, the injured party shall have recourse to remedies provided herein. The right to sue upon such breach is subject to the period of limitation prescribed under this Act; namely, three years from the date the cause of action arose. Provided that, where the breach relates to an immovable property, the period of limitation shall be five years from the date of the breach. It is further provided that any suit brought after the expiry of the applicable period of limitation may be entertained only if the injured party demonstrates exceptional circumstances rendering it just and equitable to allow such a claim. The court may, in its discretion, grant appropriate relief including damages, specific performance or injunction as deemed fit, considering the prejudice suffered by the aggrieved party.

Where notice is required to be served upon a party under this Act, the manner of service shall be deemed sufficient if it is delivered personally to that party or left at their last known place of residence or business. Provided that, where the address of such party is not ascertainable, service may be effected by registered post with acknowledgment due, and the date of dispatch shall constitute proof of service. Further, in cases involving corporations, service shall be deemed sufficient if delivered to the Secretary or other officer duly authorized to receive notices on behalf of the corporation. Any party disputing the validity of service must demonstrate a material prejudice resulting directly from any deviation from the prescribed manner of service; otherwise, such dispute shall be considered frivolous and may attract appropriate costs. The court may grant relief to a party demonstrably prejudiced by improper service as it deems just.

Where a motor vehicle is used for gain or hire, and damages are sustained by any third party due to an accident involving such vehicle, the owner of the vehicle shall be liable for recovery of dues arising from those damages. Provided that, if the driver of the vehicle was acting without the knowledge or consent of the owner, and it is established that the owner exercised reasonable care in entrusting the vehicle to the driver, the liability of the owner may be reduced as determined by a Claims Tribunal constituted under this Act. Further, recovery proceedings shall only be initiated after due notice has been served upon all potentially liable parties, specifying the amount claimed and the basis for such claim, and allowing thirty days for response. The Claims Tribunal shall consider any evidence presented regarding contributory negligence on the part of the claimant.

A statutory declaration made under this Act shall be in writing and subscribed by the declarant before a magistrate or an officer authorized to administer oaths, and it shall contain a clear and unambiguous statement of the facts declared therein. The declarant shall affirm that the contents thereof are true to the best of their knowledge, information and belief. Any person procuring a statutory declaration containing false statements shall be liable for punishment under relevant provisions relating to offences involving deception. Subject to compliance with prescribed forms and procedures, such declarations may be admitted as evidence in any court or proceeding; provided that the party seeking admission must demonstrate reasonable certainty regarding the declarant’s identity and capacity to understand the implications of the declaration.

Where a party fails to pay any sum due under an arbitration agreement or award, the claimant shall have recourse to remedies available under general law for the recovery of dues. The application for enforcement of an arbitral award seeking recovery of dues may be presented to the appropriate judicial authority as determined by applicable jurisdictional rules. Upon presentation of such application and satisfaction of prescribed procedural requirements, including payment of requisite fees, the judicial authority shall issue notice to the respondent party affording it an opportunity to raise objections under this Act. Any objection raised shall be adjudicated expeditiously in accordance with established procedures. The claimant is required to submit all relevant documentation substantiating the claim for recovery of dues alongside the application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application, subject to review by a higher appellate authority.
