An appeal against an order passed by a District Forum shall lie with the State Commission within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said order. The State Commission shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard, either in person or through duly authorised representatives. Where the State Commission considers that an investigation into any matter is necessary for the proper disposal of an appeal, it may examine witnesses under oath or affirmation and call for such evidence as it deems fit. The aggrieved party shall have the right to present documents and arguments before the State Commission. Any order passed by the State Commission may be appealed to the National Commission within thirty days. The appointed authority designated by the Central Government shall maintain a register of all appeals filed under this Act, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

The Central Pollution Control Board may, upon application from any authorized agency engaged in environmental monitoring, grant a license to access and reproduce inspection reports generated under this Act pertaining to industrial units classified as Major Sources of Pollution. Such licenses shall specify the permitted scope of utilization, restricting reproduction solely for purposes directly related to scientific research or development of pollution mitigation technologies. The Board may impose conditions on such licenses, including restrictions regarding distribution and publication of the extracted data, ensuring confidentiality where sensitive operational details are concerned. Assignment of a license granted under this provision is permissible subject to prior written consent from the Central Pollution Control Board, provided that the assignee adheres to all terms and conditions applicable to the original licensee. Any alteration or modification to an inspection report without explicit authorization constitutes a violation punishable as provided herein.

Where a claim is made against an insurance company arising from injury or loss sustained by a third party due to the operation of a motor vehicle, the appointed authority may direct the insurer to investigate such claim and provide a reasoned determination within sixty days. Any person dissatisfied with the determination of the appointed authority shall have the right to appeal to the Transport Appellate Tribunal within thirty days of receipt of that determination. The appointed authority shall consider all relevant evidence submitted by the claimant and the insurer in reaching their decision, including but not limited to police reports, medical records, and witness testimonies. Failure on the part of an insurer to comply with a direction issued under this Act may result in penalties as determined by the Transport Appellate Tribunal. This process is subject to judicial review where fundamental principles of natural justice are alleged to have been violated.

Where a party seeks to enforce an arbitral award obtained through a statutory declaration under this Act, the aggrieved party may challenge the validity of said declaration before the designated judicial forum, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising directly from any alleged irregularity in the process of its creation. Such challenges shall be limited to instances where the declarant lacked the requisite capacity or authority to make the declaration as per applicable law and regulations. The arbitral tribunal shall provide a reasoned response within sixty days addressing the allegations raised concerning the statutory declaration, failing which, such silence shall be deemed an admission against the interest of the party relying on it. Any appeal arising from this determination shall lie to the High Court within ninety days.

Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of a document submitted for authentication before an appointed authority, either party may petition the High Court within ninety days from the date of such submission. The appointed authority shall be deemed to have acted without jurisdiction if it receives evidence demonstrating demonstrable bias or undue influence in the preparation of the document. Any order passed by the appointed authority concerning the genuineness of a signature is subject to review under this Act, and any person demonstrably prejudiced by an erroneous determination may seek redress through appropriate legal proceedings. The High Court shall have power to grant such remedies as it deems just, including but not limited to injunctions preventing further action based on the disputed document. Further, costs associated with litigation relating to decisions of the appointed authority shall be determined at the discretion of the court.

The rights and obligations arising from any arbitration agreement executed pursuant to this Act are freely assignable subject to the terms of that agreement and provided that such assignment does not prejudice the existing arbitral proceedings or the interests of any party involved. A party intending to assign their right to enforce an arbitration award, or any claim related thereto, shall execute a statutory declaration before a Notary Public attesting to the validity of the assignment and confirming that no prior assignment has been made. This declaration shall be filed with the Arbitral Tribunal within thirty days of the assignment’s execution. The Tribunal may, at its discretion and after hearing representations from all affected parties, refuse to recognize an assignment deemed detrimental to the fairness or efficiency of the arbitration process under this Act.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, grant licenses to qualified entities for the purpose of establishing and maintaining designated vehicle inspection depots. Such licenses shall be subject to annual renewal based on adherence to standards specified under this Act relating to equipment calibration and personnel training. A license holder may assign their rights and obligations pertaining to a depot, including the right to conduct inspections as authorized, to another entity upon prior written consent from the Central Government, provided that such assignment does not diminish the quality of service or compromise public safety. The power of entry into premises associated with a licensed vehicle inspection depot, whether for audit purposes or investigation of alleged irregularities, is vested in officers authorised by the Central Government and shall be exercised subject to due process and respect for operational requirements.

Where a driving license has been issued under this Act, the Central Motor Vehicle Drivers Licensing Authority may revoke such license if it is determined that the licensee obtained the same through fraudulent misrepresentation concerning their physical or mental fitness, or by suppression of material facts relating to prior convictions for offences under this Act or any other relevant law. Further, revocation shall occur where the licensee has been found guilty of driving under the influence of a controlled substance and such conviction constitutes a repeated offence within a period of three years. The Authority shall provide the licensee with an opportunity to be heard before proceeding with revocation, subject to just cause being demonstrated. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding grounds of revocation may appeal to the Transport Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority shall have the power of entry into any premises where goods or services are manufactured or offered for sale, subject to notification to the occupier and production of a warrant issued by a designated officer. This power may be exercised for the purpose of verifying compliance with standards relating to product quality, service delivery, or advertising practices under this Act. Any license granted pursuant to regulations framed under this Act concerning inspection protocols shall be assignable to accredited third-party agencies, provided that such assignment is approved by the Authority and the assignee adheres strictly to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original license. The Authority may impose a penalty on any agency found to have subverted or compromised the integrity of an inspection conducted pursuant to an assigned license. Further, the power of entry shall not extend to areas deemed sensitive under national security protocols as determined by the appropriate government department.

An employer seeking to establish a workplace gratuity fund shall apply for a certificate of registration from the Controlling Authority within whose jurisdiction the principal place of business is located. The application must be submitted in Form A and include certified copies of the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association, and any subsequent alterations thereto. Any change in the constitution of the employer or alteration to its registered office requires fresh application for a certificate of registration under this Act. The Controlling Authority may require such further documentation as it deems necessary to verify compliance with the provisions herein. A provisional certificate of registration may be issued pending verification of submitted documents, and shall remain valid for a period not exceeding ninety days. Upon satisfactory review, a permanent certificate of registration shall be granted.

Where a Public Information Officer denies access to information requested under this Act, the burden of proof that the denial is justified shall rest upon the said officer. Such justification must demonstrate compliance with all applicable exemptions as provided herein, including but not limited to those pertaining to national security and commercial confidence. The applicant may challenge such denial before the Appellate Authority, who shall consider any evidence presented by both parties. Should the Appellate Authority find that the Public Information Officer failed to adequately substantiate the reasons for withholding information, they shall direct the officer to provide access within a specified timeframe. Failure to comply with this direction will render the officer liable to penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any manufacturer or service provider who fails to comply with an order issued under this Act by the relevant authority shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding ten lakh rupees; in cases of continued non-compliance, a daily fine may be imposed at the discretion of the adjudicating officer up to one thousand rupees. The period of limitation for filing complaints alleging deficiency in service or unfair trade practices is two years from the date on which the cause of action arises. Provided that this period of limitation shall not apply where the requisite information was concealed by the manufacturer or service provider, in which case the Central Authority may condone the delay. Failure to rectify defects within thirty days after notice as provided herein will attract additional penalties.

Where a generating station or transmission licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions of its license, including but not limited to adherence to standards of reliability and safety as prescribed by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, the appropriate authority may initiate proceedings for revocation of such license. The licensee shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard in respect of any proposed action under this Act. Grounds of revocation include persistent failure to provide adequate electricity supply, demonstrated negligence resulting in significant disruption to power distribution, or fraudulent practices concerning billing and consumer accounts. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding revocation may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of receiving notification of such decision, subject to just cause shown. The authority shall consider any representations made during these proceedings before issuing a final order.

Where a party to a contract possesses material information relating to the subject matter of the agreement, but omits to disclose it voluntarily to the other party prior to its execution, that party shall be deemed to have incurred a duty of disclosure. Failure to comply with this duty constitutes a breach of contract and renders the defaulting party liable for damages sustained by the aggrieved party as a direct consequence of such non-disclosure. The amount of compensation recoverable shall be determined based on principles of fairness and equity, considering all relevant circumstances surrounding the transaction. Any dispute arising under this provision may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. Repeated or willful breaches will attract enhanced penalties, potentially including rescission of the contract and prohibition from entering into similar agreements for a period not exceeding five years.

Every adjudicating officer appointed under this Act shall receive a certificate of appointment specifying the territorial limits within which their jurisdiction extends and outlining the categories of offences they are empowered to address. An adjudicating officer is obliged to maintain a register, accessible for public inspection during prescribed office hours, detailing all cases brought before them, along with dates of hearings and orders passed. Where an adjudicating officer determines that a violation has occurred, they shall issue a written notice to the alleged offender, providing details of the infraction and the penalty imposed. The offender may submit representations within thirty days of receipt of such notice; these submissions shall be duly considered by the adjudicating officer before a final order is issued. Appeals against orders passed by an adjudicating officer are subject to review by an appellate authority as provided herein.

The records pertaining to arbitral proceedings, including all pleadings, evidence adduced, awards rendered, and any other documents filed under this Act or as directed by the Arbitral Tribunal, shall remain in the custody of the designated Record Keeper appointed by the arbitration institution administering the process, unless otherwise agreed upon between the parties. Such appointment shall be subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time. The Record Keeper may grant licenses for reproduction and dissemination of anonymized portions of these records solely for academic research purposes, provided that such licenses are accompanied by a formal undertaking ensuring compliance with confidentiality obligations under this Act. Assignment of rights relating to the maintenance of records is permitted only with prior written consent of both parties to the arbitration agreement and notification to the Record Keeper.

An application for registration of an arbitration agreement or a domestic arbitral award shall be submitted to the designated Registration Authority in the prescribed manner, along with the requisite fee detailed in Schedule A. The application must include certified copies of the original arbitration agreement and any subsequent modifications thereto, clearly delineating the parties involved and the subject matter of the dispute. Upon receipt of an application, the Registration Authority shall verify that the agreement or award complies with the provisions under this Act concerning validity and enforceability. Failure to satisfy these conditions may result in rejection. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered agreements and awards, accessible for public inspection subject to restrictions imposed as provided herein relating to confidential information impacting conditions of licence granted under specific sectoral regulations.

Registration of documents relating to agricultural land shall be deemed complete only upon affixation of a digitally verifiable seal by the registering officer, confirming receipt of all required documentation. The manner of service of notices pertaining to objections raised against proposed registrations is prescribed in Schedule A appended hereto; such service shall be effected through registered post with acknowledgement due and simultaneously via electronic mail to the designated email address of the applicant as recorded during initial submission. Where an objection relates to a boundary dispute, personal service upon the concerned parties, as defined under this Act, shall also be mandatory. Provided that, in cases where the registering officer is unable to effect service through either mode, alternative methods approved by the State Government may be employed, subject to recording of reasons for such deviation in the registration record.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to respond to a request for information within the time limit stipulated under this Act, the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, upon receiving a complaint from the complainant, shall issue a notice of demand to the concerned Public Information Officer requiring him to provide the requested information within a further period not exceeding fifteen days from the date of such notice. The notice of demand shall clearly state the nature of the information sought and the consequences of non-compliance, which may include imposition of penalties as provided herein. Failure to comply with a notice of demand shall be deemed a willful disobedience of orders under this Act and render the Public Information Officer liable for action under applicable law.

For the purposes of this Act, an adjudicating officer means an individual appointed by the Central Government or designated by the State Government, possessing qualifications in environmental science, law, or engineering, and who shall exercise powers conferred upon them for expeditious disposal of cases relating to violations of environmental norms. The adjudicating officer shall be responsible for determining liability, imposing penalties as provided herein, and issuing remedial orders. Subject to appeal under this Act, the decisions of an adjudigating officer are binding. An adjudicating officer may conduct hearings, examine evidence, and issue summons.

Every establishment engaged in the manufacture or sale of goods or provision of services shall apply for a licence from the Central Authority prior to commencement of operations, submitting detailed plans outlining operational procedures and quality assurance protocols. The application shall be accompanied by a non-refundable processing fee as determined by notification issued by the Central Government. Upon receipt of an application, the Central Authority may conduct inspections at the establishment to verify compliance with prescribed standards. A licence shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates adherence to all relevant regulations under this Act and provides satisfactory evidence of consumer grievance redressal mechanisms. The conditions of licence so granted are subject to periodic review by the Central Authority, not less than once every three years. Any alteration in operational procedures requires prior written approval from the Central Authority.

The Regional Transport Authority may, upon application and subject to satisfaction of conditions as provided herein, grant licenses for the operation of commercial vehicles engaged in the transport of goods or passengers under this Act. Such licenses shall be assignable only with prior written consent from the Authority, and such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any transfer of a license granted under this Act requires registration with the designated licensing officer within thirty days of the intended assignment; failure to register shall render the assignment void. The authority may impose fees for registration of assignments as determined by notification. Where an application for assignment is rejected, the applicant shall be provided with reasons in writing and afforded opportunity for redressal through a summary procedure established under this Act.

Every State Electricity Regulatory Commission shall maintain a register of undertakings engaged in electricity generation, transmission, distribution or supply within its jurisdiction. This register shall be accessible for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Commission to protect confidential commercial information. Any person claiming that an undertaking is not duly registered may file a complaint with the Commission, and the Commission shall investigate such complaints expeditiously. If it is determined that an unregistered undertaking has engaged in activities regulated under this Act, the Commission may direct the cessation of those activities and impose penalties as provided herein. The register shall be updated periodically, reflecting changes in ownership or scope of operations for registered entities. Failure to maintain an accurate register constitutes a violation subject to remedial action by the Commission.

Where any dispute arises concerning compliance with conditions stipulated in a terms of settlement agreed upon under this Act between the Central Pollution Control Board, State Pollution Control Boards, industries, and affected persons, either party may file an appeal before the appropriate judicial forum as determined by the jurisdiction of the original cause action. Such appeals shall be accompanied by certified copies of the terms of settlement and all relevant correspondence demonstrating adherence or non-adherence to said conditions. The appellate authority shall consider evidence presented by both parties and may order further investigation if deemed necessary, provided that any such orders are subject to review under principles of natural justice. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate authority may pursue further remedies as available under the Code of Civil Procedure.

Any individual or community claiming demonstrable harm arising from activities impacting environmental quality may submit a statutory declaration affirming the nature and extent of such harm, along with supporting documentation as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The declaration shall detail specific instances of pollution, degradation, or resource depletion directly attributable to the actions of an identified entity. Such declarations are subject to verification by the competent authority, who may require additional information or site inspections. Failure to provide accurate and truthful information in a statutory declaration renders the declarant liable for penalties as determined under this Act. The findings resulting from such verification shall be considered during proceedings relating to remedial action and compensation claims, provided that the claimant demonstrates standing to sue.

Any party seeking to enforce an arbitral award obtained through a statutory declaration under this Act shall file an application before the designated District Court within ninety days of the date of the declaration. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the application inadmissible, subject to allowance by the court where exceptional circumstances are demonstrated. The Court may require production of original documents substantiating the declaration and underlying arbitration proceedings. Any person making a false statutory declaration for the purpose of obtaining enforcement shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than one year but which may extend to five years, and also to a fine extending to ten thousand rupees. Recovery of penalties imposed under this provision shall be deemed a civil debt recoverable from any property owned or controlled by the defaulting party.

Registration of documents relating to immovable property shall be deemed complete upon affixation of the official seal and signature of the Registration Officer, subject to verification of identity as mandated under this Act. Any person presenting a document for registration shall pay fees as prescribed in the Schedule of Fees annexed hereto. The Registrar may, at his discretion, waive or reduce such fees in cases involving disputes concerning agricultural land, provided that prior written approval from the District Magistrate is obtained. Further, any alteration or addition to a registered document requires fresh registration and payment of applicable fees under the schedule. Failure to pay the prescribed fee shall render the registration voidable at the option of the Registration Officer.

Where any party disputes the admissibility of evidence tendered by another party concerning a testamentary document, the presiding officer may direct that such document be submitted for examination by an expert appointed under this Act. The decision of the presiding officer regarding the evidentiary value and authenticity of the document shall be final, subject to appeal before an appellate tribunal constituted as provided herein. Any party dissatisfied with the findings of the appellate tribunal may further petition a High Court, but only on grounds of legal error apparent on the face of the record. It is provided that the appellate tribunal shall consider all submissions made by both parties and shall not be bound by any previous rulings concerning similar documents.

Every public authority, intending to make a statutory declaration regarding its compliance with Section 4(1)(b) of this Act, shall first establish an internal committee comprising not less than three officers, one of whom shall be the designated Central Information Officer or equivalent. The committee shall verify all information proposed for inclusion in the declaration against documented procedures and records maintained under this Act; provided that any discrepancies identified during verification must be rectified prior to submission. Further, a duly authenticated copy of the statutory declaration, along with supporting documentation demonstrating adherence to established protocols, shall be submitted electronically to the Central Information Commission within thirty days of its approval by the public authority’s governing body. Failure to comply with these conditions renders the declaration void ab initio.

Where a motor vehicle causes injury or damage to another individual or property, compensation shall be payable by the owner of such vehicle, subject to the provisions regarding third-party insurance as provided herein. The manner of service of notices pertaining to claims and assessments under this Act shall adhere strictly to the prescribed forms and procedures detailed in Schedule B. Failure to serve a notice according to the stipulated manner renders it void and prevents subsequent legal action based on that deficiency. A claimant aggrieved by an improperly served notice may petition the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal for redress, including but not limited to, re-issuance of the notice. The Tribunal shall consider evidence presented regarding the attempted service and determine whether due diligence was exercised in the manner of service.

Where a contract for the sale or purchase of goods involves inspection by the buyer, the seller shall provide reasonable facilities for such inspection. The buyer’s right to reject the goods following inspection is conditional upon submission of a formal Inspection Report within fourteen days from the date of completion of the inspection. This report must be registered with the designated Sub-Registrar under this Act and accompanied by an affidavit verifying its contents. Failure to register the Inspection Report within the stipulated period shall constitute a waiver of the buyer’s right to reject the goods, as provided herein. The Sub-Registrar may require additional documentation supporting the findings detailed in the Inspection Report. Any dispute arising from the validity or accuracy of an Inspection Report shall be subject to resolution through arbitration as per prevailing regulations.

Where an arbitrator is appointed under this Act, they shall ensure that all material facts relevant to the arbitration agreement or the subject matter of the dispute are disclosed by each party appearing before them. Such disclosure shall include any circumstances affecting impartiality or independence of the arbitrator, and any relationships between the arbitrator and either party which could reasonably give rise to a conflict of interest. A party failing to comply with this duty of disclosure shall be liable for costs incurred by the other parties as a consequence of that failure. The Tribunal may, subject to appeal under this Act, order discovery of documents relevant to such undisclosed facts. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the non-disclosure was intentional or negligent and is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

Where a consumer alleges that charges levied by a distribution licensee are excessive or inaccurate due to errors in meter reading, billing calculations, or unauthorized additions to load, such consumer shall have the right to file a complaint with the appropriate forum as provided herein. The forum shall entertain complaints relating to bills raised within one year from the date of issuance of the bill. Provided that, where fraud or misrepresentation is alleged on the part of the distribution licensee, the forum may condone the delay in filing such complaint and admit it on its merits. This period of limitation applies irrespective of whether the consumer has previously attempted resolution through internal grievance redressal mechanisms maintained by the licensee. Any order passed by the forum shall be binding on both the consumer and the distribution licensee subject to appeal under this Act.

Where any food business operator disputes the validity of a certificate of registration granted under this Act, or alleges that the grounds for refusal of such certificate were not supported by sufficient evidence, he may within thirty days from the date of receipt of notification of the grant or refusal, file an appeal before the State Food Safety Appellate Authority. The appellate authority shall consider any submissions made by the food business operator and any counter-submissions presented by the licensing officer. Provided that the appellant must demonstrate a clear prejudice arising directly from the decision under challenge. Any order passed by the State Food Safety Appellate Authority shall be final, subject to further appeal before the Central Food Safety Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the conditions under which a certificate of registration relating to a commercial motor vehicle may be assigned or hypothecated as security. Such assignment shall require prior approval from the Regional Transport Authority and shall be evidenced by an endorsement on the original certificate of registration. The assignee or hypothecator shall furnish a prescribed form along with the requisite fee, detailing particulars of the assignor or hypothecator and the duration of the assignment or hypothecation. No transfer of ownership through assignment shall be valid unless recorded as per the procedures detailed herein. Further, any person desiring to obtain a certificate of registration by way of transmission upon the death of the registered owner shall apply within thirty days, subject to verification of legal heirship.

Where a lessee under an agreement for lease seeks entry into leased premises occupied by the tenant, such entry shall only be permitted subject to prior written notice of at least thirty days being served upon the tenant detailing the purpose of the intended entry. The notice shall specify the date and approximate time window within which entry is proposed. Entry may be refused if the stated purpose is not reasonably related to the maintenance or repair of the premises, or if a mutually convenient alternative time can be agreed upon. Provided that such refusal is communicated in writing within seven days of receipt of the initial notice. Any person exercising power of entry shall carry identification clearly indicating their authority and purpose, and shall provide a copy thereof to the tenant upon request. The tenant may refuse access if reasonable safety precautions are not observed by those seeking entry.

Where a dispute arising from a contractual obligation is resolved through mutual agreement between parties and documented as a terms of settlement, such document shall constitute a legally binding contract enforceable by law. The execution of a terms of settlement shall require the physical presence of all parties involved or their duly authorised representatives holding valid power of attorney. Any alteration to the agreed terms within a terms of settlement must be made through a supplementary written agreement signed by all original signatories and notarised as per prevailing regulations. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements may render the terms of settlement voidable at the option of any affected party. The jurisdictional court shall, in cases of dispute concerning the interpretation or enforcement of a terms of settlement, apply principles of equity and good faith. All notices related to a terms of settlement must be served through registered post with acknowledgment due as provided herein.

Where a product or service is offered with any warranty, express or implied, the manufacturer or service provider shall ensure that all prescribed particulars relating to the quality, quantity, purity, potency, standard and price of such product or service are clearly and conspicuously displayed on the packaging or in the advertisement thereof. These prescribed particulars include, but are not limited to, the date of manufacture, expiry date, ingredients used, net weight or measure, directions for use, and any relevant safety warnings. Failure to comply with this requirement shall be deemed a deficiency in service or a violation of consumer rights under this Act. The Central Authority may issue guidelines specifying the manner in which these prescribed particulars are to be displayed, taking into consideration prevailing industry practices and technological advancements. Any dispute arising from non-compliance relating to prescribed particulars shall be subject to resolution through established mechanisms as provided herein.

Where a party to an agreement seeks access to premises necessary for the performance of their contractual obligations, and where such access is not readily granted by the owner or occupier of those premises, the District Magistrate shall have the power of entry upon any such premises. Notice of intention to exercise this power of entry shall be served upon the owner or occupier at least twenty-four hours prior to the proposed entry, specifying the date, time, and purpose thereof. Any person obstructing an officer authorised under this Act from entering premises pursuant to such notice shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable as provided herein. The officer exercising power of entry may bring with them such reasonable force as may be necessary for the purpose of gaining access. This provision is subject to review by a designated appellate authority within thirty days of the exercise of power, upon application made by the affected party.

Where a person is accused of an offence relatable to traffic regulations or violation of rules concerning motor vehicles, the Transport Department shall constitute a Compounding Committee for each district. This Committee will consist of a Motor Vehicle Inspector, a representative from the local police force, and such other officers as deemed appropriate by the Regional Transport Authority. The Committee may, subject to guidelines issued by the State Government, entertain applications for compounding of offences that are minor in nature and do not involve serious injury or death. Provided that before any compounding is considered, the accused shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard. Any amount determined as a result of such compounding shall be remitted to the Motor Vehicle Fund maintained by the State Government. The officer presiding over the Compounding Committee shall maintain detailed records of all cases processed and amounts received, which will be subject to audit under this Act.

Every complaint received concerning a violation of regulations pertaining to electricity distribution or consumer rights shall be registered by the concerned State Distribution Utility within seven working days of receipt. The utility shall promptly serve notice upon the complainant acknowledging registration and providing a reference number for tracking purposes. Upon preliminary examination, if the complaint appears to involve disputed facts or requires investigation beyond standard record review, it may be referred to an adjudicating officer appointed under this Act. Such referral shall include all relevant documentation submitted by the complainant and any initial assessment made by the utility. The adjudicating officer is empowered to summon witnesses, examine evidence, and conduct hearings as deemed necessary for a fair determination of the matter. Decisions rendered by the adjudicating officer are subject to appeal before an appellate tribunal established under this Act.

Where a party desires to serve any document or notice relating to arbitral proceedings upon another party under this Act, service shall be effected in accordance with the rules specified in Schedule G. Provided that, where the address for service of a party has been notified in writing pursuant to a prior agreement between the parties or as determined by the arbitration tribunal, service may be made at such notified address. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all notifications received under this provision and any alteration thereto. Any person registering an address for service is deemed to have accepted that address for all purposes relating to arbitral proceedings. Failure to update the register promptly will not invalidate any subsequent service effected in the manner of service prescribed herein.

The Central Authority established under this Act shall prescribe a schedule of fees for various services rendered by consumer dispute resolution mechanisms, including but not limited to registration of complaints, mediation proceedings, and facilitation of conciliation. Such schedule shall be published in the Official Gazette and made available on the website of the Central Authority. The fees specified therein may be revised periodically, subject to prior publication and a period of thirty days for public feedback. Any consumer challenging the applicability or quantum of any fee levied under this Act may file an objection with the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission having jurisdiction over the matter; provided that such objection shall not operate as a bar to the continuation of proceedings until the objection is disposed of by the Commission, and any order made by the Commission is subject to appeal.

The license granted to a distribution licensee for the supply of electricity within its licensed area may be assigned by the licensee to another entity subject to prior approval from the Central Government and the State Government. Such assignment shall include all rights, obligations, and assets pertaining to the distribution network as defined in the original license agreement. Where an undertaking is proposed to be transferred under a scheme of amalgamation or merger, the appointed authority may grant permission for such transfer without requiring fresh licensing formalities, provided that the resulting entity possesses the requisite financial stability and technical competence to maintain uninterrupted power supply. The appointed authority shall consider applications for assignment or transfer within ninety days from the date of receipt, and communicate its decision in writing. Any objection received under this Act concerning a proposed assignment must be addressed by the licensee before final approval is granted.

For the purposes of this Act, an “inspection report” means a written document prepared by an officer authorized under this Act to conduct inspections of goods or services offered for sale. Such inspection report shall detail observations made during the inspection, including but not limited to deficiencies in quality, safety standards, labeling requirements, and adherence to prescribed guidelines. The inspection report shall also specify any instances where the supplier has failed to comply with provisions as provided herein. An inspection report may include photographs, videos, or other documentary evidence collected during the course of the inspection. Every inspection report shall be signed by the inspecting officer and retained as a record under this Act.

The Authority shall, upon receiving a complaint regarding the refusal or cancellation of a certificate of registration under this Act, conduct an inquiry in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The complainant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments supporting their claim, and the employer against whom the complaint is made shall likewise have the right to defend its actions. Any order passed by the Authority affirming or reversing the original decision may be appealed within sixty days from the date of such order to the designated appellate forum. The appeal shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based, and the appellate forum’s determination shall be final, subject to further review under Article 226 of the Constitution.

For the purposes of this Act, “licence” with respect to any business or trade activity means permission granted by a competent authority in writing, authorizing the licensee to carry on such activity subject to specific conditions and limitations. These conditions of licence shall include, but are not limited to, stipulations regarding operating hours, geographical restrictions for conducting business, adherence to prescribed quality standards for goods or services offered, and payment of stipulated fees as determined by the relevant regulatory body. A condition is deemed fundamental if its breach renders the agreement voidable under this Act. Any modification to conditions of licence shall be notified in writing to the licensee at least thirty days prior to their implementation.

Any license granted under this Act conferring rights to generate, transmit, supply or distribute electricity shall be subject to revocation by the appropriate authority if the licensee fails to comply with prescribed safety standards as determined by the Central Electricity Authority, and where such failure results in demonstrable harm to consumers or damage to electrical infrastructure. Furthermore, a license may be revoked if the licensee engages in fraudulent practices regarding billing or collection of charges, or persistently neglects maintenance obligations detailed within their operational plan submitted under this Act. The authority shall issue a notice specifying the grounds of revocation and provide opportunity for hearing prior to any action being taken; failure to remedy the deficiencies identified in such notice will result in immediate license termination and imposition of penalties as provided herein.

Registration of arbitration agreements requires adherence to stipulated procedures and associated fees, ensuring transparency and enforceability under this Act. An arbitrator intending to register an agreement shall submit Form ‘A’ along with a certified copy of the agreement itself, duly attested by a notary public or equivalent officer. The prescribed schedule of fees for registration varies depending on the monetary value of the dispute covered by the arbitration agreement; agreements pertaining to disputes exceeding fifty crore rupees shall attract a fee of twenty thousand rupees, while those below this threshold incur a fee of ten thousand rupees. Provided that any party demonstrating financial hardship may apply for a waiver or reduction in the applicable fees, subject to review and approval by the designated Registration Authority. Failure to remit the requisite fee will render the registration application invalid.

For the purposes of this Act, a “competent officer” means an officer designated by the State Government, not below the rank of Assistant Engineer in electricity distribution or transmission undertakings, or an officer appointed by the Central Government for inspection and verification of accounts relating to generation companies, subject to such qualifications as may be prescribed. A competent officer shall possess expertise relevant to the specific functions assigned under this Act, including but not limited to electrical engineering, accountancy, and legal matters pertaining to electricity supply. The State Electricity Regulatory Commission may, by order, specify additional criteria for designation of a competent officer, provided that such criteria do not contradict provisions herein.

Where a consumer alleges deficiency in goods or services rendered by an entity operating as a system, the onus of establishing such deficiency shall lie upon the complainant. Provided that, where the entity provides documentary evidence demonstrating adherence to prescribed quality standards and industry best practices at the time of service, the complainant shall be required to demonstrate that despite such compliance, the consumer suffered quantifiable harm or loss directly attributable to the goods or services. The adjudicating officer may, subject to principles of natural justice, require both parties to submit relevant documentation and testimony. Failure by either party to present credible evidence as provided herein will result in an assessment based on prevailing market rates and reasonable compensation for demonstrable losses. This burden of proof is not intended to preclude claims where the entity’s actions are demonstrably negligent or fraudulent.

Appeals against orders passed by adjudicating officers shall lie before the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal constituted under this Act. The Tribunal shall have the jurisdiction to hear and decide appeals relating to any matter decided by an adjudicating officer under provisions concerning food safety standards, licensing and registration, or seizure of unsafe food articles. Any party aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer may prefer an appeal to the Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Tribunal shall follow such procedure as it deems fit, provided that notice is given to all parties concerned at least thirty days prior to any hearing. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final and binding subject to further appeals under the relevant provisions of law relating to judicial review. Records pertaining to proceedings before the adjudicating officer shall be made available to the Tribunal upon request.

Registration of Food Product Establishments – Burden of Proof Regarding Compliance Every proprietor seeking registration of a food product establishment shall submit detailed documentation pertaining to manufacturing processes, ingredient sourcing, and quality control measures, as prescribed under this Act. The registering officer may request additional information at any stage of the assessment process. Upon receipt of an application, the onus lies upon the applicant to demonstrate, through verifiable records and evidence, adherence to all applicable food safety standards and hygiene protocols stipulated herein. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation or demonstrable compliance shall result in rejection of the registration application. Any challenge to a registering officer’s determination regarding non-compliance rests with the applicant, who bears the burden of proof to substantiate their claims of conformity.

For the purposes of this Act, “environmental damage” includes pollution of any natural resource, alteration to ecosystems, or depletion of environmental resources which results in loss of biodiversity, harm to human health, or impairment of livelihoods; and where such damage is caused by an omission or negligence on the part of any person, entity, or instrumentality, that party shall be liable for recovery of dues pertaining to remediation measures. Recovery of dues under this Act shall encompass costs associated with restoring the environment to its original condition, as determined by a prescribed authority. The Central Government may, through notification, specify procedures for assessing environmental damage and calculating the amount recoverable.

Where the Central Pollution Control Board determines that an industrial unit has failed to comply with prescribed environmental standards, or has otherwise violated any provision under this Act, the Board may issue a notice of demand to the defaulting unit requiring remediation and compensation for damages caused by the non-compliance. Such notice shall specify the nature of the violation, the amount demanded as remediation costs and compensation, and the period within which payment must be made. The industrial unit aggrieved by such notice of demand may, within thirty days from the date of receipt thereof, file an appeal to the Appellate Authority constituted under this Act contesting the findings or the quantification of damages. Provided that the Appellate Authority shall consider any evidence submitted by both parties and may modify the amount demanded if it deems it necessary.

Every food business operator engaged in import of processed organic foods shall ensure that each consignment is accompanied by a certificate of origin issued by an accreditation body recognized under this Act, confirming compliance with the standards for organic production as provided herein. The Food Safety and Standards Authority may conduct inspections to verify adherence to these requirements; failure to produce the requisite certification or demonstrate such compliance will render the operator liable for penalties as determined under this Act. Appeals against orders passed by the Authority relating to import conditions shall lie before the appellate tribunal, subject to the provisions regarding timelines and procedures outlined in regulations framed pursuant to this Act. The appellate tribunal’s decision shall be final and binding.

For the purposes of this Act, "licence" means authorization granted under section 16, or subsequent sections thereof, permitting a person to generate, transmit, distribute, trade, supply, use electricity, or undertake any integrated activity related thereto. The grant of a licence is subject to conditions as may be specified therein; and such conditions shall remain binding on the licensee for the duration of the licence. A licence may be revoked by the appropriate authority if the licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions stipulated under this Act, or engages in activities detrimental to the interests of consumers. These grounds of revocation include, but are not limited to, persistent failure to maintain distribution standards, fraudulent practices, and unauthorized diversion of electricity.

Where a contract for the provision of services requires the payment of a security deposit, the parties may agree upon the conditions governing the assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to that deposit. Such agreement shall specify whether the security deposit is intended as collateral for performance obligations under the contract, or as compensation for damages arising from breach. Any licensee granted rights relating to the recovery of a security deposit shall be deemed an agent of the licensor and bound by its terms. The licensor retains ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with applicable provisions under this Act regarding unjust enrichment and undue influence. A transferor of contractual rights, including those related to a security deposit, must provide written notice to the obligee within thirty days of such transfer. This requirement is waived only if the obligee expressly consents in writing to the assignment or licensing arrangement.

Where a party claims breach of contract alleging misrepresentation concerning the quality or suitability of goods sold, it shall be incumbent upon that party to establish, by clear and convincing evidence, the existence of said misrepresentation and its materiality to the decision to enter into the agreement. The burden of proof regarding such matters rests solely with the claimant, and any failure to adequately demonstrate the elements of misrepresentation will preclude recovery under this Act. Provided that, if the defendant adduces evidence suggesting a waiver or modification of the original contract terms concerning quality standards, the onus shall shift temporarily to the defendant to substantiate said alteration. This does not relieve the claimant from ultimately proving the initial misrepresentation; it merely necessitates further evidentiary scrutiny. Any claim for damages arising from alleged breach must be supported by documented proof of losses directly attributable to the misrepresented condition.

The power of entry granted to a duly appointed Arbitral Representative for the purpose of inspecting premises relevant to a dispute under this Act shall not extend beyond areas expressly designated within a written Access Agreement executed prior to the commencement of inspection. Such Access Agreements must clearly delineate permissible activities and timeframes, subject to the consent of the property owner or their authorized representative. The Arbitral Representative may, provided that reasonable notice is given, request modification of an existing Access Agreement; such requests shall be considered expeditiously by the Arbitration Tribunal. Assignment of rights pertaining to access granted under this Act requires prior written approval from the Arbitration Tribunal and shall not prejudice the confidentiality obligations imposed upon all parties involved in the arbitration proceedings. Any unauthorized entry constitutes a breach of these provisions and may render evidence obtained inadmissible, as provided herein.

Where an employee claims gratuity under this Act, the onus of establishing entitlement rests upon the claimant; provided that, where the employer disputes the claim, it shall be incumbent on the employer to demonstrate, with documentary evidence, reasons for denying such gratuity. For the purposes of determining whether the burden of proof has been discharged, all records pertaining to employment, including but not limited to appointment letters, salary slips, and attendance registers, shall be admissible as relevant evidence. The adjudicating officer may, at their discretion, require further documentation from either party to ascertain the veracity of claims made under this Act.

Any distribution licensee failing to comply with directions issued by the appointed authority regarding metering standards shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. The State Commission may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, impose additional penalties up to fifty thousand rupees where such failure constitutes willful disregard of the appointed authority's instructions or results in demonstrable financial loss to consumers. Any person aggrieved by any order passed by the appointed authority relating to tariff determination or license conditions may appeal to the State Commission within sixty days. Failure to remit penalties as determined shall render the licensee subject to suspension of licence privileges, as provided herein.

Every Regional Transport Authority shall establish and diligently maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all vehicles registered under this Act, including but not limited to details of ownership, insurance coverage validity, fitness certificates, and emission compliance reports. Such records shall be preserved electronically and in physical form, subject to periodic audits by designated officers as provided herein. The authority may prescribe the format and content of these records through notifications issued from time to time. Any motor vehicle dealer failing to submit requisite documentation for registration within thirty days of sale shall be liable for penalties determined under this Act. Furthermore, all authorized workshops performing repairs or modifications to vehicles must document such work accurately; failure to do so constitutes a violation. The maintenance of records is crucial for ensuring road safety and efficient traffic management.

Every food business operator engaged in manufacturing, processing, or packaging of food products shall ensure that inspection reports pertaining to their premises are maintained accurately and remain accessible for a period not less than three years from the date of issuance. Such inspection reports shall detail observations made by authorized officers under this Act concerning hygiene practices, storage conditions, pest control measures, and adherence to prescribed standards. The Food Safety Officer may require submission of corrective action plans within thirty days where deficiencies are noted in the inspection report; failure to submit such a plan shall render the food business operator liable for penalties as provided herein. Any alteration or falsification of an inspection report constitutes a violation and is subject to prosecution.

Every consent granting authority shall establish and maintain a comprehensive register detailing all consents issued, renewed, or revoked under this Act. This register shall include, but not be limited to, the name and address of the industry operating within the jurisdiction, the nature and extent of its operations, the pollutants discharged, and the prescribed standards adhered to. The maintenance of records relating to environmental clearances is paramount for effective monitoring and compliance. All entries in the register shall be recorded accurately and legibly, and any amendments or corrections made thereto shall be clearly indicated with the date and initials of the officer responsible. Periodically, not less than once every six months, a certified copy of the register shall be submitted to the State Pollution Control Board for verification. Failure to maintain such records as provided herein will render the consent granting authority liable to penalties under this Act.

Where a contractual agreement contains provisions for arbitration concerning financial obligations arising from licensing arrangements relating to intellectual property, any assignment of rights under that agreement shall remain subject to the terms governing recovery of dues stipulated within the original license. The assignor retains responsibility for ensuring compliance with all pre-existing conditions precedent to the triggering of an arbitral claim, provided that the assignee undertakes to maintain records pertaining to payments and performance obligations as they relate to the licensed intellectual property. Furthermore, any subsequent assignment of the assigned rights shall not prejudice the ability of either the original licensor or licensee to pursue remedies under this Act for outstanding amounts due, irrespective of the number of times the right has been transferred. The arbitrator may order specific performance to secure recovery of dues where a breach of contract occurs following an assignment.

Every manufacturer, importer, packer, distributor, retailer and marketer of food products shall apply for a certificate of registration under this Act within thirty days from the date these regulations come into force. An application shall include particulars regarding the premises where food is manufactured, processed or handled, along with details of all equipment used in such processes. The registering officer may inspect the premises at any time to verify compliance with hygiene and safety standards as provided herein. A certificate of registration shall be renewed every two years, subject to continued adherence to prescribed conditions relating to storage, handling, and labeling practices. Any alteration to the food business operations requires prior notification and approval from the licensing authority; failure to comply may result in suspension of the certificate of registration.

Where a document is tendered under this Act as proof of the execution of a deed or contract, the Court may require that the handwriting appearing thereon be identified by comparison with any admitted writing of the party alleged to have executed it; provided that if the document contains signatures bearing variations in style or form, such variations shall not preclude admissibility unless it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Court that these differences do not reflect a genuine evolution in the person’s customary manner of signing. The prescribed particulars relating to any signature for comparison purposes include but are not limited to the relative size and slant of letters, spacing between words, and characteristic flourishes or markings consistently employed by the signatory; failure to provide such details shall render the document inadmissible as evidence.

Where a food safety officer has reason to believe that any unsafe food is being manufactured, processed, stored, distributed or sold, he may issue a notice of demand to the person responsible for the activity, requiring them to appear before him at a specified time and place to explain their actions and produce relevant records. Provided that such notice shall clearly state the alleged violation and provide particulars of the evidence upon which the belief is based. Failure to comply with a notice of demand may result in proceedings being initiated without further notice. Any party aggrieved by action taken under this Act following a failure to appear as directed, or disputing the accuracy of any information contained within the notice of demand, shall have the right to appeal to the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within thirty days of the order appealed against.

The operator of a residential complex providing accommodation services shall establish clear procedures for the collection and management of security deposits from prospective tenants. Such security deposit shall not exceed an amount equivalent to two months’ rent as determined by the Central Government, and any attempt to levy a higher sum shall be deemed unfair trade practice under this Act. The assignment or transfer of rights pertaining to such security deposit, including but not limited to claims arising from damages or unpaid utilities, may occur with the consent of all parties involved, provided that such assignment is documented in writing and registered with the relevant housing authority. Further, any sub-licensing of recovery mechanisms for a security deposit requires prior approval from the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. The operator shall furnish a detailed accounting of the security deposit upon termination of tenancy, as provided herein.

Any industrial unit engaged in the processing of hazardous materials shall ensure that effluent treatment plants operate continuously and meet standards prescribed under this Act, subject to periodic inspections by authorized officers. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the unit liable for remedial action and potential penalties as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order issued concerning compliance or non-compliance may appeal to the appellate tribunal established under this legislation within sixty days of receipt of notification. The tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented, including technical reports and expert testimony, and its decision shall be binding on both the appellant and the authority issuing the original order, provided that the tribunal’s jurisdiction is limited to matters of fact concerning environmental impact assessment.

Registration of Service Providers with Central Authority: Every person offering services falling under Schedule A shall register with the Central Consumer Protection Authority in the prescribed manner. Such registration shall be valid for a period of five years and may be renewed upon application, subject to continued compliance with standards established under this Act. The authority shall maintain a publicly accessible registry detailing registered service providers, including their area of operation and categories of services offered. Any modification to the scope or nature of services provided by a registrant must be reported to the Central Authority within thirty days; failure to do so may result in suspension of registration. The manner of service rendered by a registered provider shall adhere to guidelines issued periodically by the authority, ensuring consumer safety and satisfaction.

Where a dispute arises concerning the enforceability of an agreement entered into pursuant to these provisions, the Presiding Officer appointed under Section [reference] shall adopt a summary procedure for its determination. Such procedure shall prioritise expeditious resolution and minimise formal legal processes. The Presiding Officer may direct parties to submit written statements outlining their respective positions, and shall provide reasonable opportunity for oral arguments if deemed necessary. Decisions regarding admissibility of evidence are at the discretion of the Presiding Officer, subject to principles of natural justice. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this summary procedure may appeal to the District Judge within thirty days from the date of such order. The appellate authority shall review the decision solely on questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of these provisions and not re-examine the evidence.

The Central Food Safety Authority shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers and duties relating to inspection, sampling, and analysis of food articles to designated officers appointed in writing. Such delegation shall not extend to the power to impose monetary penalties exceeding one hundred thousand rupees or to initiate prosecution proceedings under this Act. Any officer to whom such powers are delegated shall exercise them strictly in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Food Safety Authority, and any action taken in excess of those guidelines shall be deemed void. The authority may revoke any delegation of powers at any time, provided that reasonable notice is given to the affected officer.

Applications for a licence to operate an arbitration facility shall be submitted to the Central Authority in Form A, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed in Schedule I. The application must detail the proposed location of the facility, its anticipated capacity, and the qualifications and experience of the personnel intended to manage the operations. Upon receipt of an application, the Central Authority may require further information or clarification from the applicant. Granting of a licence is subject to verification of the applicant's financial stability and adherence to standards of infrastructure as determined by regulations framed under this Act. The conditions of licence shall include mandatory continuing professional development for facility personnel and periodic audits conducted by an independent body approved by the Central Authority. Any deviation from these conditions may result in suspension or revocation of the licence, following due process and opportunity for hearing.

Where an employee has ceased employment with an establishment, a claim for gratuity shall be deemed to have arisen on the date of cessation; provided that any dispute regarding the eligibility of an employee for gratuity or the amount payable thereunder must be brought before the Grievance Redressal Committee established under this Act within six months from the date such cessation. Failure to initiate proceedings within this period of limitation will ordinarily preclude subsequent legal recourse, subject to just cause demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Labour Commissioner. The determination of "just cause" shall consider factors including but not limited to demonstrable ignorance of the applicable procedures and any documented impediment preventing timely filing. Further, where a statutory notice has been served on the employer regarding a gratuity claim, the period of limitation may be extended by a duration equivalent to the time taken for resolution through that prescribed channel.

Any agreement recorded in writing purporting to embody the terms of settlement between parties to litigation pending before any civil court shall be deemed admissible evidence only if it is accompanied by an affidavit from each party affirming its voluntary execution and understanding thereof, as provided herein. Failure to produce such affidavits shall render the purported terms of settlement inadmissible and subject the defaulting party to a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. The Court may, at its discretion, order inspection of relevant documents preceding the formulation of the terms of settlement. Any attempt to enforce a settlement agreement obtained through coercion or misrepresentation shall be void, and the party attempting such enforcement shall be liable for damages as determined by the court under this Act.

Where a Food Safety Officer conducts an inspection of any food business operator, a comprehensive inspection report detailing observations made regarding compliance with applicable standards and regulations shall be prepared and furnished to the licensee within fourteen days of conclusion of the inspection. The inspection report shall clearly specify deficiencies identified, including but not limited to violations of hygiene practices, improper storage conditions, or mislabeling. Any food business operator aggrieved by findings contained in an inspection report may submit a written representation outlining their objections and corrective actions taken within seven days of receipt thereof. Such representations shall be considered by the licensing authority, who may modify the report as deemed appropriate after due deliberation. Failure to address deficiencies highlighted in the inspection report may result in action under this Act, including suspension or revocation of licenses.

The assignment of arbitration agreements entered into pursuant to contracts for the provision of specialized engineering services shall be subject to the provisions outlined herein regarding fees. Any entity seeking to assign its rights or obligations under an arbitration agreement relating to such services must first obtain a certificate of authorization from the designated Arbitral Authority, demonstrating compliance with prevailing industry standards and professional qualifications. The schedule of fees applicable to this assignment process, as detailed in Annexure A, shall be paid upfront by the assigning party. Further, any sub-licensing or further assignment of rights granted under such an arbitration agreement requires prior consent of both original parties and is subject to additional levies outlined within the aforementioned schedule of fees. Provided that the Arbitral Authority may waive certain fees at its discretion in cases involving public interest considerations.

Where an arbitration agreement is silent or ambiguous regarding the procedure for determining the seat of arbitration, the arbitral tribunal shall, after consultation with the parties, specify the place of arbitration in its award. The designation of the seat shall be conclusive evidence of the intended location and shall not be subject to challenge under this Act except on grounds specified herein. For purposes of this determination, the parties’ written submissions regarding their commercial relationships and anticipated operational needs will be considered. Furthermore, any subsequent modification of the designated place of arbitration requires the express written consent of all parties involved. The prescribed particulars relating to the seat shall include details concerning applicable procedural rules and judicial oversight provisions. Failure to provide these prescribed particulars may render the award vulnerable to challenge on grounds of fundamental unfairness.

Any employer who fails to implement a terms of settlement arrived at between an employee and the establishment regarding gratuity entitlement, within thirty days from the date thereof, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each instance of non-implementation. The Controlling Authority may, after affording the employer an opportunity of being heard, impose such penalty under this Act. Failure to comply with the terms of settlement shall constitute a violation requiring immediate rectification as provided herein. Further, any officer responsible for ensuring compliance with the terms of settlement who wilfully neglects or omits to do so, is subject to disciplinary action and may face penalties as determined by the appropriate government authority.

Where a contract expressly or impliedly authorises one party to delegate their powers and duties to another, such delegation shall only be valid if the original party retains ultimate responsibility for performance. Any loss or damage arising from acts performed by the delegatee beyond the scope of the authorised delegation, or resulting from negligence in the supervision of the delegatee’s actions, shall remain the liability of the delegating party. A party seeking to enforce a contract based on delegated authority must demonstrate that the delegation was reasonable and did not prejudice the rights of any third parties who reasonably relied upon the original contracting party's representations. The right to claim damages for breach of contract shall extend to cover losses incurred as a direct consequence of improper delegation of powers, subject to considerations of contributory negligence.

Where a consumer files a complaint alleging deficiency in service or unfair trade practice, the District Commission shall, upon receipt of such complaint, serve notice to the party against whom the complaint is made, providing them with a reasonable opportunity to file their response under this Act. The adjudicating officer presiding over the proceedings shall ensure that both parties are afforded an equal chance to present evidence and arguments relevant to the matter. Provided that, if the complainant fails to appear before the adjudicating officer on two consecutive hearings without sufficient cause, the Commission may proceed ex parte. Further, any document submitted as evidence must be duly authenticated according to rules framed by the Central Government. The adjudicating officer shall record reasons for every decision made and ensure compliance with principles of natural justice.

Applications made under sub-section (1) shall be disposed of within a period of six months from the date of their respective receipt by the appellate tribunal. The tribunal shall follow the principles of natural justice in dealing with any application, providing each party an opportunity to present its case and relevant evidence. Any order passed by the tribunal may be appealed against to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to further appeal as may be prescribed under this Act. Where a dispute arises regarding the interpretation or application of any provision relating to costs incurred in proceedings before the appellate tribunal, the decision of the tribunal shall be final and binding. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute an advisory committee to assist the appellate tribunal in matters concerning technical expertise.

For the purposes of facilitating inspection for compliance with the provisions of this Act, an officer empowered by the Controlling Authority, not below the rank of Labour Commissioner, shall have power of entry into any premises or place where gratuity is proposed to be paid or has been paid. Such entry may be exercised only during working hours and after due notice, ordinarily twenty-four hours prior, has been given to the employer, provided that in cases of imminent threat of non-compliance or fraudulent activity, such notice may be dispensed with at the discretion of the officer. The power of entry shall be accompanied by a duly authenticated warrant specifying the purpose of inspection as provided herein.

Where a party possesses material information relating to a contract’s subject matter which, but for its suppression, would reasonably induce another party not to enter into the agreement, there arises a duty of disclosure under this Act. This duty shall apply irrespective of whether active misrepresentation or fraudulent intent is established. Failure to comply with such duty constitutes a vitiation of the contract and renders it voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. However, provided that the non-disclosure was due to inadvertence and without any intention to deceive, an appeal against a finding of breach of this duty may be entertained by the appellate court if demonstrable steps were taken to rectify the omission promptly upon discovery.

For the purposes of this Act, “minor offence” means an offence relatable to contravention of rules regarding road traffic signs, signals or markings; exceeding the speed limit specified for a motor vehicle; or failing to exhibit direction indicators. The term "aggravated minor offence" shall include any such minor offence committed while driving under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs as defined under other laws. Compounding of offences involving minor and aggravated minor offences may be undertaken by an officer authorized in this behalf, subject to guidelines framed by the Central Government. Such compounding shall involve payment of a sum determined according to scales prescribed herein, provided that the offender consents to such compounding.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission or a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum may prefer an appeal to the relevant National Commission within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Applications for registration of complaints involving disputes concerning goods or services exceeding fifty thousand rupees shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original complaint and all supporting documents filed before the lower forum. The State Government, in consultation with the Central Consumer Protection Authority, may, by notification, establish offices of an appointed authority to facilitate such registrations and manage related records. Such an appointed authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing each registered application and its current status under this Act.
