The Central Consumer Protection Authority may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, grant licenses to entities engaged in providing services relating to consumer grievance redressal, including but not limited to mediation, conciliation, and arbitration. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permissible activities and the standards for ensuring fair and efficient service delivery. A licensee may assign its rights and obligations under the license to another entity with prior written consent from the Authority, provided that the assigning entity remains jointly liable for any breaches occurring before the assignment. The manner of service rendered by a licensed entity must adhere strictly to guidelines issued periodically by the Authority concerning transparency, data security, and consumer accessibility. Any sub-licensing shall require specific authorization granted under this Act.

Every food product manufactured, processed, imported, or distributed within India shall bear prescribed particulars clearly and legibly marked on its package in English or Hindi, or both. Failure to comply with these marking requirements constitutes an offence under this Act. The Food Safety Officers may seize any misbranded food product found in violation of the regulations. Any person convicted of such an offence shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. Provided that, if the violation is repeated, the penalties will be doubled. The State Food Safety Authority may issue notices directing rectification of labelling deficiencies; non-compliance with such notice attracts additional penalties as provided herein.

Every supplier offering goods or services to consumers shall ensure full and accurate disclosure of all material terms and conditions relating to the offer, including but not limited to pricing, warranties, guarantees, return policies, and any limitations on liability. Failure to provide such a duty of disclosure, or providing information that is false or misleading, constitutes an unfair trade practice under this Act. The Central Consumer Protection Authority may, after due inquiry, impose penalties proportionate to the detriment suffered by consumers, not exceeding two times the value of the goods or services provided. Any consumer aggrieved by non-compliance with these provisions may also file a complaint before the relevant District Commission, subject to further proceedings as provided herein.

The operator of an industrial unit engaged in the processing of ferrous metals shall ensure that effluent discharge consistently meets the standards laid down under this Act and subsequent notifications issued by the Central Pollution Control Board. The conditions of licence granted for operation are subject to periodic review, not less frequently than once every three years, based on inspection reports and compliance audits. Any deviation from prescribed parameters necessitates immediate remedial action as detailed in the operational manual approved by the State Pollution Control Board. Further, the licensee shall provide access to all records pertaining to environmental monitoring and waste management to authorized officers upon request. Failure to adhere to these conditions renders the licence liable for suspension or revocation, as provided herein.

Where an inspection report pertaining to a manufacturing facility is submitted as evidence under this Act, it shall be accompanied by a certificate from the inspecting officer confirming adherence to established protocols for data collection and analysis. The report must clearly delineate any deviations observed during the inspection process and specify corrective actions recommended or implemented. Evidence derived solely from an inspection report shall not be admissible unless the inspecting officer is present in court to verify its contents, subject to provisions regarding reasonable excuse as provided herein. Any party challenging the accuracy of an inspection report may request access to raw data utilized in its compilation, provided that such request complies with procedures outlined elsewhere under this Act concerning confidential commercial information.

Where a party possesses material information, not readily ascertainable by the other party through diligent inquiry, which relates to the essential nature of the contract being proposed, that party shall have a duty of disclosure towards the prospective contracting party. This duty extends to informing the other party of such material information prior to the finalization of the agreement. Failure to disclose such information may render the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The determination of what constitutes “material” information for purposes of this provision shall be made by the adjudicating officer, based on the specific facts and circumstances presented. Any dispute regarding a breach of duty of disclosure under this Act may be referred to arbitration as provided herein, subject to the jurisdiction of civil courts. Appeals against decisions of the adjudicating officer relating to this matter are permitted before the appellate authority.

The employer intending to assign, pledge, or otherwise transfer any gratuity liability accruing under this Act relating to employees of an establishment shall first obtain a certificate of registration from the Controlling Authority. Such certificate shall specify the particulars of the establishment and the extent of gratuity liabilities intended to be transferred. The application for such certificate must include a detailed inventory of assets proposed as security, together with a valuation report certified by a chartered accountant. No transfer shall be valid unless sanctioned by the Controlling Authority after due notice is given to all relevant stakeholders including employees and employee representatives. Further, any assignment or pledge made without prior registration will be deemed void and unenforceable against the gratuity payers under this Act. The Controlling Authority may impose conditions on such registrations as it deems necessary to protect the interests of the employees.

Any party failing to comply with an order issued by the appointed authority under this Act relating to the discovery of documents or other evidence shall be guilty of contempt of court and liable to pay a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Court may, in its discretion, impose a further penalty equivalent to ten percent of the value of the disputed amount if such non-compliance is deemed willful and obstructive. Where an appointed authority determines that a party has failed to produce requested information as directed, that party shall be responsible for all costs incurred by the other party in seeking enforcement through judicial intervention. Repeated or egregious disregard for instructions from the appointed authority may result in summary dismissal of claims or defenses.

Registration of Inspection Reports relating to Licensed Food Businesses Every proprietor of a licensed food business shall, within thirty days of completion of any inspection conducted under this Act, submit an electronic copy of the resultant inspection report to the designated online portal maintained by the State Food Safety Authority. Such submission shall be deemed complete upon acknowledgement of receipt by the system. The Authority may prescribe standards for the format and content of these reports. Provided that a proprietor who fails to register an inspection report within the stipulated timeframe is liable to pay a compounding fee as determined under this Act. Any person aggrieved by the contents of a registered inspection report may file a written objection with the State Food Safety Authority, which shall be considered in accordance with procedures established therein.

Where in any proceeding relating to a contract, a party asserts the existence of a fact which, if established, would discharge their obligation or invalidate the agreement, the burden of proof shall lie upon that party to demonstrate its occurrence to the satisfaction of the court. This requirement applies equally whether the assertion concerns misrepresentation, duress, undue influence, fraud, mistake, or any other ground for relief as provided herein. The party bearing the burden of proof shall produce sufficient evidence to reasonably establish the asserted fact; failure to do so shall be construed against that party. Nothing in this provision shall preclude the court from independently examining all relevant circumstances under this Act.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to provide information within the time specified under this Act or provides inadequate responses, an aggrieved person may file a complaint with the designated appellate authority. The appellate authority shall examine such complaints and issue notices to the concerned Public Information Officers, affording them an opportunity of being heard. If, after due consideration, the appellate authority finds that the Public Information Officer has acted in contravention of this Act or failed to exercise reasonable diligence, it may direct the officer to take remedial action including providing the information, rectifying errors, and offering compensation for any loss suffered by the complainant. The appointed authority shall also review the performance of Public Information Officers periodically and submit reports to the Central Information Commission regarding compliance with directions issued under this Act.

Every adjudicating officer assessing penalties under this Act shall adhere strictly to the schedule of fees annexed hereto, which details charges applicable for various infractions related to unfair trade practices and deficient services. Provided that, where a consumer demonstrates financial hardship through submission of certified income documentation, the adjudicating officer may waive up to fifty percent of the prescribed fee, subject to review by the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. Further, any entity failing to submit required documentation within thirty days of notification shall be assessed an additional late filing penalty as detailed in the schedule of fees. The Central Authority shall revise the schedule of fees every three years, ensuring alignment with prevailing economic conditions and administrative costs, and notify such revisions through official gazette.

Where a party to an arbitration agreement seeks access to documents or records held by another party relevant to the dispute, such request shall be made through the arbitral tribunal, specifying the nature of the information sought and the reasons for its relevance. The tribunal may, after hearing representations from both parties, direct inspection of specified documents under conditions it deems appropriate, provided that such direction does not unduly prejudice the interests of either party or disrupt ongoing business operations. Any refusal to comply with a tribunal’s order regarding an inspection report shall constitute contempt of court and be dealt with accordingly. The aggrieved party may petition the tribunal for remedies including but not limited to costs associated with pursuing the inspection, and injunctive relief preventing further withholding of relevant information as provided herein.

The Central Gratuity Authority shall maintain a comprehensive register of undertakings covered under this Act, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as determined by the Authority. Every establishment required to register its details with the Authority shall submit an initial application containing prescribed information regarding its nature of business, employee strength, and registered office address. Subsequent alterations in these particulars must be reported within thirty days, accompanied by a duly certified copy of relevant documentation. The register of undertakings will be updated periodically reflecting changes as notified by establishments. Failure to maintain accurate records or promptly report modifications may result in penalties as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an entry in the register may appeal to the Central Gratuity Authority for review and rectification.

The Authority shall grant a license to operate commercial vehicle salvage yards subject to compliance with specified environmental standards and proof of financial solvency as determined under regulations framed by the Central Government. Such licenses are assignable, provided that any proposed assignee possesses equivalent qualifications and undergoes an assessment process administered by the Authority. Prior to assignment, the existing licensee must serve a notice of demand upon the prospective assignee detailing all liabilities associated with the salvage yard operation, including but not limited to outstanding taxes, employee dues, and environmental remediation obligations. The Authority may require a performance bond from the assignee guaranteeing fulfillment of these obligations. Failure to provide such a notice of demand shall render the assignment voidable at the option of any aggrieved party. Further, under this Act, the Authority retains the power to revoke licenses for non-compliance or fraudulent conveyance of liabilities.

Information published electronically shall be accompanied by particulars indicating the date of publication or last modification. Every Public Information Officer appointed under this Act shall maintain a register of applications received and disposed of, including details of fees remitted and reasons for refusal, if any. The Central Government may prescribe the form and manner in which such registers are to be maintained. Applications requiring the extraction or compilation of information from multiple sources or involving the manual examination of records exceeding twenty pages shall attract an additional processing fee as detailed in the schedule of fees annexed hereto. This schedule may be revised periodically by notification, subject to prior consultation with relevant stakeholders. Fees remitted shall be credited to a designated government account and utilized for improving public service delivery related to information dissemination.

Where a consumer seeks redress for grievances relating to billing or meter readings, the distribution licensee shall entertain such complaints within thirty days of their receipt. Provided that, if the complaint pertains to an alleged disconnection effected in violation of the provisions under this Act, the licensee must respond within fifteen days. Any claim concerning damages arising from faulty electrical installations or equipment failures shall be addressed expeditiously, with acknowledgement provided within seven days. The period of limitation for initiating legal proceedings relating to any matter adjudicated by the appropriate forum established under this Act shall be two years from the date of the order. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, appeals against such orders may be filed as provided herein.

Any public authority failing to maintain records in a manner facilitating access under this Act shall be liable to pay compensation not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees for each instance of denial of information or delay in providing it. An officer found guilty of obstructing the exercise of right to information, or knowingly providing false or misleading information, shall be subject to disciplinary action as determined by the appointing authority and may also face a penalty of up to ten thousand rupees. Any individual making a statutory declaration under this Act affirming compliance with record-keeping requirements, and subsequently proven to have acted in violation thereof, is liable for double the compensation payable under section 8(1)(b). The Central Information Commission may issue directions requiring rectification of practices where non-compliance persists.

Registration of Generating Set Installations Every owner intending to install a generating set with a total connected capacity exceeding ten kilowatts shall apply for registration under this Act. The application shall contain prescribed particulars including but not limited to the location of installation, technical specifications of the generating set, details of fuel source utilized and name and address of the authorized service personnel responsible for maintenance. Such particulars must be verified by a certified electrical engineer. Failure to submit complete or accurate information will render the registration invalid. The registering authority may request additional documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with safety regulations and grid connectivity standards. All applications shall be processed within thirty working days, subject to verification of submitted details and payment of applicable fees as provided herein.

Any person found to be operating a commercial vehicle without possessing a valid certificate of fitness, as required under this Act, shall be liable to pay a compounding fee not exceeding two thousand rupees per offence. The Motor Vehicles Inspector may, subject to due process, seize the vehicle and prevent its further operation until such time as the deficiency is rectified and the requisite certificate obtained. Repeated offences committed by the same owner or driver will result in enhanced penalties, including suspension of driving license for a period determined by the Regional Transport Authority. This summary procedure allows for expeditious resolution of violations concerning vehicular safety standards, provided that appeals may be made to an appellate authority within thirty days of notification of penalty.

Where a dispute arises concerning the interpretation or implementation of an arbitration agreement, either party may apply to the High Court for appointment of an appointed authority if the designated arbitrator fails to assume office within thirty days from the date the arbitration agreement is executed, or where the arbitrator refuses to act. The application shall specify the reasons for such failure or refusal and provide evidence thereof as deemed necessary by the court. Upon receipt of such application, the High Court may direct the appointment of an appointed authority who shall proceed with the matter in accordance with the provisions under this Act. Any order made by the appointed authority shall be binding on both parties subject to a right of appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days.

The registration of a motor vehicle shall remain valid subject to continued compliance with the provisions under this Act relating to roadworthiness and insurance coverage. Where a registered vehicle is involved in an accident resulting in serious bodily injury or death, the registering authority may initiate proceedings for revocation of such registration. Such revocation shall be predicated upon demonstrable negligence on the part of the vehicle's owner or driver, as determined by a motor accidents claims tribunal. The grounds of revocation also include persistent failure to pay applicable road taxes within the prescribed timeframe and any modification to the vehicle’s structure that compromises safety standards, provided that the owner is afforded an opportunity for hearing before any order of revocation is passed.

Where a consumer has obtained an order against an opponent under this Act, and subsequently seeks revocation of that order, application shall be made to the District Commission, State Commission or National Commission, whichever is appropriate based on the original order’s value, in prescribed Form D. The application for revocation must specify with particularity the grounds upon which it is founded; these grounds may include, but are not limited to, demonstrable fraud perpetrated by the consumer, material misrepresentation made during proceedings before the initial adjudicating body, or a significant change in circumstances rendering the original order inequitable. Notice of such application shall be served on the opponent as per the rules framed under this Act. The Commission may require production of further evidence and may afford the opponent an opportunity to present counter-arguments. Decisions regarding grounds of revocation are subject to judicial review only on limited grounds, namely error apparent on the record.

Where a contract requires the provision of a security deposit by one party to another, such deposit shall be held in trust by the recipient until all obligations undertaken within the agreement have been fully performed by the obligor. The amount constituting the security deposit may be agreed upon between the parties and shall be evidenced in writing as part of the contractual terms. Failure on the part of the obligor to perform their contractual duties entitles the recipient to utilize the security deposit towards recoupment of losses, damages, or costs incurred due to such non-performance. Any excess remaining after such recoupment shall be promptly returned to the obligor. The recipient shall provide a detailed accounting of any utilization of the security deposit upon request by the obligor and may be liable for penalties under this Act if found to have acted in bad faith regarding its management.

Where a construction contract incorporates provisions for a security deposit intended to guarantee performance of obligations under the agreement, the amount retained by the contractor as security deposit shall not exceed ten percent of the total contract value. Such retention is subject to compliance with all applicable labour laws and regulations concerning wages, statutory deductions, and provident fund contributions relating to personnel employed on the project. The disbursal of the security deposit shall occur upon satisfactory completion of the work, certification by the employer confirming adherence to specifications, and submission of a ‘no dues’ certificate from relevant government authorities and subcontractors. Provided that any claim arising under this Act against the contractor shall be satisfied first from the security deposit held by the employer.

Every authorization issued under this Act for the operation of commercial vehicles shall specify a designated route, and no vehicle so authorized shall deviate from that route unless prior written permission is obtained from the competent officer. The application for such deviation must detail the reasons necessitating the change, the proposed alternative route, and an assessment of potential impact on traffic flow. A competent officer may grant or deny such permission at their discretion, provided that any approval is subject to a review after six months. Any operator failing to adhere to the prescribed route without authorization shall be deemed to have violated the terms of their permit, rendering them liable for penalties as provided herein. The competent officer shall maintain records of all deviation requests and approvals.

For the purposes of this Act, an appellate tribunal is defined as a body established under provisions herein for hearing appeals arising from orders passed by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions or other authorities exercising powers delegated under this Act. The appellate tribunal shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two other members, all of whom shall be persons having substantial experience in legal, technical, or economic matters relating to electricity. Decisions of the appellate tribunal shall be binding on the parties involved, subject to further appeals as may be provided for under this Act. The jurisdiction of the appellate tribunal extends to both factual and legal issues arising from orders appealed against.

The Central Licensing Authority may grant licenses for the manufacture, processing, and distribution of fortified foods subject to compliance with nutritional standards as provided herein. Any licensee intending to assign their license or a portion thereof relating to specific product lines shall first obtain prior approval from the Authority. Such assignment proposals must include a statutory declaration by both the transferring and receiving entities confirming adherence to all conditions stipulated in the original license, including quality control protocols and labeling requirements. The declaration shall also detail any proposed changes to production capacity or distribution networks following the assignment. Failure to submit a complete and accurate statutory declaration will render the assignment invalid. Further, the Authority may impose additional conditions on assignments deemed necessary to safeguard public health and consumer interests under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, duty of disclosure arises where one party possesses material information concerning a transaction which, but for its communication, would preclude the other party from making an informed decision. Material information is deemed to include facts known to the possessor which he should reasonably believe are relevant to the other party’s assessment of whether or not to enter into the agreement. The duty shall apply irrespective of whether the relationship between the parties suggests a fiduciary obligation; however, such relationships may intensify the scope and nature of required disclosure as provided herein. Silence does not constitute a breach unless active concealment is proven.

Where any claim for compensation arising from injury or loss relating to a motor vehicle accident is not filed within three years from the date of the incident giving rise to the claim, the Claims Tribunal shall be satisfied that the claimant has sufficient cause for the delay. Provided that, if the claimant demonstrates reasonable excuse for such delay, which may include but is not limited to unforeseen medical incapacity or absence from the jurisdiction, the Tribunal may waive the aforementioned period of limitation and entertain the claim. Any decision regarding waiver under this provision is subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the order. The appellate court shall consider whether the claimant has indeed established sufficient cause justifying deviation from the prescribed time limits as provided herein.

Where any party disputes the findings of fact recorded by the adjudicating officer in respect of damages awarded under this Act, or challenges the reasonableness of the procedural safeguards afforded to them during arbitration proceedings, an appeal shall lie to the designated appellate tribunal. The appellate tribunal may, after affording both parties a fair hearing and considering all relevant evidence presented before the adjudicating officer, confirm, vary, or set aside such findings or orders. Provided that any challenge regarding the impartiality or competence of the adjudicating officer must be raised within thirty days from the date of the award. Further, the appellate tribunal shall not entertain appeals based solely on merits of the underlying dispute, but only on grounds relating to procedural fairness and adherence to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

Where a document purporting to be a certificate of registration issued by the Registrar of Societies is produced in evidence, the court shall presume that it was duly issued and contains particulars of the society’s name, address, and objects, subject to the evidentiary challenge available under this Act. Any party disputing the authenticity or accuracy of such certificate may present evidence demonstrating material errors or irregularities in its issuance process. The burden of proving such error lies upon the party challenging the validity of the certificate. Provided that, if a counter-affidavit from the Registrar explicitly refuting the allegations is filed, the court shall consider it as relevant and admissible under this Act. An appeal against any order determining the admissibility or weight to be given to a certificate of registration may be made to the High Court within sixty days.

Where any consumer disputes the findings of fact recorded by the District Commission or State Commission under this Act, they may file within thirty days thereafter an application for review before the same forum, stating grounds demonstrably warranting reconsideration. Such applications shall be entertained only if they demonstrate a clear error apparent on the face of the record; otherwise, they will be summarily dismissed. Any party aggrieved by an order passed pursuant to such review application may further appeal to the appropriate appellate authority within sixty days, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The appellate authority shall consider all evidence submitted and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Provided that any challenge to the summary procedure employed in a review application is itself grounds for appeal.

Where a dispute arises regarding the validity or enforceability of an arbitration agreement, the arbitral tribunal shall determine such issue solely on the basis of the written agreement and applicable laws relating to contracts. If a party claims that the arbitration agreement lacks prescribed particulars as required under this Act, the tribunal shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence pertaining to the existence and clarity of those details. Failure to provide adequate information regarding the scope of the dispute or the method for selecting arbitrators shall render the agreement voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The tribunal may order discovery relating only to matters directly relevant to ascertaining whether prescribed particulars were indeed furnished. Any award rendered based on a determination that the arbitration agreement was valid is final and binding, subject to challenge under this Act solely on limited grounds.

Where a gratuity is withheld or delayed in payment due to disputed findings within an inspection report submitted by an appointed Inspector under this Act, the employee concerned shall have the right to appeal such findings before a Grievance Redressal Committee constituted at the establishment level. The committee shall review the inspection report and any supporting documentation provided by both the employer and the employee. Any determination made by the Grievance Redressal Committee regarding the accuracy of the inspection report shall be binding on all parties involved, subject to further appeal before a Labour Court as provided herein. Failure to comply with the recommendations of the Grievance Redressal Committee may render the employer liable for penalties and interest on the unpaid gratuity amount. The employee is entitled to receive a copy of the inspection report within thirty days of its completion.

All agreements relating to the sale or exchange of immovable property shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the Sub-Registrar of Deeds designated for the relevant jurisdiction. Every party entering into such an agreement shall provide a certified copy of identification and address proof, along with three copies of the executed document. The Sub-Registrar may require additional affidavits or declarations as he deems necessary to verify the authenticity of the transaction and the capacity of the parties involved. Failure to present all required documentation will result in rejection of registration. Furthermore, meticulous maintenance of records pertaining to registered agreements is mandatory for all Sub-Registrars, ensuring accessibility for public inspection subject to applicable privacy regulations under this Act.

Where a party to a contract possesses material information which is likely to significantly influence the decision-making process of the other party, and such information is not readily ascertainable by reasonable inquiry, there shall be deemed to exist a duty of disclosure. Failure to disclose such material information, when deliberately withheld or actively concealed, renders the contracting party liable for breach under this Act. The aggrieved party may seek rescission of the contract, restitution of any benefits conferred, and compensation for losses directly attributable to the non-disclosure. Provided that, if the non-disclosing party demonstrates reasonable reliance on a third-party expert opinion regarding the undisclosed information, liability shall be mitigated proportionately. Nothing herein prevents a party from demonstrating fraudulent intent or misrepresentation, in which case remedies may extend beyond those provided herein.

The distribution licensee shall, prior to commencing supply of electricity to any consumer requiring a security deposit under this Act, execute a written agreement specifying the terms and conditions governing said deposit. Such agreement may include provisions for periodic review of the deposit amount based on consumption patterns and tariff revisions as determined by the State Commission. Assignment of rights pertaining to such security deposits shall be permissible subject to prior approval from the distribution licensee, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations associated with the original consumer’s account. The licensee may stipulate conditions regarding the financial stability and operational capacity of any entity seeking assignment. Upon termination of supply, the security deposit, less any outstanding dues or damages as assessed under this Act, shall be refunded to the consumer or their legal representative.

Where a finding of fact made by a Civil Judge Junior Division is challenged before an appellate tribunal on grounds relating solely to the admissibility of documentary evidence, the tribunal shall consider whether the evidentiary ruling prejudiced the substantial rights of either party. Any order passed by the appellate tribunal under this Act may be subject to further appeal only if it involves a question of law concerning the interpretation or application of principles regarding relevance and probative value. The aggrieved party shall have the right to apply for a stay of execution of any such order pending disposal of the appeal, provided that security is furnished as deemed appropriate by the appellate tribunal. This provision does not preclude recourse to other remedies available under this Act or any other law in force; however, the appellate tribunal may direct parties to mediation before entertaining further proceedings.

The grant of licenses for the extraction of minor minerals from ecologically sensitive areas shall be subject to prior environmental impact assessment as provided herein and require approval from the appointed authority designated under this Act. Such approvals may be assigned or sub-licensed, but only with the express written consent of the original licensee and subsequent registration with the competent regional office. The appointed authority shall maintain a public register detailing all such assignments, including the names of both assignor and assignee, the specific mineral rights transferred, and the duration of the assignment. Any alteration to the scope or conditions of an existing license, whether through modification or further extraction activities, also necessitates re-evaluation by the appointed authority. Failure to disclose any assignment or material change shall render the licensee liable for penalties as determined under this Act.

Where any party to a contract seeks to establish the genuineness of its obligations under this Act, they may submit a statutory declaration executed by an advocate or notary public, affirming the existence and terms of said agreement. Such declarations shall be admissible as evidence in court, subject to challenge regarding the competence or impartiality of the declarant. Any party disputing the validity of a contract based on a statutory declaration must demonstrate material misrepresentation or undue influence affecting the declarant at the time of execution. The burden of proof concerning such allegations rests solely upon the challenging party. Provided that, any appeal against an order admitting or excluding evidence based on a statutory declaration shall be heard expeditiously to avoid prejudice to either litigant.

Where a party institutes proceedings under this Act seeking specific performance of a contract, the adjudicating officer shall first determine whether such contract is valid and enforceable according to principles of law and equity. Provided that, if the adjudicating officer finds that the contract contains a clause excluding or limiting liability for negligence, he may only grant relief as provided herein if the party seeking specific performance demonstrates that the negligence was grossly negligent or willful. Further, where an objection is raised regarding the arbitrability of the dispute, the adjudicating officer shall consider such objection and determine its validity based on prevailing jurisprudence. The adjudicating officer shall record reasons in writing for any order declining to grant relief, and such reasons shall be made available to both parties under this Act.

Where a complaint is filed alleging deficiency in service or goods, the onus of establishing the claim shall lie upon the complainant. This burden of proof requires the complainant to demonstrate, with sufficient evidence, that the goods were not up to the claimed standards, the services rendered fell short of reasonable expectations, or an unfair trade practice was employed. Provided that, where the supplier admits liability for the deficiency, or where a presumption arises under this Act regarding the quality of goods or nature of service provided, the complainant shall be relieved from the strict application of this evidentiary requirement. The adjudicating officer may consider circumstantial evidence and consumer testimonies in determining whether the burden has been met.

Where any dispute arises between a distribution licensee and a consumer regarding the assessment of charges, disconnection notices, or other matters pertaining to electricity supply, both parties may agree to resolve the matter through terms of settlement. Such terms shall be reduced to writing and signed by authorized representatives of each party, and a copy thereof shall be filed with the appropriate State Commission under this Act within thirty days of execution. Any party dissatisfied with the implementation of the terms of settlement may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, file an application for review before the State Commission, demonstrating material breach or misrepresentation. The Commission shall consider such applications expeditiously and pass orders as it deems just, providing both parties a fair hearing.

Applications for registration of food testing laboratories, received under this Act, shall be processed initially by the designated State Food Safety Officer, who may, subject to maintaining a record of all actions taken, delegate the responsibility for preliminary scrutiny and verification of documents to any officer subordinate to him or her. Such delegation of powers shall not extend to the final decision regarding registration approval, which remains solely with the State Food Safety Officer. The applicant shall be notified in writing of any deficiencies identified during this process, providing a period of thirty days for rectification. Any subsequent application requiring further clarification may be referred back to the delegated officer for additional assessment and reporting before consideration by the State Food Safety Officer.

Registration of commercial vehicles shall proceed only upon submission of a certificate from the Regional Transport Authority confirming adherence to prescribed safety standards. The manner of service relating to vehicle registration includes the electronic uploading of all relevant documents, including proof of insurance and fitness certificates, onto the central transport database. Any alteration to the particulars recorded during initial registration requires subsequent notification to the registering authority and may necessitate a fresh inspection as provided herein. Owners shall ensure that any transfer of ownership is duly registered within thirty days, failing which penalties under this Act will apply. The registering authority may refuse registration if the application is incomplete or contains false information. Further, details regarding authorized signatories for vehicle-related communications must be maintained on record.

Where a police officer has reasonable cause to believe that evidence relating to an offence is concealed within any premises, he or she may exercise power of entry into such premises; provided that the belief is based upon information received from credible sources and recorded in writing. Such entry shall only occur during daylight hours unless exigent circumstances, duly documented, necessitate otherwise. Prior attempts to obtain access through alternative means, such as requesting voluntary cooperation from the occupant, must be demonstrably pursued before resorting to power of entry. The officer shall record the reasons for entering the premises and the time of entry in a prescribed form. Any person lawfully present within the premises at the time of entry shall be informed of the purpose under this Act and their identity recorded as provided herein.

Where an arbitral award has been challenged under this Act on grounds of fraud, misrepresentation, or any other act of deception affecting the validity of the arbitration agreement or the proceedings, the party alleging such misconduct shall bear the burden of proof to establish the same before the judicial authority. Provided that, where evidence is presented demonstrating a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of an arbitrator, the judicial authority may direct the shifting of this burden to the respondent. Failure to adduce sufficient evidence to satisfy the judicial authority regarding the existence and materiality of such fraudulent conduct shall render the challenging party liable for costs incurred by the other party in defending against the challenge, as determined under applicable rules concerning legal expenses. The judicial authority may impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for frivolous challenges lacking merit.

Licenses granted for generation of electricity, including those pertaining to transmission infrastructure, may be assigned subject to prior approval from the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission. Such approvals shall not be withheld or delayed without just cause, and an application for assignment must include details regarding the proposed assignee’s financial stability and technical competence. The Commission may conduct a summary procedure review of such applications, prioritizing those involving renewable energy sources as defined under this Act. Any licensee seeking to assign a license shall provide detailed justification for the transfer, demonstrating continued compliance with obligations stipulated herein. Further, assignment is permissible only if the proposed assignee possesses requisite experience in electricity generation or distribution. The Commission may impose conditions on any assignment deemed acceptable, ensuring uninterrupted power supply and adherence to safety standards.

Appellate Tribunals shall be constituted at the State level to hear appeals against orders passed by District Commissions. Every appeal arising out of an order passed by a District Commission shall be admitted by the Appellate Tribunal within thirty days from the date of receipt thereof, provided that the aggrieved party may file an application for condonation of delay if such delay has occurred without sufficient cause. The Tribunal may, at its discretion, require the appearance of parties before it or proceed ex parte. Decisions of the Appellate Tribunal shall be final subject to appeal to the State Commission under this Act. Parties appearing before the Appellate Tribunal shall be entitled to representation by an advocate. Costs relating to appeals heard by the Appellate Tribunal may be awarded as deemed appropriate by the Tribunal, taking into consideration the nature of the dispute and the conduct of the parties.

Where a motor vehicle owner or driver commits an offence relatable to traffic regulations, or concerning road safety, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, the concerned police officer may direct that the offender be given an opportunity to make a request for compounding of offences. Such request shall be accompanied by a sum determined as per guidelines issued by the State Government and deposited with the officer. Provided that this power of compounding shall not extend to offences involving serious injury or death, nor to repeat offenders within a period of one year from prior conviction under this Act. The victim of such offence shall have the right to object to any proposal for compounding, and their objection shall be recorded and considered by the officer before any decision is made. Failure to comply with conditions relating to compounding may result in prosecution as provided herein.

Every Regional Transport Authority and State Transport Undertaking shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to vehicle registrations, driving licenses issued, permits granted, and fitness certificates endorsed under this Act and rules made thereunder. Such records shall be preserved in a manner accessible for inspection by authorized officers of the Motor Vehicles Department and, subject to reasonable restrictions, by members of the public upon application. Failure to maintain accurate or complete records as provided herein constitutes an offense punishable with a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Further, any officer found deliberately falsifying or destroying such maintenance of records shall be liable for departmental action and criminal prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code.

Any establishment engaged in the processing or handling of hazardous materials exceeding threshold limits as notified under this Act shall apply for a certificate of registration within ninety days from the date these regulations come into force. The application shall include detailed plans demonstrating adherence to effluent discharge standards, waste management protocols, and emergency response procedures approved by the State Pollution Control Board. A certificate of registration may be refused if the proposed activity is likely to cause air or water pollution exceeding permissible limits, or poses a significant threat to public health. Renewal of the certificate of registration shall require submission of an annual compliance report verifying continued adherence to stipulated conditions, and may be subject to inspection by authorized officers as provided herein.

Any person failing to surrender a seized vehicle within thirty days from the date of seizure, as directed by the appointed authority, shall be deemed to have abandoned the said vehicle and it may be sold by public auction after due notice. The proceeds of such sale, subject to deduction of expenses incurred in holding the auction and recovering any outstanding fines or penalties under this Act, shall be deposited into the Road Fund maintained by the State Government. Any person attempting to obstruct the lawful seizure or subsequent disposal of a vehicle by the appointed authority is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both. Failure to comply with instructions issued by the appointed authority regarding vehicle inspection shall attract a penalty as prescribed.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive record of all arbitral agreements filed for registration under this Act, including details pertaining to the parties involved, the subject matter of the dispute, and the designated arbitration venue. Such records shall be preserved in both physical and electronic formats, ensuring accessibility for authorized personnel and stakeholders as provided herein. The Registrar may require additional documentation from applicants seeking registration, verifying compliance with procedural requirements. Any amendment or modification to a registered arbitral agreement must also be recorded by the Registrar, noting the date of alteration and the consent of all parties. Failure to maintain proper maintenance of records shall constitute an administrative lapse subject to review under applicable service regulations.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed particulars” relating to gratuity eligibility include, but are not limited to, the employee’s date of first appointment, continuous service rendered, last drawn salary, and any deductions or contributions made towards the gratuity fund. These prescribed particulars shall be maintained by the employer in a manner readily accessible for inspection under this Act. The determination of an employee's entitlement to gratuity is subject to verification against these prescribed particulars, as provided herein. Any alteration or amendment to the prescribed particulars must be recorded with appropriate authentication and justification. Failure to maintain accurate prescribed particulars may render the employer liable to penalties as determined under this Act.

Where a dispute arising from a contractual obligation is resolved through a terms of settlement executed between parties, the rights and obligations contained therein shall constitute legally binding agreements under this Act. Such terms of settlement may include provisions for the assignment or licensing of any intellectual property generated as a consequence of the original contract. A party to a terms of settlement shall be deemed to have expressly consented to the assignment of such rights unless otherwise stipulated within the document itself, provided that such assignment does not prejudice the interests of third parties who are not privy to the agreement. The right to license these assigned rights may also be granted subject to conditions outlined in the terms of settlement and consistent with principles of fairness and equity as determined by a competent court. No action shall lie against any party for breach of contract arising from an assignment or licensing undertaken pursuant to a duly executed terms of settlement.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to eligible entities for the purpose of facilitating the recovery of dues owed to consumers under agreements for goods or services. Such licenses shall permit the licensee to assign, pledge, or otherwise transfer rights relating to outstanding payments to a third party, provided that such assignment is accompanied by a disclosure statement outlining the terms and conditions applicable to the consumer’s original agreement. The Authority may specify criteria for eligibility including financial stability and adherence to ethical collection practices. Any entity seeking to undertake recovery activities through licensed assignment shall submit a detailed operational plan demonstrating compliance with regulations concerning data privacy and consumer communication. Further, the licensee remains ultimately responsible for ensuring fair treatment of consumers as provided herein during the entire process of debt recovery.

An employee shall be deemed eligible for gratuity under this Act if he has rendered continuous service for not less than five years; provided that any period of leave exceeding one month during the said continuous service shall not be counted towards the said five years. The determination of whether an employee satisfies the conditions relating to length of service, and the assessment of the amount of gratuity payable, shall be undertaken by a competent officer appointed under this Act, acting in accordance with established procedures. Such a competent officer may require production of relevant documents substantiating continuous service, including attendance records and employment contracts. The employer shall furnish all necessary information to the competent officer upon request. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in penalties as provided herein.

Every public authority shall maintain all records diligently and in a manner that facilitates access to information thereunder. The duty to maintain such records includes ensuring their proper indexing, cataloging, and preservation, both in physical and electronic form. Failure to adequately maintain records shall constitute an act of denial of the right to information, rendering the concerned public official liable for penalties as provided herein. Any citizen demonstrating a direct adverse effect resulting from inadequate maintenance of records by a public authority may petition the Central Information Commission seeking redressal, including compensation for demonstrable losses incurred. The Commission may order the public authority to rectify deficiencies in record keeping and impose sanctions on responsible officers. This obligation applies equally to records created before as well as after the commencement of this Act.

Any enterprise engaged in activities listed under Schedule I which results in emissions or effluents exceeding prescribed standards shall apply for a certificate of registration from the State Pollution Control Board. Application for such certificate shall include detailed project reports, environmental impact assessments and proposed mitigation measures as specified by the Board. The Board may grant or reject the application after due consideration of the submitted documentation and site inspection; reasons for rejection must be provided in writing to the applicant within sixty days. Failure to obtain a certificate of registration prior to commencement of operations shall render the enterprise liable to penalties, including fines and potential closure orders as determined by the Board. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding a certificate of registration may appeal to the Appellate Authority constituted under this Act, subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions relating to deposit of fees and time limits.

Where a service provider undertakes to provide services relating to telecommunications, including internet access, they shall ensure that the manner of service is consistent with the standards established by the relevant regulatory authority under this Act. This obligation applies irrespective of whether the service is provided through fixed lines, wireless networks or any other technology. Provided that, if a consumer explicitly consents to a modified manner of service, such as reduced bandwidth during peak hours, the provider shall provide clear and conspicuous notice detailing the limitations and potential impact on service quality. Failure to adhere to these requirements may result in penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The Central Authority may issue guidelines regarding best practices for maintaining appropriate standards in the manner of service.

Registration of documents relating to immovable property shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the fact of registration, and the date on which such document was registered as appearing in the registry book shall be taken as proof until disproved under this Act. Where a document is presented for registration, the registering officer shall require the presenter to specify the prescribed particulars concerning the parties involved, including their addresses and occupations, alongside details pertaining to the property’s boundaries and extent. Failure to provide these prescribed particulars accurately may result in refusal of registration, provided that the presenter shall be afforded an opportunity to rectify any discrepancies before such a determination is made. The registering officer may also require supporting documentation to verify the accuracy of information submitted.

Any public authority failing to comply with an order issued under this Act directing the recovery of dues owed to it, or any subordinate officer obstructing such recovery, shall be liable to a monetary penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, determined by the Central Information Commission. The Commission may, after affording the concerned public authority and officer an opportunity for being heard, issue directions specifying the mode and manner of recovery. Failure to comply with these directions within the time specified therein shall attract a daily penalty of one thousand rupees until compliance is made. Further, any employee found deliberately concealing information to evade recovery proceedings will face disciplinary action as provided herein.

The findings contained within any inspection report prepared pursuant to a dispute resolution agreement undertaken under this Act shall remain confidential between the parties involved and the appointed arbitrator or conciliator. Subject to an order of Court issued upon application by either party demonstrating compelling need, such reports may be disclosed only for the purpose of facilitating settlement discussions or in support of a reasoned award. Any assignment of rights arising from the utilization of data derived from an inspection report requires prior written consent from the original reporting agency; such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, the licensee of an inspection report shall adhere to all quality assurance protocols mandated by the originating body and may sub-license access for internal review purposes only, provided that confidentiality obligations remain strictly enforced as provided herein.

Every undertaking engaged in the manufacture or processing of goods exceeding a threshold value as determined by notification issued by the Central Government shall maintain a register of undertakings detailing all transactions pertaining to raw materials, finished products, and inter-unit transfers. This register shall be preserved for a period not less than seven years from the date of each transaction recorded therein and made available for inspection upon request by an authorized officer under this Act. The register must accurately reflect quantities, values, dates, and parties involved in each transaction. Failure to maintain such a register or providing false information within it will render the undertaking liable to penalties as provided herein. Any alteration to entries shall be clearly indicated with supporting documentation and duly attested.

The Authority granting environmental clearances for industrial projects involving ecologically sensitive areas shall require submission of a security deposit from the project proponent as a condition precedent to commencement of operations. This security deposit, calculated at a rate not exceeding ten percent of the total estimated project cost, serves as an assurance against potential environmental degradation and remediation expenses. The Authority may assign its right to recover funds from this security deposit to a designated financial institution or agency through a written agreement. Such assignment shall not relieve the project proponent of their primary obligation under this Act to comply with all stipulated conditions. Any transfer of ownership or management control of the project requires prior notification to and approval by the Authority, who may adjust the amount held as security deposit accordingly. The release of the security deposit is subject to a post-operational audit confirming satisfactory environmental performance.

For the purposes of this Act, “material information” with respect to a generating station, transmission line, or distribution network means any fact, matter, circumstance, report, or statement which is likely to affect significantly the financial condition, performance, or operations thereof; and includes, but is not limited to, details regarding planned outages, projected demand fluctuations, and assessments of infrastructure vulnerability. Every licensee shall have a duty of disclosure to provide accurate and complete material information to the appropriate regulatory authority as provided herein. This duty extends to proactively informing the Authority of any foreseeable event likely to impact electricity supply stability. Failure to disclose such information constitutes a violation under this Act.

Every public authority shall maintain a register of undertakings, detailing all contracts entered into, agreements executed, and memoranda of understanding finalized by such authority, irrespective of their monetary value. This register shall be conspicuously displayed on the designated website of the public authority and made available for inspection at its offices during working hours. Any citizen seeking access to information pertaining to any undertaking listed in the register is entitled to receive a certified copy thereof, subject to payment of applicable fees as prescribed under this Act. Failure to provide such copies or maintain an accurate and updated register shall constitute a denial of information and render the public authority liable for penalties as provided herein. The Central Information Commission may, upon receiving complaints regarding deficiencies in the maintenance of the register of undertakings, issue directions for rectification and compliance.

Where a contract involves the creation of digital records pertaining to performance obligations, the parties shall jointly establish protocols for the secure maintenance of records. Such protocols must specify retention periods commensurate with applicable statutory limitations and industry best practices. Any party intending to assign or transfer their rights and obligations under this Act concerning the aforementioned digital records may do so subject to obtaining prior written consent from the other contracting party. This consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, provided that the assigning party demonstrates compliance with all stipulated protocols for maintenance of records. Further, any assignee shall assume responsibility for continued adherence to these protocols, as if originally bound by them under this Act. The original contracting party retains the right to audit the assignee’s record-keeping practices and ensure ongoing compliance.

Every public authority shall maintain a register of undertakings, both ongoing and completed, detailing all projects undertaken by that authority for the delivery of services or benefits to citizens. This register shall include, but not be limited to, information regarding project commencement dates, anticipated completion timelines, total budgetary allocations, and details of contractors engaged. The register of undertakings shall be maintained in a readily accessible format, both electronically and in physical form at designated locations as determined by the Public Information Officer. Any officer responsible for maintaining this register shall ensure its accuracy and update it regularly, not less frequently than once every three months. Requests for information pertaining to entries within the register of undertakings are deemed requests under this Act and shall be processed accordingly, subject to any exemptions provided herein.

Every food business operator engaged in manufacturing, processing, packing, storage or wholesale trading of food products shall have a positive duty of disclosure regarding material information affecting consumer safety and quality. This includes, but is not limited to, details concerning ingredients, allergens, nutritional content, production processes, and any known defects or contamination risks. Failure to provide such disclosures, or providing false or misleading information, renders the operator liable for damages suffered by consumers as a direct consequence of reliance on that undisclosed information. Compensation shall include medical expenses, loss of earnings, and consequential losses reasonably foreseeable. A consumer aggrieved may pursue remedies under this Act, including claims for injunctions preventing further deceptive practices and orders compelling full disclosure.

Where a claim arising under this Act relates to injury or loss of life sustained by reason of a motor vehicle accident, parties involved may agree to a settlement subject to approval by the Motor Accidents Settlement Tribunal established under this Act. Such agreement shall specify the amount agreed upon and the manner in which it is to be disbursed amongst all claimants entitled to compensation. The Tribunal shall not approve any terms of settlement if it determines that the proposed sum is manifestly inadequate or fails to adequately address future medical needs, as certified by a qualified physician. Further, approval shall only be granted provided that all parties have executed the agreement voluntarily and without undue influence or coercion. Any party may petition the Tribunal for review of an approved settlement within thirty days.

The licensing of documentary evidence obtained through summary procedure, as provided herein, shall be subject to the approval of the Central Licensing Authority constituted under this Act. Any person intending to assign or otherwise transfer rights pertaining to such evidence must first obtain a ‘No Objection Certificate’ from the original evidentiary source, confirming consent for said assignment. The Central Licensing Authority may, after due consideration and public notice, grant permission for assignments where it is satisfied that the assignee possesses demonstrable expertise in legal analysis and adheres to principles of impartiality. Further, any sub-licensing or further assignment shall require renewed application and approval under this Act. Failure to secure prior authorization will render such transfer void ab initio. The Authority may impose conditions regarding confidentiality and usage restrictions as deemed necessary to protect public interest and the integrity of judicial proceedings.

Any public authority failing to grant access to information requested under this Act, or unduly delaying the provision of such access, shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Central Information Commission. Such compensation may include, but is not limited to, monetary penalties levied against responsible officers and disciplinary action taken against defaulting employees. The conditions of licence granted to private entities providing services related to information dissemination are subject to review and revocation if found to impede access or transparency guaranteed herein. Failure to comply with directives issued by the Commission regarding procedural adherence and timely responses will attract progressively increasing financial penalties, as prescribed in regulations framed under this Act.

Where any public authority fails to provide information requested under this Act within the time frame stipulated therein, or provides information that is incomplete or inaccurate, an aggrieved party may file a complaint with the Information Commission. Such complaints shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating the failure or deficiency in response. The Information Commission shall entertain such complaints only if filed within six months from the date of the alleged infraction, as provided herein. This period of limitation may be extended by the Commission for reasons to be recorded in writing, but not beyond a further three months. Any order passed by the Commission regarding extension of time is subject to appeal before the Central Information Commission.

The Central Information Commission may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses for the automated extraction and dissemination of information held by public authorities, provided that such licenses are granted only to entities demonstrating a commitment to responsible data handling practices as defined under guidelines issued by the Commission. Any license so granted shall be assignable, but only with prior written consent from the Central Information Commission, which may impose conditions regarding continued compliance with these guidelines upon assignment. The period of limitation for challenging the grant or refusal of such a license before any appellate authority shall be sixty days from the date of communication of the decision. Further, any entity acquiring a license through assignment shall inherit all obligations and liabilities associated therewith, including adherence to stipulated timelines for responding to information requests under this Act.

A statutory declaration made under this Act shall be in writing and subscribed by the declarant before a person authorized to administer oaths, being a Magistrate, Notary Public, or other officer of like rank as may be notified by the Central Government. The declaration shall contain a clear and unambiguous statement of the facts intended to be proved, accompanied by a solemn affirmation that such facts are true to the best of the declarant's knowledge, information and belief. Every statutory declaration shall conclude with a clause explicitly stating that the declarant understands that making a false declaration is punishable under the Indian Penal Code. The person before whom the declaration is made shall attest it by signing and affixing their official seal, indicating verification of the declarant’s identity. Any document presented as evidence which purports to be a statutory declaration but fails to comply with these requirements shall be deemed inadmissible.

For the purposes of this Act, a “competent officer” means an individual appointed by the Central Government or State Government, possessing qualifications deemed appropriate for environmental management and enforcement, which includes, but is not limited to, officers from the departments of environment, forests, pollution control boards, and any other department specifically authorized under notification. A competent officer shall be empowered to conduct inspections, take samples, seize materials, and issue directions as provided herein. The designation of a competent officer shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any individual acting as a competent officer must possess such training and experience as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where a service provider furnishes services involving transportation of passengers or goods, the manner of service shall conform to standards prescribed by the Central Government, published in the Official Gazette. These standards shall specify requirements relating to safety protocols, passenger comfort, cleanliness, and accessibility for persons with disabilities. A service provider failing to adhere to these prescribed standards may be directed by the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission to implement corrective measures, including but not limited to remedial training for personnel and modification of operational procedures. The Central Government may, from time to time, revise these standards based on recommendations received from consumer advocacy groups or industry consultations. Any revision shall be published at least thirty days prior to its effective date. Service providers are obliged to prominently display the applicable standards in a language readily understood by consumers accessing their services.

Where a service provider offers access to digital content relating to financial products through a subscription-based platform, they shall provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms governing the licensing of that content to subscribers. This duty of disclosure includes, but is not limited to, information regarding any restrictions on redistribution or secondary use permitted under this Act. A service provider may grant rights to assign or sublicense access to such digital content to affiliated entities, provided that such assignment does not diminish the quality of service offered to the original subscriber and is disclosed prominently at the point of subscription. Any attempt to circumvent these disclosure requirements through obfuscation or misleading representations shall be deemed an unfair trade practice. Subscribers are entitled to a refund proportional to any unfulfilled licensing terms arising from unauthorized assignments, as provided herein.

Where a contract for the supply of goods involves an inspection report prepared by an independent surveyor acting on behalf of the buyer, the rights pertaining to that report shall be subject to the provisions herein. The seller may, with prior written consent of the buyer, assign or license any right relating to the preparation, dissemination, and use of such inspection reports, provided that such assignment or license does not alter the fundamental terms of the underlying contract for supply. Any party receiving a license under this clause shall be bound by the conditions stipulated in the original agreement between the seller and the buyer regarding confidentiality and data protection. The buyer may require verification of any proposed assignee’s professional competence before granting consent, as provided herein. Further, no assignment or license shall relieve the seller from liabilities arising under this Act concerning the quality or conformity of the goods supplied.

Fees leviable under this Act shall be paid to the designated Government account as per rules framed by the Central Government. The schedule of fees prescribed herein is indicative and may be revised periodically based on administrative costs and prevailing economic factors; any such revision shall be notified in the Official Gazette at least thirty days prior to its effective date. Applications for registration, appeals against rejection, and requests for rectification of contracts are all subject to the applicable fee as detailed within the schedule of fees annexed hereto. Failure to pay the prescribed fee within the stipulated time period may result in the application being deemed withdrawn or the appeal rendered inadmissible. The Central Government may, by notification, delegate powers relating to the assessment and recovery of these fees to designated officers. Any dispute concerning the applicability or amount of a fee shall be resolved through an internal grievance redressal mechanism established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an inspection report means a document prepared by an authorized inspecting officer following an examination of a motor vehicle, detailing observations pertaining to its roadworthiness and compliance with applicable standards. The inspection report shall include, but not be limited to, assessments of braking systems, steering mechanisms, suspension components, lighting equipment, and tyre condition. It may also record any modifications made to the vehicle deviating from original specifications. An inspection report is deemed valid for a period as provided herein, subject to the inspecting officer’s certification and adherence to prescribed procedures under this Act.

Any distribution licensee failing to rectify a reported interruption in electricity supply within the timeframe specified under this Act, or otherwise than as prescribed, shall be liable to pay compensation at rates determined by the State Commission. Such compensation shall be paid directly to the affected consumer and may be recovered from the distribution licensee through deductions from its revenue collected under this Act. The period of limitation for claims relating to such compensation shall be three years from the date of the interruption. Failure to file a claim within this period shall bar any subsequent action, subject to just cause demonstrated before the State Commission. Recovery proceedings against defaulting licensees may be initiated by the appropriate authority without prejudice to other penalties as provided herein.

Any person engaged in activities involving hazardous substances requiring a certificate of registration under this Act shall maintain records pertaining to emissions, effluents, and waste generated, accessible for inspection by authorized officers. Failure to do so constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years or a fine extending to one lakh rupees, or both. Any alteration or falsification of such records will attract enhanced penalties, including suspension of the certificate of registration. Furthermore, any person found knowingly obstructing an officer in the performance of his duties related to verification of compliance shall be liable to prosecution under this Act and may face additional fines as determined by the competent authority.

Any distribution licensee desiring to resolve disputes concerning tariff determination or service agreements relating to electricity supply shall first attempt amicable resolution through negotiations facilitated by a mutually agreed mediator. Should such negotiations fail to yield a satisfactory outcome within ninety days, the parties may proceed towards establishing terms of settlement. These terms shall be documented in writing and signed by authorized representatives of both the licensee and the complainant, accompanied by verification under oath as provided herein. The State Electricity Regulatory Commission may, upon application from either party, review any proposed terms of settlement to ensure compliance with applicable regulations and safeguard consumer interests. Any deviation from these established terms requires prior written consent from the Commission.

Where an individual is charged under this Act with causing injury to another person due to negligent driving of a motor vehicle, the prosecution shall bear the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged negligence occurred and directly resulted in said injury. Provided that, if the accused presents evidence suggesting contributory negligence on the part of the injured party, the prosecution may then be required to demonstrate, by affirmative evidence, that the injuries sustained were primarily attributable to the actions or omissions of the accused driver. Failure to satisfy this evidentiary standard shall result in acquittal. The adjudicating authority may, at its discretion, require the production of expert testimony regarding road conditions and vehicle performance. Any appeal against a finding under this Act concerning the burden of proof is subject to review by the appellate tribunal.

Where an analysis of a food sample reveals the presence of a prohibited substance exceeding permissible limits as determined under this Act, the burden of proof shall lie upon the manufacturer or importer to demonstrate that the excess is attributable solely to unavoidable contamination arising from circumstances beyond their reasonable control and preventative measures. Such demonstration must be supported by documented evidence including records pertaining to raw material sourcing, processing protocols, storage conditions, and quality assurance procedures maintained throughout the production chain.
