Every owner of a motor vehicle involved in an accident resulting in injury or death shall, within seven days of the occurrence, file a statutory declaration before a notified Magistrate, affirming the accuracy of information provided to the investigating officer regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident and the identities of all parties involved. Failure to submit such a declaration will render the owner liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees, and may result in suspension of the vehicle’s registration certificate for a period as determined by the Regional Transport Authority. The Magistrate shall verify the declaration based on records maintained under this Act and may require further clarification from the declarant. Any false statement made within the statutory declaration is punishable with imprisonment extending to two years, or fine, or both, as provided herein.

Where a licence is granted under this Act for the operation of a consumer dispute resolution mechanism, the conditions of licence shall be prominently displayed at all points of contact with consumers, including but not limited to physical offices and online platforms. Any alteration or modification to these conditions requires prior written approval from the Central Authority, and such approval may only be granted if deemed consistent with the objectives of this Act. Failure to adhere strictly to the prescribed conditions shall constitute a material breach of the licence agreement, rendering the licensee liable for penalties as determined by the Central Authority. An aggrieved party may appeal any decision regarding a breach or modification of these conditions to the Appellate Tribunal, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from such action.

Any party failing to furnish the prescribed particulars relating to an arbitral agreement within the time specified under this Act shall incur a monetary penalty of fifty thousand rupees for the initial default, and ten thousand rupees for each subsequent day of non-compliance. The Arbitrator may, notwithstanding any order made by the Court, direct recovery of such penalties as arrears of land revenue. Provided that, if the failure to furnish the prescribed particulars is attributable to demonstrable fraud or misrepresentation on the part of a party, the Court shall enhance the penalty up to two hundred thousand rupees and may issue an order restraining further proceedings until full compliance is achieved. The adjudicating officer shall submit a quarterly report detailing penalties imposed and recoveries effected as provided herein.

Any license granted under this Act may be revoked if the licensee is found to have wilfully violated any provision relating to food safety standards or has failed to comply with prescribed hygiene practices. The Food Safety Officer shall issue a notice to the licensee, detailing the alleged violation and providing an opportunity for a hearing within thirty days of the date of such notice. Following the hearing, the adjudicating officer may determine whether grounds of revocation exist based on evidence presented. Where the adjudicating officer finds that the violation is substantial and persistent, or constitutes fraud, the license shall be revoked immediately. An appeal against an order of revocation lies with the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The authority’s decision shall be final.

Where a Public Information Officer disputes the existence of information requested under this Act, or challenges the veracity of information provided by another Public Information Officer, the burden of proof shall lie upon the applicant seeking the information to demonstrate that the information exists and is held by the concerned public authority. The Central Information Commission may require the Public Information Officer to produce documentary evidence substantiating their claims regarding non-existence or inaccuracy of records. Failure on the part of a Public Information Officer to provide adequate justification for denying access, or providing incorrect information, shall be deemed a violation under this Act and subject to penalty as provided herein. The Central Information Commission may, in its discretion, direct the public authority to undertake a search for the requested information if it finds reasonable grounds to believe that such information may exist but has not been disclosed.

Every arbitration agreement shall require each party to the agreement to maintain a register of undertakings relating to that agreement, accessible for inspection by the other party upon written request. The format and content of the register of undertakings shall conform to guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time, published in the Official Gazette. Failure to provide access to the register within thirty days of such request may result in a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees imposed on the defaulting party by an adjudicating officer appointed under this Act. The adjudicating officer’s order shall be final and binding subject to appeal to the High Court. Any entry made in the register of undertakings is deemed admissible as evidence unless proven otherwise, provided that the register itself has been duly maintained according to prescribed procedures. Parties may apply to the arbitral tribunal for directions regarding interpretation or implementation of these provisions.

Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or enforceability of an agreement relating to the supply of essential goods, the adjudicating officer appointed under this Act shall have the power to order interim relief pending final determination of the matter. Such relief may include, but is not limited to, injunctions preventing further action detrimental to the aggrieved party and directions for the provision of the essential goods at a reasonable price. The adjudicating officer shall provide both parties with an opportunity to be heard and present evidence in support of their respective claims. Any order made by the adjudicating officer may be appealed to a higher appellate authority as provided herein, subject to such conditions regarding costs and timelines as are prescribed. Failure to comply with any order issued by the adjudicating officer shall render the defaulting party liable for penalties under this Act.

Where a consumer establishes that goods or services were procured as a result of misleading advertising or unfair trade practices, they shall be entitled to seek redressal under this Act. Such redressal may include, but is not limited to, damages proportionate to the loss suffered, discontinuation of the offending practice, and corrective advertising measures. Further, where a product proves defective or deficient in quality, leading to demonstrable harm or injury to the consumer, the consumer retains the right to claim compensation for such losses. The Central Authority may, upon receiving complaints regarding persistent unfair practices, issue orders directing businesses to cease operations or modify their conduct. Consumers are afforded grounds of revocation of contracts entered into under conditions of misrepresentation and shall be entitled to a refund of any consideration paid.

Every consumer dispute relating to goods or services involving a deficiency in service shall be investigated by a competent officer appointed under this Act. Such competent officer shall, upon receipt of a complaint, issue notice to the relevant party against whom the complaint is made, providing them with a reasonable opportunity to submit their response within thirty days from the date of such notice. The competent officer may conduct site visits and examine documents as deemed necessary for ascertaining the facts giving rise to the dispute. Provided that any evidence submitted by either party shall be verified through affidavit. If, after due consideration, the competent officer finds merit in the complaint, they shall pass orders directing compliance within a stipulated timeframe, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where in an arbitration proceeding, a party seeks to establish a fact or circumstance relevant to the determination of the dispute, that party shall bear the burden of proof pertaining thereto, unless expressly provided otherwise under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. The standard of proof required shall be that which is appropriate given the nature of the fact or circumstance sought to be established and the applicable rules of evidence as determined by the arbitral tribunal. Nothing herein shall prevent the arbitral tribunal from directing a party to produce documents or information relevant to the dispute, subject to principles of fairness and confidentiality as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “licence” with regard to mining operations includes any authorization granted by a competent authority permitting the extraction of minerals from specified land, and is deemed to incorporate all conditions attached thereto at the time of grant or subsequent modification. These conditions of licence shall be binding on the licensee and their successors in interest. Any dispute arising concerning the interpretation or enforcement of such conditions may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. The term “competent authority” means the body designated under relevant regulations for issuing mining licences, and its designation shall not invalidate any action taken prior to formal notification.

For the purposes of this Act, “terms of settlement” with respect to disputes arising between distribution licensees and consumers or between generation companies and transmission licensees shall mean a written agreement reached through mediation, conciliation, or arbitration, wherein both parties voluntarily agree to resolve their differences relating to billing, service connection, power supply, or any other matter governed under this Act. Such terms of settlement shall be binding on the parties thereto unless they are subsequently modified by mutual consent or set aside by an appropriate forum as provided herein. The acceptance of such terms constitutes a waiver of further remedies available to either party concerning the subject matter addressed within those terms.

For the purposes of claims arising under this Act, “notice of demand” means a written communication served upon an individual or entity alleged to be liable for damages, specifying the amount claimed and providing particulars of the loss or injury giving rise to such claim. Such notice shall clearly state the basis on which the liability is asserted and include contact information for the claimant or their representative. A notice of demand may be sent by registered post with acknowledgement due or through any other mode that provides verifiable proof of receipt. Failure to serve a valid notice of demand does not, however, preclude recovery, subject to judicial discretion as provided herein.

Where an inspection is conducted pursuant to directions issued under this Act, the inspecting officer shall prepare a detailed inspection report documenting all observations made, deficiencies identified, and remedial measures recommended. This inspection report shall be submitted to the prescribed authority within thirty days of completion of the inspection. Any party directly affected by the findings contained in the inspection report may, within fifteen days from its receipt, submit written objections or clarifications to the prescribed authority. The prescribed authority shall consider such objections before finalizing the report and shall record reasons for any modifications made. Disputes arising regarding the accuracy or completeness of an inspection report are subject to review under procedures as provided herein.

Every applicant seeking a learner’s permit shall submit Form A duly completed and verified by two persons resident within the jurisdiction of the Regional Transport Authority concerned. The attending medical practitioner, designated under this Act, must certify on Form A that the applicant meets the prescribed physical fitness standards as provided herein. Upon receipt of the application and verification thereof, the Motor Vehicles Inspector may conduct a practical test assessing the applicant’s basic understanding of traffic rules and road safety procedures. Failure to pass such inspection shall render the application liable for rejection, with reasons recorded in writing. The conditions of licence relating to age, physical fitness, vision standards, and driving experience are strictly enforced under this Act. Any person found violating these conditions is subject to suspension or revocation of their license as determined by the Appellate Authority. Renewal applications must be submitted at least thirty days prior to expiry, accompanied by a medical certificate conforming to Form B.

Every distribution licensee shall furnish a notice of demand to a consumer intending to draw electricity from the licensee’s distribution system, specifying the anticipated load requirements and the associated tariff applicable. Such notice shall be issued at least thirty days prior to the commencement of supply, or such shorter period as may be prescribed by regulations made under this Act. The notice must clearly state the terms and conditions governing the connection agreement, including provisions relating to payment schedules and potential penalties for default. A consumer aggrieved by any condition stipulated in a notice of demand may file an objection with the appropriate appellate authority within fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice. The licensee shall consider such objections and provide reasoned responses within another fifteen days. Failure to comply with this procedure will render the subsequent supply agreement voidable at the option of the consumer.

Every motor vehicle presented for registration under this Act shall comply with all applicable standards of safety and emissions as determined by the Central Government. The application for a certificate of registration must include a valid insurance policy, proof of ownership, and a declaration confirming that the vehicle conforms to the requirements outlined in Schedule A. Where a vehicle has been modified from its original design, such modifications must be approved prior to registration; failure to obtain this approval will render the certificate of registration void. The Regional Transport Authority may require an inspection of the vehicle to verify compliance with these provisions. Any alteration to the chassis or engine number without notification and authorization shall invalidate any existing certificate of registration.

Any distribution licensee failing to furnish information regarding electricity supply connections in the prescribed particulars, including but not limited to consumer name, address, connected load, tariff category, and date of connection, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty as determined by the State Commission. Such penalty shall be recoverable as an arrears of revenue under this Act. The State Government may, through notification published in the Official Gazette, increase the amount of such penalties where non-compliance persists or demonstrates systemic failure. Failure to rectify deficiencies identified during inspection regarding prescribed particulars constitutes a violation subject to further enforcement action and potential suspension of distribution license privileges, provided that due notice is given prior to any such action.

Where an offence involving moral turpitude has been committed, or where the offender is a minor, no suit shall be brought for compensation by way of compounding of offences against any person aggrieved, and the matter shall be solely within the purview of the courts to adjudicate upon guilt and appropriate punishment. In cases other than those excluded under this provision, an application for compounding may be made to the court at any stage prior to the recording of evidence, provided that both parties consent in writing to such a resolution. The Court shall consider factors including the nature and gravity of the offence, the extent of harm caused to the victim, and the willingness of the offender to make restitution. If the Court deems it appropriate, it may order compounding of offences on terms and conditions as it considers just, which shall be recorded in its judgment. Any agreement reached must comply with principles of fairness and equity.

The Central Authority may grant a certificate of registration to any entity engaged in providing services related to consumer dispute redressal, subject to fulfilling specified criteria as provided herein. Such certificates shall remain valid for a period not exceeding five years and are renewable upon application and payment of the prescribed fee. The holder of a certificate of registration shall be entitled to offer mediation, arbitration, or conciliation services relating to consumer grievances, but may not undertake any activity that directly competes with the functions of District Commissions, State Commissions, or the National Commission under this Act. A certificate of registration may be assigned to another entity upon prior approval from the Central Authority and subject to conditions safeguarding consumer interests. Any assignment shall be recorded in a register maintained by the Authority.

Where a Sub-Divisional Magistrate, or other officer empowered under this Act to administer oaths, requires attendance of witnesses or production of documents, the fees payable to such witnesses and for the certified copies of documents produced shall be determined in accordance with the schedule of fees annexed hereto. Such schedule shall specify rates applicable based on the status of the witness, being differentiated between Government servants, judicial officers, and private individuals; provided that where a witness is required to travel beyond their usual place of residence, additional allowances for mileage and daily sustenance shall also be paid as detailed in the said schedule. The officer administering oaths may, subject to guidelines issued by the State Government from time to time, adjust these fees if circumstances warrant, ensuring equitable compensation under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “service” with respect to any notice or communication required to be served upon any person, includes delivery in physical form, transmission via registered post acknowledgment due, and electronic transmission where the recipient has consented to receive such communications electronically, subject to verification of receipt. The manner of service shall be deemed sufficient if evidence of dispatch is maintained by the sender, unless otherwise specified under this Act. Any notice served electronically shall be considered duly served upon confirmation of delivery or access by the recipient, as provided herein. Failure to obtain acknowledgement does not invalidate a notice sent via registered post.

The Central Registering Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all motor vehicles registered within its jurisdiction, detailing particulars including but not limited to chassis numbers, engine capacities, and permitted usage classifications. Upon successful verification of submitted documentation and payment of prescribed fees, a certificate of registration shall be issued to the registered owner, constituting prima facie evidence of ownership and compliance with requirements under this Act. Any alteration or modification to a vehicle after initial registration necessitates notification to the Central Registering Authority and may require updated endorsement on the existing certificate of registration. Failure to update such details as provided herein is deemed an offence subject to penalty. The authority shall have power to revoke a certificate of registration where fraudulent misrepresentation occurred during the application process.

Where any adjudicating officer finds that a food business operator has contravened any provision under this Act or regulations made thereunder, he may, following a summary procedure, issue an order directing the rectification of the violation and imposing a monetary penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for the first offence. Any party dissatisfied with such order may appeal to the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within thirty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate authority shall consider any objections raised by the appellant and the respondent, affording both parties an opportunity for argument, and may confirm, vary, or annul the original order. Such appeals shall be decided expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice.

Where any information requested under this Act pertains to matters involving commercial confidence or trade secrets, the Public Information Officer shall consult with a competent officer designated by the concerned public authority for assessment. The competent officer’s determination regarding whether the information qualifies as exempt from disclosure, subject to the proviso that such determination must be accompanied by reasoned justification recorded in writing, may be challenged before the appellate authority. Any appeal against an order of the Public Information Officer upholding the exemption claim shall be entertained only if the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the withheld information; otherwise, the appeal shall stand dismissed. The appellate authority may direct the competent officer to reconsider their assessment and provide further clarification.

For the purposes of arbitration proceedings under this Act, a party’s duty of disclosure shall encompass the obligation to promptly inform the other party of any material fact known to the party which is or may be relevant to the resolution of the dispute. This duty extends to facts whether obtained from public records, internal documents, communications with third parties, or any other source. A material fact is deemed such if it would likely influence the arbitral tribunal’s decision. Provided that a party reasonably believes a fact to be immaterial, no breach of this duty shall arise; however, wilful suppression of information as provided herein constitutes a ground for challenging the award.

Where a contract for the provision of services relating to infrastructure development has been entered into, and the consideration remains unpaid due to circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the service provider, the right to recovery of dues arising from that contract may be assigned by the service provider to a financing institution or other approved entity. Such assignment shall include all rights, title, and interest in the outstanding receivables under the original contract, subject to the terms and conditions specified in the assignment agreement. The assignor shall provide prior written notice to the contracting party of such assignment, detailing the assignee’s contact information. No recovery action may be initiated by the assignee without first providing a further opportunity for dispute resolution as provided herein. The contracting party shall cooperate fully with the assignee regarding all matters pertaining to the recovery of dues and shall not impede or obstruct any actions taken in good faith towards that end.

For the purposes of arbitration proceedings under this Act, an inspection report means a written document prepared by a qualified engineer or surveyor appointed by either party or jointly by the parties, detailing observations and findings relating to the condition, performance, or functionality of property subject to the dispute. Such reports shall include photographic or video evidence as deemed necessary for clarity. An inspection report is considered documentary evidence and may be presented before the arbitral tribunal. The scope of an inspection report shall be limited to matters directly relevant to resolving the issues in contention, provided that any party may challenge the qualifications or methodology employed in preparing the inspection report.

Registration of Food Service Establishments: Detailed Procedures Every proprietor intending to register a food service establishment shall submit an Application Form in triplicate to the designated Licensing Officer, along with requisite documentation pertaining to premises layout and employee training records. The manner of service of food, including but not limited to presentation, packaging, and delivery protocols, must be clearly detailed within this application. Such details shall encompass descriptions of serving utensils, temperature control mechanisms for hot or cold items, and adherence to prescribed hygiene standards during preparation and dispatch. The Licensing Officer may inspect the premises to verify compliance with the information provided. Any deviation from the declared manner of service discovered during inspection will necessitate resubmission of the Application Form and payment of a revised registration fee.

For the purposes of this Act, “outstanding dues” with respect to a public authority shall include all sums due from a third party pursuant to a contract entered into on behalf of the public authority, or arising from any statutory obligation imposed upon the public authority; such dues shall encompass fees, charges, penalties, and interest accrued thereon. The term "third party" includes, but is not limited to, contractors, suppliers, beneficiaries of government schemes, and individuals receiving services under this Act. Recovery of dues outstanding for a period exceeding one year may be pursued by the public authority through civil remedies as provided herein, subject to due process and without prejudice to any criminal proceedings that may be initiated.

For the purposes of this Act, “compounding of offences” means the settlement of a case involving an offence triable under this Act or regulations framed thereunder through negotiation between the offender and the Food Safety Officer, subject to approval from the State Food Safety Authority. Such compounding shall be permissible only for specified minor violations as notified by the Central Government, and may involve payment of a monetary penalty determined according to guidelines prescribed herein. The acceptance of such settlement constitutes an admission of guilt by the offender. Further, no compounding shall be allowed where the offence involves loss of life or serious injury, or where the Food Safety Officer deems it necessary for public interest that prosecution continues as provided herein.

Any person found to have wilfully obstructed an adjudicating officer in the performance of their duties under this Act, including but not limited to preventing access to premises or documents relevant to an inquiry, shall be liable to imprisonment for a term that may extend to six months, or with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both. Where such obstruction results in demonstrable prejudice to the fairness and efficiency of proceedings before the adjudicating officer, the court may enhance the penalty as it deems fit. Furthermore, any individual who knowingly provides false information to an adjudicating officer shall be subject to penalties under this Act, including potential liability for costs incurred by the relevant authority. Repeated offences shall attract progressively higher fines.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate any officer of the government to be a competent officer for the purposes of facilitating the assignment of information deemed sensitive under this Act. Such designation shall specify the qualifications and experience required of the designated officer, including but not limited to familiarity with data security protocols and procedures relating to public sector undertakings. Any license granted by a Public Information Officer permitting access to information may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to prior approval from the competent officer. This approval will consider potential risks to national security and commercial confidentiality, as provided herein. The competent officer shall maintain a register of all assignments and sub-licenses, accessible for inspection under this Act. Any person assigning such a license must provide full disclosure regarding the intended recipient’s capabilities in safeguarding information.

Where a consumer dispute is resolved through a terms of settlement arrived at between the complainant and the service provider under this Act, either party may, within thirty days from the date of execution of such settlement, file an application before the District Commission seeking modification or rescission thereof. Such application shall state specifically the grounds upon which the settlement is challenged, including but not limited to allegations of coercion, misrepresentation, or manifest unfairness. The Commission shall consider the application and provide both parties with a reasonable opportunity to present their arguments and evidence. Provided that the Commission may dismiss an application if it finds that the terms of settlement were arrived at freely and fairly, subject to any subsequent appeal as provided herein.

Fees payable under this Act shall be determined according to the schedule of fees annexed hereto. The Arbitral Tribunal may, with the prior approval of the High Court exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction over the territory where the arbitration is conducted, recommend an increase in any fee specified in the said schedule, provided that such recommendation is made only if circumstances warrant and are duly justified on record. Any application for such approval shall be accompanied by a detailed assessment of the increased costs incurred. The Registrar may require further documentation to substantiate the Tribunal’s findings. Fees collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. Where an arbitration agreement specifies fees different from those prescribed in the schedule, the agreement shall prevail, subject to judicial review as provided herein.

A generating station license granted under this Act may be revoked if the licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions stipulated therein, or contravenes any provision of this Act or regulations made thereunder. Such revocation shall occur where the licensee has persistently failed to maintain adequate operational safety standards as determined by inspections conducted by the Central Electricity Authority, or where the generating station’s output consistently falls below the guaranteed level specified in the license agreement for a period exceeding six months. Further, grounds of revocation include demonstrable evidence that the licensee has engaged in fraudulent practices concerning energy accounting or has wilfully obstructed investigations undertaken by authorized officers. The State Commission shall provide an opportunity to be heard prior to any order of revocation being issued.

Where an appeal lies against an order passed by a Public Information Officer, the Central or State Information Commission shall designate an adjudicating officer for hearing the appeal. The adjudicating officer shall exercise all powers necessary for conducting hearings, including the power to summon witnesses and examine documents relevant to the dispute. An aggrieved party may present evidence in support of their claim before the adjudicating officer, subject to rules of procedure determined by the Information Commission. The adjudicating officer shall provide each party with a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to submit written arguments under this Act. Decisions regarding procedural matters are at the discretion of the adjudicating officer. Any order passed by the adjudicating officer is appealable before the Central or State Information Commission, provided that such appeals are filed within thirty days from the date of receipt of the order.

Where a mining concession is granted pursuant to an agreement containing an arbitration clause, the conditions of licence stipulated therein shall be deemed incorporated into the terms of the arbitration agreement itself. Any dispute arising from a breach of these conditions, or relating to their interpretation, shall be subject to resolution through arbitration as provided herein. The arbitrator shall have the power to award damages for loss suffered by either party due to non-compliance with the stated conditions, including but not limited to remediation costs and lost profits. Further, failure by the licensee to adhere to specified environmental safeguards detailed within the licence conditions shall constitute a material breach of the underlying agreement, entitling the grantor to seek injunctive relief under this Act. The arbitrator may also order specific performance to compel compliance with any condition deemed essential for the proper operation of the mine.

Registration of Renewable Energy Certificates – Disclosure Requirements Every generator seeking registration for the issuance of Renewable Energy Certificates under this Act shall submit a detailed project report alongside the application form. This report must include, but is not limited to, information pertaining to land acquisition, environmental clearances obtained, and projected energy generation capacity. Furthermore, any material change in these particulars occurring after initial submission requires immediate notification to the registering authority through an addendum filed within thirty days of such alteration. Failure to adhere to this requirement constitutes a breach of registration terms. The duty of disclosure extends to all financial arrangements impacting project viability; details thereof must be clearly outlined. False or misleading information provided during registration renders the certificate invalid, subject to penalties as prescribed herein.

Where a dispute arises concerning the enforceability of a contract entered into under this Act, and either party seeks immediate resolution without prejudice to subsequent remedies, the court may, at its discretion, adopt a summary procedure for determination. This procedure shall apply only if both parties consent in writing prior to commencement of proceedings or if the value of the subject matter of the dispute does not exceed ten thousand rupees. The court shall provide reasonable opportunity for each party to present evidence and arguments relevant to the disputed terms. Any order made under this summary procedure is binding, provided that it complies with principles of natural justice and fairness as understood in law. Further proceedings may be instituted notwithstanding any such order, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where a party seeks to establish a fact relating to a contract or agreement, the burden of proof shall lie upon that party unless it is provided by law or these rules that the onus lies elsewhere. Provided that, where the existence of a particular circumstance is alleged by one party as rendering a contract voidable, the burden shall be on such party to prove the existence of that circumstance and its material effect on the validity of the agreement. Furthermore, if a defendant asserts an affirmative defence requiring proof of a specific event or action, the burden of proving that event or action shall rest upon the defendant; subject to any exceptions prescribed under this Act relating to presumptions. Any party failing to satisfy the requisite evidentiary standard as provided herein shall be deemed not to have established the fact in question.

Where a construction contract incorporates provisions relating to a security deposit furnished by the contractor to the procuring entity, the amount so retained shall be deemed an arbitration matter for the purposes of resolving disputes arising from the contract. The disbursal of such security deposit shall be subject to verification by an independent engineer appointed under this Act, whose report shall detail any deficiencies in work performed or outstanding liabilities owed by the contractor. Any claim made by the procuring entity against the security deposit must be accompanied by detailed documentation substantiating the alleged breach and the quantification of damages incurred. The arbitrator may require production of such documents and may conduct site inspections as deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the claim. Failure to provide adequate evidence supporting a claim shall result in its rejection, and costs associated with the arbitration shall be borne by the claimant. A dispute concerning the application of a security deposit is final once an award has been made under this Act.

Every undertaking registered under this Act shall maintain a register of undertakings in the prescribed form, detailing all transactions affecting its assets or liabilities, including but not limited to transfers of ownership, encumbrances, and changes in management. Failure to do so shall render the responsible officer liable for a penalty as determined by the adjudicating authority. The register must be produced for inspection upon demand by an investigating officer authorized under this Act. Any person found to have knowingly falsified or concealed entries within the register of undertakings shall face imprisonment extending to seven years and a fine, subject to appeal before the appellate tribunal. Tampering with the register constitutes a cognizable offence under this Act.

Every industrial unit engaged in the processing of hazardous materials shall submit a statutory declaration annually to the State Pollution Control Board, confirming compliance with effluent discharge standards as provided under this Act. This declaration must detail the types and quantities of pollutants released, alongside measures implemented for waste minimization and pollution prevention. Failure to furnish the statutory declaration within the prescribed timeframe will render the unit liable for penalties as determined by the Board. The Board may conduct inspections at any time to verify the accuracy of information contained in the declaration. Any discrepancy found during inspection shall necessitate immediate corrective action and subsequent resubmission of the statutory declaration, duly certified by a chartered environmental auditor.

The licensing of commercial vehicle operators shall be subject to conditions as provided herein, concerning the assignment of operational territories and associated permits. An operator seeking to assign a portion of their licensed territory or any attached permit relating to goods transport must apply to the appointed authority for prior approval. Such application shall detail the proposed assignee’s qualifications, including experience in similar operations and financial stability. The appointed authority may grant permission only if satisfied that the assignment will not compromise public safety or disrupt established transportation networks. Further, any assignment is conditional upon the continued adherence of both the original operator and the assignee to all regulations under this Act. Failure to comply with these conditions renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the appointed authority.

Where a gratuity becomes payable to any legal heir or nominee of a deceased employee, the employer shall issue a notice of demand specifying the amount due and the mode of payment, within thirty days from the date of death. Such notice may be served by registered post with acknowledgement due to the address provided by the claimant or, failing that, at the last known place of residence of the deceased employee. The right to receive gratuity under this Act is deemed property and may be assigned by a written agreement executed prior to the occurrence of any event triggering its payment; however, such assignment shall only permit the transfer of the right to receive payments as stipulated in the agreement. Any subsequent alteration or modification to the terms of an assignment requires consent from both assignor and assignee and must be registered with the designated Gratuity Authority.

The Central Pollution Control Board shall, upon granting approval for any industrial project involving ecologically sensitive areas, require submission of a security deposit from the project proponent. This security deposit shall be calculated based on the potential environmental impact assessment and may be adjusted against remediation costs incurred by the Board in the event of non-compliance with stipulated conditions under this Act. Disputes regarding the amount or application of such security deposit are subject to appeal before the jurisdictional Environment Appellate Authority, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the initial determination. The authority shall consider evidence presented by both the proponent and the Board and may order adjustments to the deposit as deemed appropriate, with reasons recorded in writing.

Where an offence involving a breach of contract or other civil wrong has been committed, the offender shall, upon application made by him to the Arbitral Tribunal, be permitted to apply for compounding of offences with the aggrieved party. Such application must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the circumstances giving rise to the offence and detailing any proposed restitution or compensation offered to the injured party. The Arbitral Tribunal may, after affording both parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, direct that the offender make such payment or do such other act as it deems fit to compensate the aggrieved party for the loss suffered. Provided that the amount determined under this process shall be subject to judicial review by an appropriate court on petition filed within thirty days of the order. The Tribunal shall record its reasons for allowing or refusing the application for compounding of offences in writing.

Every registered consumer dispute resolution agency shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to all complaints received, proceedings conducted, and orders passed, for a period not less than eight years from the date of their final disposition. Such records shall include, but are not limited to, copies of complaint applications, written statements, rejoinders, evidence submitted by parties, minutes of hearings, and reasoned judgments or orders. The Central Authority may prescribe the form and manner in which these records are maintained, including provisions for electronic storage and retrieval, ensuring accessibility for authorized personnel only. Failure to maintain adequate records as provided herein shall be deemed a violation under this Act, attracting penalties as determined by the competent authority. All officers entrusted with maintaining such records shall undergo periodic training on record management practices. The maintenance of records is crucial for transparency and accountability in consumer redressal mechanisms.

Where any establishment seeks to obtain or renew a licence under this Act for the purpose of determining eligibility for gratuity payments, the licensing authority shall be satisfied that the establishment maintains adequate records pertaining to employees’ length of service and salary drawn, in accordance with regulations framed by the Central Government. Failure to demonstrate such compliance may result in refusal or revocation of the licence. An appeal lies to the Labour Court against any decision regarding the conditions of licence, including but not limited to assessments of record-keeping adequacy. Such appeals shall be filed within thirty days from the date of communication of the order and are subject to judicial review on grounds of perversity or demonstrable error in the application of principles under this Act.

Every vehicle registered under this Act shall display a registration certificate prominently affixed to its windscreen, conforming precisely to the format detailed in Schedule A appended hereto. The particulars recorded therein shall include, but not be limited to, the make and model of the vehicle, the chassis number, the engine number, the name and address of the registered owner, and the class of vehicle as determined under this Act. Any alteration to the prescribed particulars without prior authorization from the Regional Transport Authority renders the registration certificate invalid. Provided that, a change in ownership shall necessitate an endorsement on the existing certificate reflecting the new owner’s details; failure to comply will result in penalties as provided herein. The authority may, at any time, require submission of original documents for verification of prescribed particulars.

The authorization to operate a commercial vehicle as defined under this Act shall remain subject to the terms of settlement agreed upon between the vehicle owner and any third-party insurance provider engaged for comprehensive coverage. Such settlements may include, but are not limited to, stipulations regarding assignment of claim recovery rights pertaining to accidents involving damage to property or injury to persons. The owner shall be deemed to have irrevocably assigned all rights arising from such terms of settlement to the insurer upon commencement of commercial operation, provided that a written acknowledgment is retained by the vehicle owner as evidence of this assignment. Any subsequent alteration or modification to these terms requires mutual consent and must be formally documented with both parties involved; failure to do so renders the amendment unenforceable. The State Government may prescribe guidelines for standardizing such agreements to ensure transparency and fairness in claim resolution processes.

The Regional Transport Authority may, subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, grant a learner's licence to any person who applies in the prescribed form and satisfies the authority that he possesses the qualifications specified herein. A driving licence shall not be issued unless the applicant has held a learner’s licence for at least one month and successfully completed the practical tests as determined by the Authority. The conditions of licence include, but are not limited to, maintaining good health and fitness, adhering to traffic regulations, and ensuring that the vehicle operated is properly insured. Any alteration in the particulars furnished during application or any subsequent violation of these conditions may render the driving licence liable for suspension or revocation. Furthermore, a licence holder may assign operating rights pertaining to commercial vehicles to another individual with prior authorization from the Authority, provided that such assignment does not compromise road safety.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appointed authority” means an officer designated by the Central Government, State Government or District Authority, as applicable, to exercise powers and discharge duties relating to the redressal of consumer disputes. The appointed authority shall possess qualifications prescribed in regulations framed under this Act, including experience in law, economics, or consumer affairs. An appointed authority may be assisted by such staff as the relevant government deems necessary. Decisions made by an appointed authority are subject to appeal as provided herein and shall be binding on the parties involved unless modified by a higher appellate forum.

The Central Licensing Authority may, upon application from a food business operator holding a State-level license under this Act, grant a multi-State license authorizing operation across multiple states, provided that the applicant demonstrates adherence to hygiene and safety protocols as specified by the competent authority. Any existing licenses granted prior to the commencement of these provisions shall remain valid until their expiry date; however, renewal applications must be submitted with updated operational details reflecting any changes in processing units or distribution networks. The Authority may assign portions of a multi-State license to authorized distributors, subject to conditions regarding quality control and traceability. Failure to comply with assigned responsibilities by a distributor shall render the primary licensee liable for penalties as provided herein. Recovery of dues owed to the Central Government under this Act pertaining to licensing fees or penalties shall be pursued through established debt recovery mechanisms.

Where any dispute arises concerning the reasonableness or necessity of the exercise of power of entry by an officer authorized under this Act, either party may file an objection before the Controlling Authority within thirty days from the date of the alleged intrusion. The Controlling Authority shall consider all submitted evidence and hear representations from both the employer and the employee, affording each a fair opportunity to present their case. Any order passed by the Controlling Authority regarding such disputes is appealable to the Labour Court within sixty days thereafter. Provided that the Labour Court shall only entertain appeals based on demonstrable errors of law or fact appearing on the face of the record; fresh evidence may not be adduced unless specifically permitted under rules framed for this purpose.

Where an investigating officer is required or authorised under this Act to enter upon or into any premises for the purpose of searching for any document or thing, or for collecting evidence, he shall produce for inspection a copy of the warrant or order authorising such entry, and proceed no further unless that warrant or order expressly authorises otherwise. The occupier of the premises, or any person authorised by him to act on his behalf, shall be called upon to permit such entry. Failure to comply with this provision does not invalidate subsequent actions taken under this Act. The investigating officer may use reasonable force to effect entry if necessary, provided that such force is proportionate to the resistance encountered and in accordance with established procedures. Any person obstructing a lawful exercise of power of entry shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable as prescribed herein. The investigating officer shall prepare a detailed inventory of all documents and things seized during the search, which shall be signed by himself and at least one independent witness present at the time.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appointed authority” means an officer designated by the State Government, generally not below the rank of Labour Commissioner, to exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred or imposed upon him under this Act. The designation shall be published in the Official Gazette. An appointed authority may be empowered to inquire into any matter relating to the payment of gratuity and to determine disputes arising between an employer and an employee concerning eligibility for gratuity, amount payable, or other matters as provided herein. Every such authority shall act according to the principles of natural justice.

For the purposes of this Act, "manner of service" with respect to goods or services includes, but is not limited to, the speed of delivery, the method of providing access to digital content, the responsiveness of customer support channels, and the clarity and accuracy of information provided during the transaction. The manner of service shall be assessed having regard to prevailing industry standards and practices, as well as the reasonable expectations of consumers in relation to the nature of the goods or services offered. Nothing herein shall require a supplier to provide a level of service that is technically unfeasible or commercially unreasonable, provided that such limitations are clearly disclosed to the consumer prior to the transaction.

Where any food business operator is charged with contravention of prescribed standards of quality or safety under this Act, the burden of proof shall lie upon the prosecuting officer to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that such contravention has occurred. Provided that, if the accused food business operator presents evidence suggesting compliance with applicable regulations, the onus shifts to the prosecuting officer to rebut such evidence. Any appeal against a determination made by an adjudicating officer regarding alleged violations may be filed within sixty days of the order’s communication; however, any delay in filing shall be condoned only where sufficient cause is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the appellate authority. The appellate authority may require further investigation or analysis as deemed necessary for just resolution.

Any party to an arbitration agreement may apply to the Arbitral Tribunal for access to an inspection report pertaining to immovable property relevant to the dispute, subject to demonstrating that the information contained therein is material to the resolution of the issues before the Tribunal and that reasonable efforts to obtain the report through other means have failed. The Tribunal shall consider such applications within fifteen days and may grant or deny access based on a balancing of the interests of all parties involved, provided that confidentiality obligations previously undertaken concerning the inspection report are duly respected. Failure by any person to produce an inspection report when ordered by the Arbitral Tribunal constitutes contempt under this Act and is punishable with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt.

The Central Information Commission shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, determine its own procedure for carrying out its functions. Where an authority is empowered under this Act to delegate any power or duty, such delegation shall only be to a subordinate officer within the same department. Delegation of powers does not extend to the transfer of responsibility for ensuring compliance with the obligations imposed upon the original authority as provided herein. Any function delegated may be resumed by the delegating authority at any time and from time to time. The exercise of power under this Act shall not, however, preclude the Central Information Commission from issuing directions to improve public information dissemination practices.

The licensing of intellectual property rights arising from contracts entered into under this Act shall be subject to prior written consent from the adjudicating officer appointed for the purpose. Such consent will not be withheld if the proposed licensee possesses demonstrable expertise in the relevant field and undertakes to maintain standards consistent with prevailing industry best practices. Assignment of a contract, or any right pertaining thereto, including but not limited to rights relating to confidential information exchanged during negotiations, requires notification to the adjudicating officer at least thirty days prior to the effective date of assignment. The adjudicating officer may impose reasonable conditions on such assignments to safeguard the interests of all parties involved and ensure compliance with obligations under this Act. Failure to obtain requisite consent or provide timely notification shall render the contract voidable at the option of an aggrieved party.

Where any Public Information Officer fails to provide information in accordance with the provisions under this Act, or provides information which is incomplete, misleading, or false, an aggrieved person may file a complaint before the designated Grievance Redressal Officer. The Grievance Redressal Officer shall conduct inquiry into such complaints expeditiously and shall afford both the complainant and the Public Information Officer opportunity for hearing. Decisions of the Grievance Redressal Officer are subject to appeal under this Act, and appeals shall be processed through a summary procedure designed to ensure prompt resolution. Provided that any order made by the Grievance Redressal Officer may be challenged before the Central Information Commission if deemed manifestly unjust or in violation of principles of natural justice.

Where an Inspector is satisfied that a gratuity has not been paid within the time limit stipulated under this Act, or that any other contravention of its provisions has occurred, he may exercise his power of entry into the premises of the employer for the purpose of ascertaining whether the requirements of this Act have been complied with. Such entry shall be exercised only after due notice, in writing, is given to the employer, specifying the time and date intended for inspection and the reasons for such proposed entry. Provided that where the Inspector has reasonable cause to believe that evidence relating to an offence under this Act is being destroyed or concealed, he may enter without prior notice. The employer shall provide all necessary assistance to the Inspector during his investigation, failing which penalties as provided herein may be imposed.

Registration of Generating Stations shall be undertaken upon submission of a detailed project report, including but not limited to land acquisition documents, environmental clearances, and grid connectivity agreements, to the appropriate State Electricity Regulatory Commission. The Commission may, after due consideration of the submitted documentation and any supplementary information sought, register the generating station subject to compliance with technical standards as provided herein. Any dispute concerning registration shall be referred to a competent officer appointed by the Central Government for resolution. Further, an annual declaration regarding operational status and power generation figures must be filed under this Act. Failure to file such declarations may result in penalties as determined by the Commission. A designated competent officer will verify these filings against actual grid dispatch data.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to provide information within the time specified under this Act, or provides incomplete or inaccurate information, the complainant shall have recourse to file an appeal before the appellate authority as provided herein. The appellate authority may, after affording the Public Information Officer an opportunity of being heard, direct him to rectify the deficiencies and furnish the complete and correct information within a further period not exceeding thirty days. Failure by the Public Information Officer to comply with such direction shall render him liable for penalty under this Act. Further, the manner of service of notices and orders issued under this Act shall be deemed sufficient if sent through registered post with acknowledgment due or delivered personally. Any complainant aggrieved by the manner of service may petition the Central Information Commission for redressal.

For the purposes of this Act, a “certificate of registration” means a document issued by the registering authority in the form specified in Schedule A, confirming that an arbitration agreement or a list of arbitrators has been registered with that authority. Such certificate shall contain particulars as may be prescribed and shall be deemed prima facie evidence of the date on which the application for registration was received, subject to any proof tendered to the contrary. An applicant shall receive the certificate of registration within the time stipulated under this Act, provided that the required fees have been duly paid. The registering authority may refuse to issue a certificate of registration if the application is incomplete or does not comply with requirements as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘public authority’ includes any body owned, controlled or substantially financed by the appropriate government; provided that an entity which is managed by board of directors where fifty percent or more members of such Board are in office by election shall not be considered a public authority. The time within which an information request may be filed under this Act shall ordinarily be deemed to commence from the date the citizen becomes aware of the existence of the relevant record, subject to justifiable reasons for delay duly recorded and accepted by the Public Information Officer. Any action taken beyond the prescribed period of limitation may be challenged before a designated appellate authority.

Where an information provider is required to furnish information under this Act, the burden of proof regarding whether such information was furnished within the stipulated time period shall lie upon the information provider. For the purposes of establishing non-furnishing, documentary evidence including but not limited to postal receipts, electronic mail confirmations, and server logs may be presented by the complainant. The Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, as provided herein, may consider such evidence along with any oral testimony offered by either party. Nothing in this provision shall prevent a complainant from presenting direct evidence of non-receipt of information.

Any person entering into an agreement in violation of the restrictions imposed under this Act relating to price controls shall be deemed to have committed an offence cognizable by a police officer. Upon discovery of such violation, the competent officer empowered under these regulations may immediately seize all relevant documentation pertaining to the transaction and freeze assets connected thereto. Failure to comply with directions issued by the competent officer regarding the restitution of affected parties shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. Further, any party found deliberately obstructing investigations conducted by a competent officer is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or until such obstruction ceases, whichever is shorter.

Where service of any document relating to arbitral proceedings is required under this Act or in pursuance of an arbitration agreement, such service shall be effected by personal delivery or by sending the document by registered post with acknowledgment due. Provided that, if the party to be served fails to acknowledge receipt of the document sent by registered post within seven days from the date of dispatch, it shall be presumed that the document was not received and the sender may petition the arbitral tribunal for directions regarding alternative manner of service. The arbitral tribunal shall then determine a suitable method, which determination is subject to appeal to the High Court on grounds of manifest error or procedural unfairness.

Licenses granted for intra-State transmission of electricity, whether relating to infrastructure or services, are assignable subject to prior written consent from the concerned State Commission and approval from the Appellate Tribunal. Such consent shall not be withheld if the proposed assignee possesses equivalent technical expertise and financial stability as the original licensee, as determined by the Commission. The transferor shall provide a detailed inventory of assets and liabilities associated with the license to both the Commission and the transferee. Any condition imposed on a license under this Act may be transferred along with the license itself, provided that such conditions are clearly stated in the assignment agreement. The Appellate Tribunal may entertain appeals against orders passed by the State Commission refusing consent for assignment, adhering to procedures as provided herein.

Where a consumer has suffered loss or injury due to a deficiency in goods or services provided by an undertaking, the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission shall, upon receiving a complaint, initiate proceedings for recovery of dues owed to the complainant. The Commission may require the undertaking to produce documents and records relevant to the assessment of damages. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the State Commission within sixty days from the date of such order. The State Commission shall consider any objections raised during appellate proceedings regarding the calculation or validity of the recovery amount. Further, the Recovery Officer appointed by the appropriate authority shall be responsible for implementing orders relating to recovery of dues and shall follow procedures as prescribed in the relevant rules. Subject to appeal, all orders concerning recovery are final.

Where a distribution licensee fails to provide electricity service within a reasonable period from the date of application by a consumer, or where the quality of supply falls below established standards, the aggrieved consumer may file a complaint with the appropriate State Electricity Regulatory Commission. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Commission shall investigate and determine whether the licensee has violated its obligations under this Act. If, after investigation, the Commission finds that a violation occurred, it may direct the licensee to compensate the affected consumers for losses incurred due to the deficient service. The licensee shall submit a statutory declaration within thirty days of receiving such direction, detailing the steps taken to rectify the deficiency and prevent future occurrences. Failure to comply with this requirement will attract penalties as provided herein.

Applications for registration of premises where environmental offences have occurred shall be submitted to the Regional Officer within thirty days of notification of the intended compounding amount under this Act. Such applications must detail the nature of the offence, remedial measures undertaken by the offender, and a plan for preventing recurrence. The Regional Officer may require additional documentation verifying compliance with prescribed standards or mitigation strategies. Where an application is received, the Regional Officer shall verify its contents against records maintained by the State Pollution Control Board. Upon satisfactory verification and payment of the prescribed fee, the premises shall be registered in the designated register maintained under this Act, subject to periodic inspections as provided herein. The compounding of offences does not preclude further legal action under any other law for the time being in force.

An arbitration tribunal shall have the power to order a party to produce documents relevant to the dispute for inspection by the other parties and the tribunal itself. Such an order shall only be made after consideration of any objection raised by the concerned party regarding confidentiality or privilege, and following an opportunity afforded to that party to present arguments against disclosure. The tribunal may direct that specific portions of any document are redacted prior to inspection, subject to ensuring that the essence of the information remains accessible for assessment. Where a dispute arises concerning the scope or validity of an inspection report generated pursuant to such an order, the tribunal shall resolve it in accordance with principles of natural justice and fairness. The production of documents under this Act does not constitute a waiver of any other legal right or remedy available to either party.

Registration of land-use change proposals involving ecologically sensitive areas shall be undertaken through a designated online portal maintained by the Central Pollution Control Board. Applications for registration must include detailed environmental impact assessments and mitigation plans conforming to guidelines issued under this Act, along with proof of public consultation as mandated. The prescribed fee for registration is non-refundable, irrespective of whether the proposal is subsequently approved or rejected. A person aggrieved by a rejection may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of such rejection. This period of limitation shall be strictly adhered to and no appeals received beyond this timeframe will be entertained. Further, any alteration to registered proposals requires fresh registration, subject to similar conditions as originally applied.

Where an employee seeks recovery of gratuity from an employer, and disputes arise regarding eligibility or amount payable, the Controlling Authority shall adopt a summary procedure for resolution. The application shall be accompanied by requisite documents as prescribed under this Act, and notice thereof shall be served upon the employer within thirty days of receipt. The employer shall then have fifteen days to submit its response in writing. Failure to respond within that period shall be deemed acceptance of the employee’s claim. Oral hearings may be conducted at the discretion of the Authority, but are not mandatory. Decisions regarding entitlement and calculation shall be based solely on documentary evidence presented and relevant provisions herein. The Authority is empowered to direct payment of gratuity along with interest as it deems appropriate. Appeals against orders passed under this Act lie before a higher appellate authority within sixty days.

Registration of Power Purchase Agreements relating to Renewable Energy Sources shall be undertaken within thirty days from the date of execution by all distribution licensees and generating companies engaged in procurement of electricity through power purchase agreements. The Registrar shall maintain a register containing details of each agreement, including but not limited to the parties involved, tariff structure, duration, and projected energy output. Any objection to the registration may be submitted to the Registrar within fifteen days from the date of public notice of the proposed registration. Such objections shall be considered by the Registrar, who may require further documentation or clarification as deemed necessary. The period of limitation for challenging the validity of a registered power purchase agreement under this Act shall be two years from the date of registration.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed particulars” with respect to information held by a public authority shall include, but not be limited to, the date of creation of the record, the format in which it is stored, the medium on which it is recorded, and any indexing or classification system employed for its retrieval. The term "prescribed particulars" also encompasses details relating to the custodianship of such records, including names and designations of officers responsible for their maintenance. These particulars shall be provided alongside information disclosed under this Act, as may be deemed necessary by the Central Information Commission. Further, any amendment or modification to these prescribed particulars shall be documented and accessible.

Where any individual or entity alleges that activities undertaken by another party are in violation of standards prescribed under this Act concerning air quality, water resources, or waste management, they may file a complaint with the adjudicating officer appointed for the relevant jurisdiction. The adjudicating officer shall provide all parties an opportunity to present evidence and arguments pertaining to the alleged infraction. Any order issued by the adjudicating officer determining liability or prescribing remedial action may be appealed within sixty days of its publication to the State Environment Appellate Authority, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Provided that the appellate authority shall not entertain appeals where the complainant has failed to demonstrate demonstrable prejudice arising from the actions under scrutiny.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appellate tribunal” means a body established under notification by the Central Government for hearing appeals arising from orders passed by Controlling Authorities constituted under this Act. The appellate tribunal shall consist of a judicial member and a technical member, both possessing expertise in industrial relations or labour law matters. Decisions of the appellate tribunal shall be final subject to further appeal only to the Supreme Court on a point of law. An order establishing an appellate tribunal shall specify its jurisdiction, powers, and procedures as provided herein. The Central Government may issue guidelines for the conduct of proceedings before the appellate tribunal.

Where a motor vehicle causes injury or death, the owner of the vehicle shall, within thirty days from the date of the incident, serve upon the injured party or their legal representative a written notice of demand specifying the amount claimed in respect of damages, medical expenses, and loss of earnings. Such notice shall be served by registered post with acknowledgment due to the address specified by the claimant or ascertainable through public records. The notice of demand may include supporting documentation substantiating the claim; provided that failure to provide such documentation does not preclude subsequent presentation of evidence under this Act. Any dispute regarding the reasonableness of the amount claimed, as detailed in the notice of demand, shall be subject to resolution by a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal constituted under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “information” includes any material in any form, whether recorded or reproduced or transmitted, including but not limited to records, documents, memos, reports, e-mails, contracts, and data stored electronically; and for clarity, information shall encompass both publicly available materials and those held by public authorities. The duty of disclosure imposed under this Act requires a public authority to proactively disseminate information relating to its functions and operations unless such dissemination would constitute a denial of access permissible as provided herein. This obligation extends to ensuring that information is presented in an accessible format, subject to reasonable limitations regarding resource availability.

Every distribution licensee shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to electricity generated, transmitted, distributed, and supplied under this Act, including but not limited to metering data, consumer connection details, fault reports, and payment histories. Such records shall be preserved electronically or in durable physical form for a minimum period of ten years from the date of creation, subject to audit by the State Commission. A licensee may assign the right to access and utilize anonymized data derived from these records to third-party entities engaged in energy research or grid optimization projects, provided that such assignment is approved by the Commission and includes contractual safeguards ensuring confidentiality and preventing misuse. The maintenance of records shall be deemed a fundamental obligation under this Act, and any failure to comply may result in penalties as determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission.

Where a dispute is resolved by means of terms of settlement executed between parties, such terms shall be admissible as evidence only if they are accompanied by an affidavit verifying their voluntary nature and understanding by each party involved. The Court may require further clarification or additional documentation to ascertain the genuineness of consent, particularly where one party is significantly disadvantaged in bargaining power. Any alteration made to the original document after its execution shall render it inadmissible unless such alteration is initialed by all parties and accompanied by a similar affidavit confirming their continued agreement to the amended terms. The Court may disregard any term within the settlement if it finds that it contravenes public policy or existing legislation, provided that evidence substantiating this contention is presented under this Act.

Where a tenant fails to vacate premises upon expiry of a lease agreement, or breaches any material term thereof, the landlord shall be entitled to retain so much of the security deposit as is reasonably necessary to cover outstanding rent, damages to the property beyond fair wear and tear, and costs incurred in recovering possession. The amount retained shall not exceed the total sum initially paid as security deposit, provided that a detailed account of such deductions, along with supporting documentation including repair invoices and legal fee statements, must be furnished to the tenant within thirty days of vacation. Any dispute regarding the reasonableness of the landlord’s retention under this Act may be referred to an arbitrator appointed by mutual consent or, failing agreement, by the District Magistrate. The tenant shall have recourse to civil remedies as provided herein should the landlord fail to provide a proper accounting.

Where a dispute arises under this Act concerning goods or services provided by an enterprise, either party may propose a terms of settlement to resolve the matter amicably. Such proposal shall clearly outline the concessions offered by each party, including but not limited to refunds, replacements, repairs, and compensation for damages suffered. The Central Authority may facilitate negotiations towards reaching such terms of settlement, subject to ensuring fairness and transparency in the process. Any agreement reached as a terms of settlement shall be recorded in writing and signed by both parties, and shall be binding on them under this Act. Failure to adhere to the agreed terms constitutes a violation, actionable as provided herein.

Where gratuity is payable to an employee who has ceased employment or died while in service, the amount thereof shall be determined according to the schedule of fees prescribed by the appropriate Government, which fees are subject to periodic revision as deemed necessary to reflect prevailing economic conditions and ensure equitable compensation. An employer failing to remit gratuity payments within thirty days of becoming due is liable to pay interest at a rate not less than twelve per centum per annum on the outstanding amount until such payment is made. Any employee or nominee aggrieved by an assessment under this Act may, within sixty days from receipt of notification thereof, file an appeal with the Grievance Redressal Authority constituted for this purpose. The authority shall provide opportunity for hearing and pass orders as provided herein, ensuring just and timely redressal.

Where a party to an agreement fails to perform his obligations as agreed, and a claim for recovery of dues arises therefrom, any creditor seeking redressal shall first file a written complaint with the jurisdictional Revenue Officer, detailing the nature of the breach, the amount due, and supporting documentation. The Revenue Officer shall serve notice upon the debtor within seven days of receipt of the complaint, affording him an opportunity to submit his response or counter-claim within fourteen days thereafter. Upon consideration of both submissions, the Revenue Officer may conduct a preliminary assessment and issue an order directing payment of the dues as determined by him.
