Any party aggrieved by such order may appeal to the Assistant Collector within thirty days, who shall review the matter de novo. The Assistant Collector’s decision shall be final subject to further appeal only to the District Magistrate under this Act.

Where an arbitration agreement is challenged under this Act on the ground that it is invalid or unenforceable, a party seeking to restrain enforcement of the agreement shall apply to the designated judicial authority within ninety days from the date the challenge arises; provided that the authority may entertain an application made after the expiration of said period if it is satisfied that the delay was caused by sufficient reason. The judicial authority shall not entertain any such application if, following the expiry of a further thirty days from the date of presentation of the application, arbitral proceedings have been duly commenced under this Act. Any order passed by the judicial authority regarding the validity or enforceability of an arbitration agreement shall be final subject to appeal within sixty days as provided herein; and the period of limitation for any claim arising out of the underlying dispute remains unaffected.

Where a gratuity has become payable to any employee as determined under this Act, and where the employer has failed to remit said gratuity within the stipulated period, the aggrieved employee or their nominee may pursue remedies available through civil courts. However, an agreement for the compounding of offences relating to delayed payment of gratuity shall be permissible only with prior written consent from the Labour Commissioner having jurisdiction over the establishment concerned. Such agreements must specify a revised date of remittance and include provisions for compensatory interest as deemed appropriate by the said Labour Commissioner. The right to enter into such an arrangement is assignable, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, ensuring equitable treatment of employees and upholding principles of industrial harmony. Any assignment shall require registration with the designated authority.

Where an arbitration agreement is silent regarding the appointment of an arbitrator or the method of appointing him, the Court shall, upon application by a party to the dispute, appoint an authority for the purpose of facilitating the selection process. Such appointed authority shall first endeavour to achieve consensus between the parties on the identity of the arbitrator. If consensus cannot be reached within thirty days from the date of the application, the appointed authority shall prepare a panel of three qualified individuals and submit it to the Court. The Court shall then, by order, select one individual from this panel to act as the sole arbitrator for the dispute. Any communication regarding the selection process between the parties and the appointed authority shall be in writing and maintained as part of the record under this Act. The appointed authority is obligated to provide a written report detailing the steps taken towards appointment to the Court within fifteen days of submission of the panel.

Where a contract for the assignment of rights arising from a performance bond contains provisions relating to intellectual property developed during the course of that performance, the assignor may grant licenses ancillary to the assigned rights subject to conditions specified within the original contractual agreement. Such licenses shall not extend beyond the scope of the work contemplated under this Act and must clearly delineate the permitted uses and geographic limitations. The prescribed particulars of any such license granted pursuant to an assignment shall include a detailed description of the intellectual property licensed, the duration of the license, and the royalty rates applicable, if any. Further, any sub-assignment of rights or licenses requires prior written consent from the original obligee, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. The assignor warrants that it possesses full authority to grant these licenses and assignments as provided herein.

An inspection report prepared pursuant to investigations undertaken under this Act shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding before a court or tribunal; provided that the party offering such report shall tender alongside it a certificate from the inspecting officer confirming their identity and detailing the scope of their mandate, failing which the report may be excluded at the discretion of the presiding authority. The opposing party may challenge the validity of the inspection report by demonstrating material irregularities in its preparation or bias on the part of the inspecting officer, and such challenge shall be determined before any other evidence is considered. Any appeal against a finding based upon an inspection report shall be subject to the provisions regarding appellate jurisdiction as provided herein.

Where an actionable claim arises from a breach of contract, the period of limitation for instituting legal proceedings shall be three years from the date the cause of action accrues. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend this period to a maximum of five years where, owing to special circumstances or local conditions, it considers such extension necessary and expedient. Applications for extension beyond the initial three-year period must be submitted to the designated District Court along with supporting documentation demonstrating exceptional hardship. The court shall consider these applications and may grant extensions subject to judicial discretion. Any suit brought after the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation is liable to dismissal, unless it is shown that the delay was caused by factors beyond the plaintiff’s reasonable control and did not prejudice the defendant's rights as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “security deposit” means an amount paid or agreed to be paid by an employee to his employer as security against loss, destruction or damage of goods, materials, records or other property entrusted to the care and control of the employee; provided that such amount shall not exceed fifteen percentum of the average salary earned by the employee in the twelve months preceding the date of such payment. The term “security deposit” includes any sum deducted from the wages of an employee towards reimbursement for losses incurred as a consequence of acts or omissions attributable to him, his negligence or default; and nothing contained herein shall prevent an employer from recovering demonstrable financial loss through due process under this Act.

Every establishment shall maintain a register of gratuity recipients in Form A, accessible for inspection by employees and designated trade union representatives during working hours. The register shall contain particulars including employee name, date of joining, designation, last drawn salary, amount of gratuity payable, and date of disbursement. Failure to accurately record such information constitutes an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding one thousand rupees. An employer who fails to provide this register for inspection upon request from the Controlling Authority is deemed to be in default under this Act. The duty of disclosure extends to providing supporting documentation relating to gratuity calculations when requested by the Assessing Officer, subject to reasonable restrictions regarding confidential business information. Any dispute concerning the accuracy or completeness of the register may be referred to the Grievance Redressal Committee established as provided herein.

An officer appointed under this Act shall be deemed a competent officer only if that officer holds a post of at least Assistant Director or equivalent within the relevant governmental department, and has served continuously in that capacity for a minimum period of three years immediately preceding the date of appointment. Such an appointment shall require prior approval from the Secretary to the Government of India, Department of Legal Affairs, provided that the appointing authority certifies compliance with prescribed training modules relating to forensic analysis and evidence handling. A competent officer may be required to submit periodic reports detailing all examinations conducted and opinions rendered, subject to review by a designated oversight committee as constituted under rules framed for this purpose. Any deviation from established protocols shall render the officer’s findings potentially inadmissible.

The Central Pollution Control Board may grant a certificate of registration to any entity intending to establish or operate a facility handling hazardous materials, subject to compliance with prescribed standards and guidelines. Such certificates shall be valid for a period not exceeding five years and are renewable upon application and demonstration of continued adherence to environmental regulations. A holder of a certificate of registration may assign the benefit of such registration to another entity through an endorsement duly approved by the Board, provided that the assigning entity remains jointly liable for any non-compliance occurring prior to the assignment. Any alteration in the nature or scale of operations at a facility requiring registration shall necessitate obtaining a revised certificate. The Board may revoke a certificate of registration if it finds evidence of wilful negligence causing environmental harm, as provided herein.

The Gratuity Registration Rules provide that every establishment intending to register under this Act shall submit a statutory declaration from an officer authorized by the employer, not below the rank of Director or General Manager, verifying compliance with the provisions relating to gratuity eligibility and payment procedures. This declaration must explicitly state whether the establishment maintains adequate insurance cover for gratuity payments as mandated herein. The registering authority may request additional documentation supporting the declarations made, including details of employee contracts and disbursement records. Failure to provide a true and accurate statutory declaration shall render the registration application liable for rejection, and subsequent attempts at registration will be subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act.

Applications for registration as a food vendor shall be submitted to the designated Food Safety Officer within whose jurisdiction the proposed establishment is located, along with the requisite documentation pertaining to premises layout, equipment inventory, and employee training records. Upon receipt of an application, the Food Safety Officer shall verify the information provided and may conduct on-site inspections to ascertain compliance with applicable hygiene standards. Any discrepancies or non-compliance observed during inspection will be duly recorded and communicated to the applicant for rectification. Following verification and satisfactory resolution of any deficiencies, the Food Safety Officer shall forward the file to the adjudicating officer for final registration approval. The adjudicating officer may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, grant or refuse registration as deemed appropriate under this Act.

An individual seeking registration as an adjudicating officer under this Act shall submit a duly completed Form A to the designated Central Registration Authority, along with supporting documentation establishing eligibility criteria as specified in the First Schedule. The application must include proof of academic qualifications, professional experience relevant to legal or administrative matters, and a declaration affirming adherence to ethical conduct guidelines. Upon receipt, the Central Registration Authority may verify the submitted information through cross-referencing with official records and conducting background checks. Any discrepancies identified during verification shall be communicated to the applicant for clarification or rectification. Successful applicants will receive a Certificate of Registration, valid for a period as determined by the Government, renewable subject to periodic performance evaluations.

Where a party seeks to initiate arbitration proceedings pursuant to an agreement, they shall serve upon the respondent a written notice of demand specifying the nature of the dispute, the relief sought, and the venue proposed for the arbitral seat. Such notice must be served in accordance with the methods prescribed under this Act for service of legal documents. Failure to provide such a notice of demand prior to commencing any court proceedings related to the arbitration agreement shall render those proceedings void ab initio. The respondent may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of the notice of demand, communicate their consent to the proposed arbitral seat or nominate an alternative venue. If the respondent fails to respond within that period, the claimant may proceed as if such consent had been given to the initially specified venue. Provided that any challenge to the validity of the arbitration agreement must be raised within this thirty-day window; otherwise it shall be deemed waived.

Where a consumer forum proposes to conduct an inspection relating to deficiency in service or defect in goods, it shall provide written notice to the business establishment at least seven days prior to the proposed date and time of inspection. Such notice shall specify the nature of the complaint investigated and the scope of the inspection. The business establishment may nominate a representative to be present during the inspection proceedings. Any person obstructing an inspection conducted under this Act, or refusing access to premises as required by the forum, shall be deemed to have violated provisions herein. A comprehensive inspection report documenting observations made, evidence collected, and any statements recorded during the inspection shall be prepared by the consumer forum and maintained in its records.

Every public authority shall provide information relating to any concluded activity under this Act within a period of one hundred eighty days from the date of receipt of the request, provided that the request pertains to matters which have ceased to exist or where the requested record has been destroyed in accordance with the records management policy formulated by the Central Government or State Government as applicable. Where the information relates to ongoing activities, the public authority may extend this period subject to a written explanation being furnished to the applicant within thirty days of receipt of the request. The period of limitation for filing an appeal under this Act shall be governed by regulations framed by the Central Information Commission and is deemed conclusive unless demonstrable prejudice arises from non-compliance.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the enforcement of a contract, or the determination of damages arising from its breach, may appeal to the appellate tribunal constituted as provided herein. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall render the aggrieved party ineligible for relief under this Act. The appellate tribunal may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the original order. Any penalty imposed by the original adjudicating authority shall be subject to review and modification by the appellate tribunal.

The assignment of a commercial vehicle permit, issued under this Act, shall require prior approval from the Regional Transport Authority, provided that the proposed assignee possesses a valid driving license appropriate for the class of vehicle specified on the permit and satisfies all requirements pertaining to fitness and good character as determined by the authority. The burden of proof regarding compliance with these conditions rests upon the assignor, who must submit an affidavit attesting to the accuracy of information furnished concerning the assignee’s qualifications and operational capacity. Failure to disclose material facts or provide false representations shall render the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Regional Transport Authority. Any subsequent transfer of such assigned permit is subject to similar scrutiny and approval processes as provided herein, maintaining the same evidentiary obligations on the assignor.

For the purposes of this Act, a “register of undertakings” means a record maintained by a corporate body or partnership firm detailing all material contracts entered into on its behalf, including but not limited to agreements for sale, lease, service provision, and financing arrangements. Such register shall include particulars relating to each contract, such as the date of execution, parties involved, subject matter, duration, and consideration. The register may be maintained in physical or electronic form, provided that it is accessible to authorized personnel under this Act. Any alteration or deletion made within a register of undertakings must be recorded with appropriate authentication.

Where any occupier fails to comply with directions issued under this Act regarding pollution control measures or remediation of environmental damage, the Central Pollution Control Board may initiate proceedings for assessment of environmental compensation and punitive damages. Any person aggrieved by an order determining such compensation or damages has the right to appeal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Appeals shall be made to the National Environment Appellate Tribunal constituted under this Act. The appellate tribunal shall consider evidence submitted by all parties, including any technical reports presented, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Provided that the appellant must demonstrate a substantial error in the initial assessment.

Where evidence is adduced to establish the existence of a contractual obligation relating to the assignment of rights under any license granted pursuant to a governmental authority’s directive, the burden of proof shall lie upon the party asserting the validity and enforceability of said contract. This provision applies irrespective of whether such assertion arises in proceedings concerning specific performance, damages, or declaratory relief. Provided that the licensee has diligently maintained records pertaining to assignment transactions as required under this Act, any presumption established by those records shall be conclusive against a contrary claim unless rebutted by evidence demonstrating manifest error or fraud. The governmental authority may, by notification published in the Official Gazette, prescribe forms and procedures for maintaining such records. Any assignee seeking to enforce rights acquired through an assignment subject to these provisions must demonstrate proper notification of said assignment to the licensor.

Any environmental clearance granted under this Act may be revoked if it is subsequently determined that the recipient has wilfully misrepresented material facts or suppressed relevant information pertaining to the project’s potential impact on ecologically sensitive areas. Such revocation shall be preceded by a written notice detailing the specific grounds of revocation and affording the recipient an opportunity for a hearing, as provided herein. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated in the environmental clearance, leading to demonstrable harm to the environment, also constitutes sufficient cause for revocation. Upon revocation, all financial incentives or tax benefits previously granted relating to the project shall be immediately forfeited, and the recipient shall be liable for costs incurred by the Central Government in remediation efforts.

Where an employee aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the determination of gratuity payable or eligibility for gratuity, appeals to the appellate tribunal, the appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; provided that the appellate tribunal may entertain an appeal if sufficient cause is shown for such delay. The appellate tribunal shall give notice to both the employer and the employee concerned at least thirty days before any hearing takes place, and opportunity shall be afforded to both parties to present their case and relevant evidence. Decisions made by the appellate tribunal are final subject to further appeals under this Act only on a question of law.

Every registered undertaking providing goods or services shall maintain a register of undertakings accessible for inspection by consumers during specified business hours, subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed. This register shall contain particulars including the name and address of the undertaking, the nature of goods or services offered, details of any complaints received under this Act and their resolution, and information regarding dispute resolution mechanisms available to consumers. Failure to maintain such a register, or hindering access thereto, constitutes an unfair trade practice, rendering the undertaking liable for compensation as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. Consumers aggrieved by deficiencies in goods or services may utilize this register to verify compliance with consumer protection standards and pursue appropriate remedies provided herein.

Where a public authority requires a security deposit from any contractor or vendor undertaking works or providing services under contract, the amount so determined shall be commensurate with the value of the work or service and subject to guidelines issued by the Central Information Commission. Any dispute arising concerning the adequacy of such security deposit, or regarding claims made against it for breach of contractual obligations, may be referred to a Grievance Redressal Officer appointed under this Act. The Public Authority shall provide reasons in writing for rejecting any claim against the security deposit and the contractor or vendor aggrieved by such rejection may appeal to the appellate authority. Provided that the appellate authority’s decision shall be final, subject to judicial review on grounds limited to violation of principles of natural justice.

For the purposes of this Act, a statutory declaration is a written statement made before an authorised officer, affirming facts to be true under penalty of perjury, and presented as evidence in lieu of formal testimony or oath. An authorised officer shall include, but not be limited to, magistrates first class, motor vehicle inspectors appointed under this Act, and any other person specifically designated by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. A statutory declaration shall conform precisely to the prescribed format detailed in Schedule B; deviations from said format render the declaration invalid. Any person making a false statement within a statutory declaration is liable for offences as provided herein.

The Central Pollution Control Board shall maintain a publicly accessible register of Environmental Impact Assessments undertaken for projects requiring environmental clearance under this Act. Any entity holding a license to operate a facility subject to an EIA requirement shall provide the Board with comprehensive data pertaining to emissions, effluents, and waste generation, as determined by the assessment methodology outlined in Schedule III. This duty of disclosure extends to any subsequent assignment or transfer of ownership or operational control of said facility. The assignee is deemed to be bound by all prior disclosures made under this Act. Furthermore, the Board may grant a limited license for third-party access to anonymized data within the register, subject to conditions safeguarding commercial confidentiality and provided that such access does not compromise ongoing enforcement actions.

Where a dispute arises regarding the interpretation or enforceability of an arbitration agreement, either party may apply to the designated Arbitral Tribunal for determination thereof. The Tribunal shall conduct proceedings with due regard to principles of natural justice and fairness. An application made under this provision shall be accompanied by such documentation as the Tribunal deems necessary to understand the nature of the dispute. Where the Tribunal determines that the arbitration agreement is manifestly invalid or incapable of being performed, it shall provide reasons for its determination in writing. Parties aggrieved by a decision regarding validity may seek review before the judicial authority, but only upon demonstrating substantial grounds relating to jurisdiction or procedural fairness. This process shall be subject to a summary procedure designed to expedite resolution and minimize undue delay, as provided herein.

Registration of Food Product Establishments – Statutory Declarations Every proprietor or authorized person operating a food product establishment shall register such establishment with the designated registering officer under this Act. Upon registration, the proprietor shall submit a statutory declaration in Form A, duly notarized, affirming adherence to all applicable hygiene and sanitation protocols as prescribed herein. This declaration must also explicitly state the intended production capacity of the establishment and list all ingredients utilized in food manufacturing processes. The registering officer may require supplementary documentation substantiating claims made within the statutory declaration. Any alteration to the declared production capacity or ingredient list necessitates a fresh statutory declaration, submitted promptly to the registering officer for record. Failure to comply with this provision renders the establishment liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any person found to have tampered with electricity meters, abstracted power illegally, or otherwise violated provisions relating to distribution under this Act shall be liable for penalties as determined by the concerned Distribution Licensee. The quantum of such penalty shall be commensurate with the magnitude of the loss caused to the utility and may include recovery of costs incurred in detection and rectification. Where an offence is committed involving minor irregularities, the offender may apply for compounding of offences with the jurisdictional officer, subject to conditions prescribed herein. Such compounding shall involve payment of a sum determined by the officer, without prejudice to further action under this Act or any other law. Repeated violations will preclude the option of compounding and attract enhanced penalties.

Any generating station failing to submit its annual schedule of fees within thirty days from the close of the financial year shall be liable to pay a late submission fee equivalent to two percent of the assessed charges for that year. The State Electricity Regulatory Commission may, upon receiving a complaint regarding an inaccurate or excessive charge levied under this Act, initiate an inquiry and direct the generating station to rectify the error within sixty days. Failure to comply with such direction shall attract a penalty of ten thousand rupees per day until compliance is achieved. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Commission concerning the schedule of fees may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal as provided herein, subject to a filing fee of five hundred rupees.

Every undertaking subject to mandatory arbitration under this Act shall register itself within thirty days of commencement of operations with the designated Registering Authority constituted by the Central Government. Registration shall involve submission of a certified copy of the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association, or equivalent governing document, along with a declaration confirming adherence to applicable industry standards and dispute resolution protocols. The Register of Undertakings maintained by the authority shall be accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein. Failure to register, or providing false information during registration, shall render the undertaking liable to penalties under this Act. Any modification in the registered details must be reported to the Registering Authority within fourteen days and approved before taking effect.

In claims arising from injury or loss sustained due to motor vehicle accidents, the claimant shall bear the initial burden of proof demonstrating a causal link between the accident and the resultant damage or harm suffered. This obligation includes presenting evidence establishing the date, location, and circumstances surrounding the incident, as well as substantiating the nature and extent of the claimed losses, whether those be in respect of medical expenses, property damage, or personal injury. Provided that the claimant satisfies this preliminary burden, the onus shall shift to the respondent—the vehicle owner or operator—to rebut such evidence or present alternative explanations for the claimant’s suffering. The Tribunal may consider all available documentation and testimony when assessing whether the burden of proof has been discharged by either party, acting fairly and impartially under this Act.

Every food business operator engaged in manufacturing or processing of milk and milk products shall ensure that all premises are constructed and maintained in a manner conforming to hygienic design principles as detailed in Schedule Fourth; provided that any deviation from these standards requires prior written approval obtained from the adjudicating officer, specifying remedial measures. The adjudicating officer may conduct inspections at reasonable intervals to verify compliance with prescribed hygiene protocols. Any food business operator failing to rectify deficiencies identified during inspection within a period of thirty days shall be liable for penalties as determined under this Act. Records pertaining to cleaning and sanitation schedules must be readily accessible for review by authorized officers, including the adjudicating officer.

Any individual seeking authorization under this Act for the operation of a warehousing facility shall submit an application to the appointed authority, detailing the proposed location, infrastructure specifications, and security protocols. The appointed authority may require submission of detailed architectural plans certified by a qualified engineer, alongside an environmental impact assessment report as provided herein. Approval shall be contingent upon compliance with all applicable regulations concerning fire safety and storage capacity limits. Further, the applicant must demonstrate adequate financial solvency through audited accounts for the preceding three years. Any alteration to the approved facility’s design or operational procedures requires prior written consent from the appointed authority, failing which such deviation constitutes a breach of this Act.

The assignment of rights pertaining to contracts entered into for the provision of specialized logistical services shall require prior registration with the Central Registry of Contractual Assignments. Any entity seeking to assign a contract involving the transportation of hazardous materials must first obtain a certificate of registration from the Authority, demonstrating compliance with regulations concerning safety protocols and liability insurance. The Authority may grant or deny such certificates at its discretion, subject to appeal before a designated appellate tribunal. A certificate of registration shall remain valid for a period of five years, renewable upon application and demonstration of continued adherence to applicable standards. No assignment shall be deemed legally effective until the Central Registry confirms that a corresponding certificate of registration has been duly filed.

The assignment of contractual obligations relating to infrastructure projects undertaken pursuant to agreements governed by this Act shall require prior registration with the designated Register of Undertakings maintained by the Central Government. Such registration shall constitute conclusive evidence of the assignor’s consent and vest the assignee with all rights, title, and interest in the assigned undertaking. An application for registration may be submitted jointly by both the assignor and assignee, accompanied by a detailed inventory of assets and liabilities being transferred. The Register of Undertakings shall maintain an updated record accessible to authorized government agencies and prospective investors. Assignment without prior registration is void; however, the Central Government may grant exemptions in exceptional circumstances, provided that such exemptions are published in the Official Gazette. Further, any attempt to assign obligations relating to environmental remediation or community resettlement projects requires explicit approval from relevant regulatory bodies as provided herein.

Where a generating company is granted a licence under this Act, the conditions of that licence shall be subject to review by the State Commission upon application by any distribution licensee or consumer’s association demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from those conditions. Such applications may allege unreasonable restrictions on access to transmission infrastructure or discriminatory tariff structures imposed as part of the licensing agreement. The generating company shall have the right to present its defence and counter-evidence before the Commission. Any order made by the State Commission varying the conditions of licence is subject to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, provided that the aggrieved party files a notice of appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; failure to do so shall preclude further recourse under this Act.

Any person found to have violated provisions relating to the manufacturing, processing, import, export, sale or distribution of any article of food, subject to the conditions hereinafter specified, shall be liable for compounding of offences as provided herein. The adjudicating officer may, where deemed appropriate and considering the nature and gravity of the violation, direct such person to pay a sum not exceeding twice the value of goods involved in the offence, or with an equivalent monetary penalty. Provided that, this power of compounding shall not extend to violations involving public health emergencies or instances of adulteration endangering life. Failure to comply with the order for compounding may result in further prosecution under this Act and imposition of more severe penalties as determined by a court.

Where a contract for the provision of digital content delivery services is entered into, the rights accruing to the service provider under this Act relating to access keys, subscriber data, and network infrastructure shall be deemed assignable subject to prior written consent from the contracting party receiving such services. Such consent may be withheld if the proposed assignee fails to demonstrate compliance with applicable data protection regulations or possesses a history of contract breaches concerning similar digital content delivery agreements. Notice of demand for assignment approval must be served upon the contracting party at least sixty days before the intended effective date, and failure to respond within thirty days shall constitute deemed acceptance. The service provider may, however, unilaterally assign these rights if reasonable attempts to provide notice have been made and acknowledged.

Where a claim is made before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal alleging negligence on the part of a driver resulting in injury or death, the burden of proof shall lie upon the claimant to establish, by documentary evidence and witness testimony, that the accident occurred due to such negligence. The Tribunal may require the claimant to produce records pertaining to vehicle registration, insurance policies, and police investigation reports relevant to the incident. Provided that, if the claimant is unable to adduce sufficient evidence demonstrating a causal link between the driver’s actions and the resultant harm, the claim shall be dismissed. Further, the Tribunal shall consider any counter-evidence presented by the respondent seeking to negate or mitigate the alleged negligence. The adjudicating officer shall meticulously examine all submissions and determine the veracity of claims based on established principles of evidence as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appointed authority” means an officer designated by the Central Government, State Government, or Union Territory Administration, as applicable, to exercise powers and perform duties relating to environmental protection and pollution control. Such designation shall specify the geographical area within which the appointed authority’s jurisdiction extends. An appointed authority may be empowered to issue directions, conduct inspections, collect fees, and initiate legal proceedings under this Act. The functions of an appointed authority are subject to such guidelines as the Central Government may prescribe from time to time. Any officer so designated shall continue in that capacity until relieved by order of the appointing authority.

Service of notices issued under this Act shall be effected in the manner prescribed by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Such notifications shall specify the modes of service permissible, including but not limited to registered post with acknowledgement due, courier service, or personal delivery. Where a notice is sent by registered post, it shall be deemed to have been served on the date indicated as received on the postal acknowledgement card. The Central Government may also prescribe alternative methods for ensuring proof of service, subject to their consistency with principles of natural justice and fairness. Any person aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the manner of service may file a representation before the Appellate Authority established under Section [relevant section]. The Appellate Authority shall consider such representations and pass orders as it deems fit, providing reasons for its decision.

Any Public Information Officer failing to provide information within the time specified under this Act, or providing incomplete or misleading information, shall be liable to pay a compensatory amount as determined by the Central Information Commission, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. This amount may be recovered from the salary of the defaulting officer. The aggrieved person may file an appeal against such determination before the appellate authority established under this Act. Further, any delay in providing information beyond the prescribed period of limitation shall attract additional penalties, calculated at a rate proportionate to the duration of the delay and the severity of the informational deficiency. These penalties are without prejudice to any other action that may be taken under this Act.

Any person failing to maintain an accurate and updated register of undertakings within their jurisdiction, as required under this Act, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for the first instance of non-compliance, and one hundred thousand rupees for subsequent instances. The adjudicating authority may issue directions compelling compliance with the requirements regarding the register of undertakings, and failure to comply with such directions shall attract an additional daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. Any officer found wilfully obstructing or hindering the inspection of a register of undertakings by authorized personnel shall be deemed guilty of an offence and subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months.

Any party failing to comply with the requirements regarding a notice of demand under this Act shall be liable to pay liquidated damages equivalent to two percentum of the claimed amount, recoverable from the defaulting party as part of costs incurred by the aggrieved party in initiating or continuing arbitration proceedings. Provided that such liquidated damages shall not exceed ten thousand rupees unless the arbitral tribunal, after considering the nature of the dispute and the conduct of the parties, determines a higher sum to be just and equitable. Failure to serve a notice of demand within the prescribed time period shall constitute a material breach entitling the other party to seek injunctive relief preventing further action under this Act until compliance is demonstrated.

Where a gratuity has become due to an employee and the employer fails to make payment within thirty days from the date it fell due, or such further period as may be prescribed, the aggrieved employee shall have recourse to civil remedies as provided herein. The recovery of unpaid gratuity shall be deemed a debt owed by the employer to the employee, subject to any orders passed by an adjudicating officer under this Act. Further, where an employer has contravened any provision relating to the payment of gratuity or failure thereof, the adjudicating officer may order compounding of offences in such manner as is just and equitable, considering the nature of the default and its impact on the employee’s right to gratuity. Any amount determined through compounding shall be paid by the employer within a period specified by the adjudicating officer.

Any enterprise engaged in activities listed under Schedule I which causes environmental pollution or degradation shall furnish a security deposit prior to commencement of operations, as determined by the competent authority based on the scale and nature of the proposed activity. This security deposit shall be held in trust by the Board and may be forfeited wholly or partially if the enterprise fails to comply with any condition stipulated under this Act or pollutes the environment beyond permissible limits. The amount so forfeited shall be utilized for remedial measures, including but not limited to restoration of degraded areas and compensation to affected parties. Reimbursement of the security deposit, less any amounts forfeited, may be sought by the enterprise after a period of five years from cessation of operations, subject to satisfactory demonstration of environmental compliance.

Where a party claims performance of an agreement has been prevented by the act or omission of another party, the burden of proof shall lie upon that claiming party to establish the existence of the preventing event and its direct causal link to non-performance. Failure to adequately substantiate this claim through admissible evidence will render the claim untenable under this Act. Any person found to have deliberately fabricated evidence in an attempt to shift such a burden shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or both. The adjudicating authority may, subject to appeal, order costs against any party failing to discharge the requisite burden of proof as provided herein.

Failure to furnish a security deposit, as required under this Act in respect of an arbitral award, shall constitute a civil offence subject to penalties prescribed herein. The adjudicating authority may, upon finding of default, impose a monetary fine not exceeding ten percentum of the awarded sum. Such fine shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Repeated failure to remit installments of the security deposit, or any portion thereof, will render the party liable for an additional penalty equal to fifteen percentum of the outstanding amount. The adjudicating authority may also order attachment of assets belonging to the defaulting party until full compliance is achieved. Recovery proceedings shall be initiated without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act.

Where a party claims performance of a contract based on alleged oral assurances supplementing a written agreement, the burden of proof shall lie entirely upon that party to establish the existence, content, and materiality of such assurances. This obligation extends to demonstrating that the assurances were contemporaneously made with the execution of the written contract or shortly thereafter, and induced the claimant to enter into said contract. Provided that the written agreement contains a clause excluding oral modifications, the burden shall remain on the claimant to demonstrate that such exclusion was not intended to be binding under the circumstances. Failure to satisfy this burden shall constitute conclusive evidence against the claim’s validity, subject to appeal to a higher judicial authority as provided herein.

For the purposes of carrying out inspections or investigations relating to environmental protection, an officer authorized by the Central Government or State Government, as provided herein, shall have the power of entry into any premises. Such authorization shall specify the scope and limitations of the entry. Entry may be effected only during daylight hours unless accompanied by a police officer who is satisfied that such entry is necessary and safe. The officer exercising this power of entry shall produce evidence of their authority upon request. No person shall obstruct or attempt to obstruct an authorized entry, nor shall any person withhold information relevant to the inspection.

For the purposes of this Act, “service” with respect to goods or performance of work undertaken in consideration for payment, shall include delivery of documents, notices, and other communications relating thereto. The manner of service shall be deemed sufficient if such communication is transmitted through registered post with acknowledgement due, or delivered personally by a duly authorized representative to the address specified by the recipient at the time of contract formation. Provided that, where no specific address has been provided, service may be effected by publication in a widely circulated newspaper. The onus of proving deficient manner of service shall lie upon the party alleging such deficiency.

Where a party to an arbitration agreement fails to perform its contractual obligations pertaining to the supply of goods or provision of services, the other party may initiate proceedings under this Act seeking recovery of dues. Such proceedings shall only be entertained if the claimant demonstrates, through documented evidence including but not limited to invoices, delivery receipts and correspondence, that the outstanding amount is directly attributable to the non-performance specified in the agreement. Provided that, any dispute regarding the quantum of such recovery shall first be subject to a preliminary assessment by an independent valuer appointed jointly by both parties; failure to agree on a valuer will result in appointment by the Arbitral Tribunal. The claimant shall also satisfy the Tribunal that all reasonable attempts at amicable resolution have been exhausted prior to initiating arbitration proceedings, as provided herein.

Where a Notary Public certifies any document relating to an agreement for the sale of immovable property, or executes a power of attorney under this Act, they shall adhere strictly to the schedule of fees annexed hereto. The schedule prescribes varying amounts dependent upon the declared value of the transaction and the number of pages comprising the document submitted for attestation. Provided that, if the Notary Public determines, based on reasonable assessment, that the declared value is manifestly inaccurate, they may demand supporting documentation before proceeding with certification; failure to provide such documentation shall result in refusal of service. Further, any application for rectification or amendment to a previously certified document will incur an additional fee as detailed within the schedule of fees. All payments received by Notaries Public under this provision shall be accounted for and remitted according to established procedures.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to respond to a request for information within the time limit prescribed under this Act, or provides a response that is incomplete or evasive, the Central Information Commission may issue a notice of demand to the officer concerned, requiring him to submit a written explanation for the deficiency. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the alleged non-compliance and provide a period not exceeding fifteen days within which the explanation must be furnished. Failure to comply with a notice of demand shall render the Public Information Officer liable to proceedings before the Commission as if it were an original complaint under this Act, subject to appeal to the appropriate appellate authority. The appellate authority may confirm, vary or reverse any order made by the Commission in relation to such proceedings.

Where any gratuity becomes payable under this Act, the employer shall serve upon the employee or his nominee, as the case may be, a notice of demand specifying the amount due and the manner in which it has been calculated, within thirty days of the date on which the employee ceases to be in service. Failure to provide such notice shall not, however, preclude recovery of the gratuity sum. An appeal against the determination of gratuity under this Act may be made to the Controlling Authority if the employee or nominee disputes the amount specified in the notice of demand, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said notice. The Controlling Authority shall consider any evidence submitted and pass an order which shall be final.

Where a food vendor is required to furnish a security deposit under this Act, the amount so deposited shall be refunded within thirty days of cessation of their license, provided that an account of all transactions relating to the security deposit is submitted by the licensing officer to the vendor and duly acknowledged. Any dispute arising concerning the deduction from such security deposit may be referred to the Food Safety Appellate Authority, whose decision shall be final. The vendor aggrieved by a determination made under this provision may appeal to the appellate authority within sixty days of receiving notification of the deduction, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Failure to comply with these procedures renders any subsequent claim for refund void and without merit.

Every distribution licensee shall, prior to entering into a contract with any consumer for the supply of electricity, furnish to that consumer a detailed statement outlining all applicable tariffs, surcharges, and associated fees. This statement must also clearly articulate the procedures for redressal of grievances relating to billing disputes. The licensee shall maintain records of such statements provided to consumers for a period not less than three years from the date of issuance. Failure to provide this information constitutes a breach of duty of disclosure under this Act. Any consumer aggrieved by non-compliance with these provisions may file a complaint before the appropriate State Commission, which shall have power to impose penalties as deemed fit. The Commission may require licensees to conduct awareness campaigns regarding tariff structures and consumer rights.

Every establishment engaged in manufacturing or selling packaged consumer goods shall obtain a licence under this Act prior to commencement of operations. The grant of such licence is subject to compliance with all applicable standards relating to product safety, quality, and fair trade practices. Conditions of licence include the maintenance of adequate insurance coverage against liability for injury or damage caused by defective products, and the provision of readily accessible grievance redressal mechanisms for consumers. Further, every licensee shall submit annual reports detailing production volumes, sales figures, and consumer complaints received and resolved, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these conditions may result in suspension or revocation of the licence, along with imposition of penalties as determined under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “summary procedure” means a process designed for expeditious resolution of consumer disputes, undertaken in accordance with principles of natural justice and fairness. This summary procedure shall apply only to cases where the value of goods or services involved does not exceed an amount as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time. The adjudicating officer conducting proceedings under this summary procedure may grant such relief as is provided for under this Act, subject to limitations on compensation amounts determined by regulations. Any party aggrieved by a decision reached through summary procedure may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as specified herein.

Where gratuity has become payable to an employee by virtue of his death whilst in service, or due to disability rendering him unable to continue in service, the employer shall, within thirty days from the date on which the gratuity becomes payable, make a statutory declaration before a notary public or gazetted officer. This declaration shall attest that all requisite notices have been served upon the legal heirs or nominee of the deceased employee, or where applicable, the disabled employee, and that the amount calculated as due under this Act is accurate and complete. Failure to provide such a declaration will render the employer liable for penalty as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may challenge the veracity of the statutory declaration in an appropriate forum, and recovery of gratuity shall be stayed pending resolution of such challenges.

Every food business operator seeking a licence under this Act shall comply with prescribed conditions of licence relating to premises, equipment, personnel hygiene, and storage facilities. Failure to maintain these standards constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein. Any person alleging violation of these conditions may submit a written complaint to the licensing officer detailing the specific deficiencies observed and providing supporting evidence. The licensing officer shall investigate such complaints promptly and issue notice to the food business operator affording them an opportunity for a hearing. If, after due consideration, the officer finds the allegations substantiated, they may impose penalties including suspension or revocation of the licence. Compensation for losses arising from non-compliance with conditions of licence may be awarded by appropriate authorities as determined under this Act.

Where a dispute arises concerning the interpretation or enforceability of a terms of settlement submitted pursuant to an application filed under this Act, the Central Information Commission shall not adjudicate upon the merits of the underlying disagreement but may entertain petitions solely relating to procedural compliance with the requirements outlined herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding such compliance may file an appeal before the appellate authority as provided herein. The appellate authority shall consider only whether the Public Authority adhered to the prescribed timelines for acknowledging receipt, processing, and responding to the terms of settlement document. Failure to provide adequate notice or opportunity for reasoned objection prior to finalisation shall be grounds for review. The Commission reserves the right to direct the Public Authority to rectify any deficiencies in its procedural actions relating to the agreed resolution.

For the purposes of ascertaining compliance with the provisions relating to gratuity payments, an inspection report shall be defined as a written document prepared by an inspecting officer appointed under this Act. Such report shall detail observations made during an inspection of an establishment’s records and practices pertaining to gratuity eligibility, computation, and disbursement. The inspection report shall include findings concerning adherence to the requirements specified herein regarding employee service length and termination conditions. An inspection report may also contain recommendations for corrective action to ensure future compliance with obligations under this Act; provided that such recommendations do not constitute a determination of liability.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules framed thereunder, every industrial unit engaged in activities resulting in emissions or effluents exceeding prescribed standards shall be required to obtain a license from the State Pollution Control Board. The conditions of licence granted under this Act are binding on the licensee and failure to comply with such conditions renders the unit liable for prosecution and penalties as provided herein. Any dispute arising regarding the interpretation or enforcement of these conditions may be referred to the Environment Appellate Tribunal, whose decision shall be final subject to appeal to the appellate authority within sixty days from the date of notification of the order. The Board may, at any time, modify the conditions of a licence if it deems necessary in the interest of environmental protection.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the prevention or control of pollution, or remedial measures taken pursuant thereto, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Authority constituted under section 8, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order. The Appellate Authority shall give notice to all concerned parties and opportunity for being heard before passing any order. Appeals arising out of orders passed by the Appellate Authority may be made to the appropriate judicial forum as specified in Schedule I. Subject to provisions regarding interim relief granted under section 20, no suit or other proceeding relating to any matter which is required to be determined under this Act shall be entertained by any court until the prescribed period of limitation for preferring an appeal has expired and such appeal has been disposed of.

Every manufacturer of packaged drinking water shall ensure that each container bears, conspicuously and legibly, the prescribed particulars relating to the product’s origin, manufacturing date, expiry date, and net quantity. These particulars must adhere precisely to the format detailed in the Food Safety Standards Regulations. Provided that, where a product is intended for export, the prescribing authority may permit deviations from these regulations regarding metrication standards, subject to prior written approval. Any alteration or erasure of information printed on the container shall render the batch liable for rejection under this Act. Furthermore, every importer of such water shall verify compliance with these requirements before distribution and maintain records demonstrating due diligence in ensuring adherence to prescribed particulars.

Where any party to an arbitration agreement fails to promptly comply with a notice of demand served by the other party in accordance with the provisions herein relating to the commencement of arbitral proceedings, and such failure continues for a period exceeding thirty days from the date of service, the party serving the notice may petition the designated judicial authority seeking direction regarding the validity of the subsequent arbitration agreement. The judicial authority shall consider whether the delay in responding to the notice of demand prejudiced the defaulting party’s ability to effectively participate in the arbitral process. Any order issued by the judicial authority under this provision is subject to appeal before a higher appellate forum, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the initial determination.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice of demand” means a written communication addressed to a party against whom an arbitral claim is asserted, indicating the existence of a dispute and specifying the nature of the claim, the amount claimed, and demanding that the recipient indicate within a stipulated period their willingness to submit to arbitration. Such notice shall be deemed validly served when dispatched by registered post or through any other mode prescribed under this Act for service of legal notices. The recipient is considered to have received the notice of demand upon its actual receipt or the expiry of the prescribed time for delivery, whichever occurs earlier.

Where a dispute is resolved through a written agreement embodying the terms of settlement between parties, such agreement shall constitute admissible evidence of the facts stated therein, subject to the provisions regarding presumptions under this Act. The court may, at its discretion, permit further examination of any party involved in formulating the terms of settlement to ascertain the genuineness and understanding of said agreement. Provided that, if it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the court that the terms of settlement were arrived at through coercion, undue influence or misrepresentation, such agreement shall be deemed inadmissible. Any claim arising subsequent to a finalized term of settlement shall be barred unless expressly reserved for adjudication within the agreement itself. The burden of proving any deviation from the agreed terms rests upon the party alleging such breach, as provided herein.

Every State Food Safety Authority shall, within three months from the date of notification under this Act, designate an appointed authority for each district within its jurisdiction. The appointed authority shall receive complaints relating to food safety standards and conduct preliminary inquiries into such complaints, recording all findings in a register maintained for that purpose. Any person aggrieved by an order passed during these preliminary inquiries may appeal to the State Food Safety Authority within thirty days of receipt of the order. The appointed authority is empowered to summon witnesses, examine evidence, and require production of documents relevant to the inquiry. Subject to this, the procedures followed shall be consistent with principles of natural justice. An officer acting as an appointed authority shall submit a monthly report detailing complaints received, inquiries conducted, and orders passed, to the State Food Safety Authority.

For the purpose of efficient administration and recovery, a schedule of fees is hereby established for services rendered by Gratuity Authorities in connection with applications filed under this Act. This schedule details charges applicable to verification of employment records, assessment of gratuity amounts, and processing appeals against determination orders. The fees specified within the schedule shall be payable by the applicant or employer, as determined by the Authority based on the nature of the application. Provided that no fee shall be charged for applications pertaining to deceased employees where the nomination is duly registered. Any revision to this schedule of fees may be undertaken periodically and notified in the Official Gazette.

Any party failing to comply with an arbitral award within thirty days from the date thereof shall be liable to pay simple interest on the amount due at the rate of ten percent per annum until actual payment. Further, where enforcement proceedings are initiated under this Act against a defaulting party and such proceedings extend beyond sixty days from the date of initiation, the adjudicating authority may, subject to just cause shown, impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each day of delay in ensuring compliance. The adjudicating authority shall designate a competent officer to oversee the implementation of these provisions and assess penalties. Any appeal against an order imposing such penalty shall lie before the appellate tribunal within sixty days from the date of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, a "schedule of fees" means a tabular statement specifying monetary charges levied for various services rendered in connection with contracts, agreements, and related instruments. The schedule of fees shall detail charges applicable to registration, attestation, verification, and other processes as may be determined by the Central Government. Such fees are subject to periodic revision under this Act, notification whereof shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any alteration to the schedule of fees shall apply prospectively, provided that existing contracts remain governed by the fee structure prevailing at their inception. The precise categories of services covered within the schedule of fees may be elaborated upon through subordinate legislation as provided herein.

Any generating station intending to generate electricity for distribution within a State shall apply for a certificate of registration from the appropriate authority, furnishing such particulars as may be prescribed. Failure to obtain this certificate prior to commencement of operation constitutes an offence punishable with monetary penalties, and renders any electricity generated liable to disconnection by the distribution licensee. A person aggrieved by the refusal or revocation of a certificate of registration may appeal to the appellate tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The authority shall consider such appeals expeditiously and pass reasoned orders. Any consumer demonstrably prejudiced by operations conducted without valid registration under this Act is entitled to compensation determined by the State Commission, subject to principles of fairness and equity as provided herein.

Every holder of a driving licence shall comply strictly with all conditions of licence specified in the notification issued by the State Government under this Act. Failure to maintain the physical fitness standards as determined by the licensing authority constitutes an offence and is subject to revocation of the licence, along with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees. Any alteration or fraudulent representation concerning information provided during the application process for obtaining a driving licence shall render the licence void ab initio and attract penalties including imprisonment for up to six months. The State Transport Department may, without prejudice to any other action under this Act, suspend a licence if it is brought to their notice that the holder has failed to adhere to conditions of licence regarding medical fitness or vehicle maintenance.

Where an arbitration agreement contains provisions relating to the delegation of powers to a sole arbitrator for conducting certain procedural aspects of the arbitral proceedings, such delegation shall only be effective if expressly stated in writing and signed by all parties to the arbitration agreement. The power delegated under this provision may include, but is not limited to, decisions regarding document production, witness examination, and interim measures as defined herein. Provided that any party objects to the exercise of delegated powers within fourteen days of notification, the arbitrator shall refer the matter back for determination by the arbitral tribunal constituted as per the arbitration agreement. Further, if the delegation relates to a decision impacting substantive rights or obligations under the underlying contract, consent of all parties is mandatory and must be recorded in writing.

The Public Information Officer receiving a request for information in physical form shall prescribe fees for providing copies of documents or transcripts thereof, subject to the provisions regarding exemptions under this Act. The schedule of fees shall differentiate between requests filed by citizens and those filed by other persons, with fees for citizens being generally lower. Fees may be revised periodically as determined by the Central Information Commission, provided that prior notice of such revisions is published in a widely circulated newspaper. Any fee prescribed under this section shall be remitted if the request relates to information concerning human rights or matters of public interest.

Where an offence involving personal injury or loss of property is compounded between the offender and the injured party, a written instrument executed in the presence of at least two witnesses, attesting to the terms of the compromise, shall be registered with the Sub-Divisional Magistrate having jurisdiction over the place where the offence occurred. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the agreement for purposes of admissibility under this Act. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate may, after reviewing the instrument and ensuring fairness in the agreed settlement, refuse registration if it appears that undue influence or coercion was employed during the negotiation process. Any subsequent legal proceedings relating to the offence shall be barred following successful completion of the terms outlined within the registered compound deed, provided that the victim has unequivocally consented to the compounding of offences as recorded therein.

Where any food business operator is found to be in contravention of the standards of quality or safety prescribed under this Act, or fails to comply with directions issued by a competent officer, that officer may, after affording an opportunity for explanation, issue a notice proposing penalty and specifying the grounds on which such penalty is proposed. The food business operator shall have fifteen days from the date of receipt of such notice within which to submit its response in writing. Any representation made by the food business operator shall be considered by the competent officer, who may then either withdraw the notice or proceed with the imposition of a penalty as provided herein. An appeal against an order imposing a penalty under this Act lies to the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within thirty days of such order.

Any generating station license granted under this Act may be revoked by the appropriate authority if the licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions stipulated in the license or contravenes any provision of this Act or regulations made thereunder. The grounds of revocation shall include, but not be limited to, persistent failure to maintain adequate operational standards as determined by inspection reports submitted annually, demonstrable diversion of power intended for distribution without prior written consent, and fraudulent misrepresentation concerning infrastructure capacity during the licensing process. Prior to initiating proceedings for revocation, the authority shall issue a show cause notice to the licensee detailing the alleged violations and providing a reasonable opportunity for response and remediation. The decision to revoke a license shall be made after considering any submissions received from the licensee and recording the reasons in writing. An appeal against such a decision lies with the Appellate Tribunal.

An application for registration of a food processing unit shall be submitted to the designated State Food Safety Officer in Form A, along with the requisite processing fees detailed in Schedule III. The State Food Safety Officer shall forward the application within seven days to the appointed authority for assessment and verification. Any person intending to establish or operate a food processing unit must register under this Act. The appointed authority may conduct inspections of the premises described in the application to ascertain compliance with hygiene standards as provided herein. Failure to provide access during inspection, or submission of false information, shall render the applicant liable for penalties prescribed elsewhere under this Act. The appointed authority shall notify the applicant of its decision within thirty days.

For the purposes of this Act, “summary procedure” means an arbitration conducted in accordance with principles designed to expedite resolution and reduce costs, and includes proceedings where the arbitral tribunal is empowered to determine its own procedures subject to applicable mandatory provisions under this Act. A summary procedure shall be initiated by written application from one or more parties to the arbitration agreement, provided that such application specifies the reasons for seeking a summary procedure and demonstrates that the nature of the dispute lends itself reasonably to such expedited treatment. The arbitral tribunal may decline an application if it considers that a summary procedure would prejudice the rights of any party.

Any licensed food vendor failing to maintain a security deposit as prescribed under this Act shall be deemed to have violated the conditions of their license and subject to immediate suspension of operations until full compliance is demonstrated. The amount of the security deposit shall be determined based on the scale of operation, as detailed in the regulations framed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority. Any damage to property or loss incurred due to negligence or misconduct attributable to the vendor may be recovered from this security deposit. Failure to replenish a depleted security deposit within thirty days of written notice will result in further penalties, including revocation of the license. The authority may also initiate prosecution under provisions relating to fraudulent practices if evidence suggests deliberate manipulation of the security deposit.

For the purposes of this Act, “learner’s permit” means a document issued by the Licensing Authority authorizing a person to operate a motor vehicle in connection with their practical driving instruction, subject to conditions specified therein. Such conditions include, but are not limited to, mandatory supervision by a qualified instructor holding a valid driving license and adherence to designated learning zones as determined by the Regional Transport Authority. A learner’s permit shall be deemed invalid if the holder fails to demonstrate satisfactory progress in driving skills during periodic assessments conducted under this Act or if any of the conditions of licence are violated.

Where an arbitral award has been challenged on the grounds of revocation under this Act, the challenge shall be deemed to relate solely to matters of law affecting the jurisdiction of the tribunal or the validity of the contract. The appellate court may entertain appeals against orders dismissing applications for revocation only if it is demonstrated that the order was manifestly unjust or based upon an erroneous interpretation of established legal principles. Provided that the respondent party files a counter-affidavit within thirty days, refuting the allegations forming the basis of the challenge, the appellant shall be required to submit comprehensive rejoinders addressing each point raised in the said counter-affidavit; failure to do so may result in dismissal of the appeal. Any order passed by the appellate court concerning revocation is subject to further review under Article 136 of the Constitution.

Registration of immovable property relating to trusts involving benami transactions shall be governed by these provisions. Where a trust is created for the purpose of holding or managing immovable property, and the beneficial ownership thereof vests in a person other than the registered trustees, the instrument creating such trust must explicitly declare the identity of the cestui que trust. Failure to disclose the true beneficiary constitutes a material omission under this Act. The registering officer shall require an affidavit from the settlor confirming full compliance with this duty of disclosure. Any subsequent alteration or addition to the trust deed affecting beneficial ownership necessitates fresh registration and reaffirmation of the declaration, ensuring continued transparency as provided herein.

The rights and obligations arising from a contract for the supply of agricultural produce to processing units may be assigned by the contracting farmer to any other entity engaged in similar agricultural activities, subject to prior written consent obtained from the processing unit. Such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed. Where a processing unit desires to transfer its contractual obligations relating to the purchase of agricultural produce, it shall apply to the appointed authority for approval. The appointed authority may grant such approval if satisfied that the proposed assignee possesses the requisite infrastructure and financial capacity to fulfill the terms of the original contract. Any assignment effected without the prescribed consent or lacking registration with the appointed authority shall be deemed voidable at the option of the processing unit, provided notice is given within six months of the assignment’s execution.

The adjudication of disputes arising from agreements containing arbitration clauses shall permit the assignment of rights and obligations under the agreement to a third party with the prior written consent of the adjudicating officer. Such consent may be granted subject to conditions deemed necessary by the adjudicating officer to ensure fairness and impartiality in the proceedings, including but not limited to requirements regarding disclosure of beneficial ownership. Any attempt to assign an arbitration agreement or ongoing arbitral process without such consent shall render the assignment void ab initio. The adjudicating officer may issue directions for the rectification of any procedural irregularities arising from unauthorized assignments. Further, a licensee granted rights under an agreement subject to arbitration may sub-license those rights provided that notice is given to the adjudicating officer and no prejudice is caused to other parties involved in the arbitration.

Any person failing to comply with directions issued by an appointed authority under this Act relating to the production of documents or attendance of witnesses shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees, or both. The appointed authority may, at their discretion, grant reasonable adjournments; however, any deliberate obstruction of proceedings and wilful disregard of such directions will attract enhanced penalties as determined by the court. Repeated failure to obey an order from the appointed authority shall render the offender liable for further prosecution and a penalty not less than five thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance.
