Where any contravention of environmental standards or conditions stipulated in any consent to establish or operate is alleged, the Director or any other competent officer authorized by the Central Government may issue a notice requiring the person against whom the allegation is made to appear before him or another designated officer at a time and place specified therein. Such notice shall state the nature of the contravention and the remedial measures proposed. The recipient of such notice may submit objections, in writing, within thirty days from the date of receipt. Any order passed by a competent officer under this Act may be appealed against to the appellate authority constituted for that purpose, provided that the appeal is made within sixty days of the date of communication of the order and subject to any fees prescribed herein.

The gratuity payable under this Act relating to a terminated employment relationship shall remain the property of the employee until formally assigned through a written agreement executed prior to the commencement of new employment with another employer. Such assignment must explicitly detail the amount of gratuity being transferred and the terms governing its disbursement, subject to approval by the adjudicating officer. The original employing entity retains the right to audit any proposed assignment for compliance with regulations concerning employee financial security. Any third party receiving a gratuity assignment shall be deemed a licensee and is bound by the conditions stipulated in the initial agreement and as interpreted by the adjudigating officer. Further, sub-licensing of such assignments is prohibited without express written consent from both the original employer and the employee, provided that the employee’s consent must be obtained through a notarized declaration.

Any person seeking registration of a cooperative society engaged in the warehousing of agricultural produce shall, upon submission of the prescribed memorandum and articles of association, deposit with the Registrar a security deposit calculated at one percentum of the estimated initial working capital of the proposed society. This security deposit shall be deemed to be held in trust by the State Government and may be forfeited under this Act if the society contravenes any provision relating to the proper storage and handling of stored commodities or fails to maintain adequate records as provided herein. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require an increase in the security deposit where the scale of operations undertaken by the cooperative society warrants such adjustment. Reimbursement of the security deposit shall be made upon voluntary liquidation of the society, subject to verification of compliance with all applicable regulations.

The registration of commercial vehicles operating for hire or reward shall proceed only upon submission of Form MV-37, duly completed and verified by the vehicle owner and a designated representative of the transport company employing said vehicle. An acknowledgement receipt, bearing a unique identification number, will be issued immediately to the applicant upon initial processing. Any alteration to the registered particulars of such vehicles, including but not limited to changes in ownership or operational base, necessitates fresh application under this Act. The appointed authority shall review each submission and may request additional documentation pertaining to vehicle fitness certificates and driver qualifications. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the registration invalid, subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where a will is revoked under this Act, the revocation shall be deemed absolute unless evidence is adduced demonstrating an intention to revive the same. The party seeking to establish revival of a revoked will bears the burden of proving such intention clearly and convincingly before the court. Grounds of revocation are limited to express declarations within a subsequent instrument or conduct unequivocally indicating an intent to undo the prior testamentary disposition. Any action taken by the executor or legatee following the purported revocation shall be considered conclusive evidence against any claim for revival unless demonstrable fraud or undue influence is established. The court may, upon application and after due notice to all interested parties, inquire into the circumstances surrounding a claimed revival. Decisions regarding revival are subject to judicial review based solely on the evidentiary record presented before the presiding officer.

Every arbitral tribunal shall maintain a record of all proceedings, including pleadings, evidence adduced, awards rendered, and orders made during the arbitration process. Such records shall be preserved securely by the designated Secretariat or Tribunal Secretary, as determined under this Act. The format for maintaining these records shall conform to guidelines issued periodically by the Central Arbitral Authority; provided that any deviation from such guidelines must be approved in advance by the said Authority. Access to the arbitral record is restricted to the parties involved and authorized representatives, subject to orders of the Tribunal regarding public interest disclosures. Any request for inspection or copies of records shall be processed within fifteen working days. The Central Arbitral Authority may conduct periodic audits to ensure compliance with procedures relating to maintenance of records. Failure to adhere to these provisions may result in sanctions as determined by the Authority.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act involving a violation of procedural safeguards relating to the disclosure of information, the Central Information Commission may, subject to prior notice being served upon the offender detailing the nature of the infraction, entertain representations for compounding of offences. Such compounding shall only be considered where the offender demonstrates a clear commitment to rectifying the lapse and implementing measures preventing recurrence. The Commission may impose a monetary penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees as a condition precedent to any such compounding order. Provided that if the offender fails to comply with the terms of the compounding agreement, including timely payment of the prescribed penalty or adherence to corrective actions, the matter shall be referred for adjudication under applicable law.

Any person holding possession or control over documents relevant to ongoing judicial proceedings shall have a duty of disclosure regarding those documents, irrespective of whether such documents are admissible under this Act or any other law. Failure to comply with this duty, including but not limited to the deliberate suppression or concealment of material information contained within said documents, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to pay a fine as determined by the Court. The Court may, subject to applicable rules of evidence, consider non-compliance with this duty when assessing the credibility of witnesses involved in the proceedings. This obligation applies equally to natural persons and corporate entities. Provided that an inadvertent omission does not constitute an offence unless it is established beyond reasonable doubt that such omission was made with fraudulent intent.

The register of undertakings maintained under this Act shall record particulars of any assignment or licensing agreement relating to a construction contract subject to arbitration. Any undertaking seeking to assign its rights or grant a license concerning work performed pursuant to such a contract shall first file a notice with the registering authority, specifying the details of the proposed transfer and identifying the original contractor. The registering authority may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence in assessing the assignee’s or licensee's capacity to fulfil contractual obligations. Such assignment or licensing agreement shall not be valid against the original contractor until its registration is complete and a certificate issued. Further, any subsequent transfers or licenses relating to the same undertaking are also subject to this process of registration. The registering authority may refuse registration if it deems the proposed transfer detrimental to the interests of the arbitration proceedings.

Every employer shall furnish to each employee entitled to gratuity under this Act, within thirty days of their cessation of employment, a detailed statement outlining all factors considered in determining the gratuity amount payable, including but not limited to salary drawn, length of service, and any deductions made. Failure to provide such a statement constitutes an offence, rendering the employer liable to pay a penalty of fifty thousand rupees for the first instance and twenty-five thousand rupees for each subsequent instance. Any employee aggrieved by the omission or inadequacy of this duty of disclosure may file a complaint before the Controlling Authority, who shall investigate and impose further penalties as deemed appropriate, subject to appeal to an appellate authority.

Where an inspection is required under this Act relating to compliance with environmental standards or the prevention of pollution, any officer authorized by the Central Government for this purpose shall have power of entry upon any premises appearing to be connected with the matter to be inspected. Such entry shall only occur during daylight hours and after due notice has been given to the owner or occupier of the premises, provided that in cases where imminent danger exists to human health or the environment, such notice may be dispensed with at the discretion of the authorizing officer. The officer shall produce evidence of their authority upon demand. Entry is subject to conditions ensuring minimal disruption to ongoing operations and respecting privacy, as determined by guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

Where an information-giving public authority reasonably believes that inspection of records is necessary to ascertain the facts relevant to a request, or where access to records cannot otherwise be readily obtained, it shall have the power of entry into any premises under its control for the purpose of examining such records. Such entry shall only be permitted during working hours and after providing written notice to the occupier of the premises, unless exigent circumstances preclude prior notification; in which case, a written explanation for the lack of notice must be recorded by the officer exercising the power. The authority shall designate an appropriate officer to exercise this power, who shall carry official identification visibly at all times during entry. Any person obstructing such entry or failing to cooperate with the designated officer shall be deemed to have violated provisions under this Act and may be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Applications for registration of gratuity-paying establishments shall be submitted to the Controlling Authority in the prescribed format, along with requisite documentation establishing employee strength exceeding one hundred persons at any time during the preceding calendar year. The authority may request additional information or clarification from the applicant regarding operational details and employee records; such requests must be complied with within thirty days. Failure to provide requested documentation may result in rejection of registration. Where an application is deemed incomplete, a notice shall be issued affording fifteen days for rectification. Any dispute concerning eligibility for registration shall be resolved through a summary procedure as provided herein, prioritizing expeditious determination and minimizing procedural delays to ensure timely compliance under this Act.

The records pertaining to any inquiry conducted under this Act shall remain in the custody of the designated Record Keeper appointed by the relevant authority. Such Record Keeper shall maintain these records diligently, ensuring their legibility, accuracy, and proper indexing for ease of retrieval. The assignment or delegation of responsibility for the maintenance of records is permitted, subject to prior written approval from the appointing authority and adherence to prescribed protocols regarding data security and access control. Any person authorized to handle such records under this provision shall be bound by a confidentiality agreement as specified in Schedule A. Further, the digitization of these records may be undertaken with the consent of the Record Keeper, provided that the original physical documents remain securely stored. The transfer of ownership or operational responsibility for record-keeping functions requires notification and verification as provided herein.

Where a party claims damages arising from alleged misrepresentation concerning the ownership of immovable property, the burden of proof shall lie upon such claimant to establish both the existence of the representation and its materiality to the transaction. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrates reasonable reliance on documents officially recorded at the relevant jurisdictional office, the claimant must further prove that those records were demonstrably inaccurate or fraudulently procured. The Court may consider evidence pertaining to the conduct of all parties involved in the transfer, including any subsequent actions taken to rectify perceived discrepancies. Failure to satisfy this burden shall preclude recovery of damages as provided herein. This obligation does not relieve a party from disclosing material facts under this Act; such non-disclosure constitutes actionable deceit irrespective of the claimant’s success in establishing the initial burden of proof.

For the purposes of this Act, “security deposit” with regard to rental agreements for residential premises means an amount paid or agreed to be paid by a tenant to a landlord as security against loss, damage, or dilapidation of the rented property, or in respect of any contractual obligations undertaken by the tenant under the agreement. Such security deposit shall not exceed two months’ rent, calculated on the basis of the monthly rent stipulated in the rental agreement. The term “security deposit” includes any sum paid as advance rent beyond one month and held by the landlord as a guarantee for performance of the tenant's obligations as provided herein. It excludes payments made towards utility charges or maintenance fees.

Where any sum is due from a food vendor or manufacturer to the Food Safety and Standards Authority under this Act, the Authority shall serve upon the defaulter a notice of demand specifying the amount due and requiring payment within thirty days from the date of the notice. The notice shall be served by registered post with acknowledgment due or delivered personally. If the sum is not paid within the stipulated period, the Authority may initiate recovery proceedings as provided herein. Recovery of dues shall be deemed to be a civil debt owed to the Government. The designated recovery officer appointed under this Act shall proceed to recover the amount in accordance with prescribed procedures. Any property attached for recovery purposes shall be sold by public auction and the proceeds applied towards satisfaction of the outstanding liability, subject to any order passed by an appellate authority.

Where any officer has reason to believe that any premises contain material evidence relating to an offence under this Act or are affected by conditions prejudicial to environmental protection, such officer may, subject to providing forty-eight hours’ written notice to the occupier, enter upon and inspect those premises. Provided that where immediate action is necessary to prevent further damage to the environment, the officer may exercise the power of entry without prior notice. Any person obstructing an officer exercising powers under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable as provided herein. Disputes regarding the reasonableness of a notice or the necessity for warrantless entry are subject to judicial review and appeal to the jurisdictional High Court within thirty days of the action taken, with appropriate remedies available to aggrieved parties.

Registration of Mineral Concession Agreements relating to Bauxite Mining Where a Mineral Concession Agreement pertaining to bauxite mining is executed between the State Government and a licensee, such agreement shall be deemed admissible as evidence under this Act only upon its registration with the Sub-Divisional Magistrate having jurisdiction over the area specified in Schedule A annexed hereto. The application for registration shall contain particulars of the parties involved, the duration of the concession, and the extent of the mining lease area. Any alteration to the terms of a registered agreement requires fresh registration, subject to prior approval from the Department of Mining and Geology. Failure to register an agreement or any subsequent amendment thereof renders it void ab initio and unenforceable in any court. The conditions of licence stipulated within the unregistered agreement shall not be recognized for purposes of dispute resolution.

An information-providing public authority shall not be required to furnish any requested information if the request relates to matters concerning the security, defence, or foreign relations of India; or where providing such information would likely contravene any lease agreement entered into by the public authority. However, a decision under this Act determining that an exemption applies shall be subject to review upon appeal before the Central Information Commission. The Commission may allow appeals if it finds that the Public Authority failed to adequately demonstrate the applicability of the exemption or acted in bad faith. Further, grounds of revocation of such exemptions shall be established by demonstrable prejudice to national interests and a clear record of prior disclosure attempts.

Where a dispute arises concerning the interpretation or enforceability of any terms of settlement agreed upon between parties in resolution of a contractual matter, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before a civil court having jurisdiction. Such proceedings shall be subject to the provisions regarding limitation and maintainability under this Act. The burden of proving the genuineness and validity of the terms of settlement shall lie on the party relying thereon, and the court shall consider all relevant circumstances including any evidence demonstrating coercion or misrepresentation in the negotiation process. Any appeal against a judgment relating to such terms of settlement may be made to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that reasons for delay are satisfactorily explained.

For the purposes of this Act, “entry” with respect to any premises means the physical intrusion into or upon those premises by an officer authorized under this Act; entry shall only be permitted subject to reasonable notice being given to the occupier of the premises, provided that in cases involving imminent danger to public health or safety, such notice may be dispensed with at the discretion of the authorizing officer. An “officer” for the purposes of exercising power of entry shall include any Food Safety Officer, Designated Officer, or Assistant Director appointed under this Act and specifically authorized by written order to exercise such powers. Entry does not extend to areas clearly marked as private residences unless accompanied by a warrant obtained in accordance with procedures prescribed herein.

The assignment of contractual rights arising from arbitral agreements entered into under this Act shall be permitted subject to the consent of all parties initially bound by the agreement. Such assignments may include, but are not limited to, rights relating to claims for damages, costs, and interest awarded pursuant to an arbitration award. Where an assignment is made, the assignee shall be deemed a party to the arbitral agreement and entitled to participate in the proceedings as if originally named. The prescribed particulars of any such assignment must be filed with the Arbitrators appointed under this Act within thirty days of the execution thereof; failure to do so may render the assignment unenforceable against the original parties. Further, any sub-assignment shall require prior written approval from each party whose consent was required for the initial assignment and must include the prescribed particulars detailing the chain of assignments.

Where a local authority determines that an industrial activity is causing environmental pollution exceeding permissible limits, it shall issue a notice of demand to the operator of such industry requiring them to implement remedial measures within a specified timeframe. Such notice shall clearly state the nature of the pollution, the prescribed standards exceeded, and the penalties for non-compliance as provided herein. The operator may submit a written response to the local authority contesting the findings or proposing alternative remediation plans within thirty days from the date of receipt of the notice of demand. Failure by the operator to respond or implement the required measures within the stipulated period shall render them liable to pay environmental compensation, determined based on the severity and duration of the pollution. The local authority may also initiate further legal action under this Act for continued violations.

The register of undertakings maintained pursuant to this Act shall be deemed a public record for the purposes of accessing information pertaining to corporate governance structures. Any person authorized under this Act to maintain or update said register may, subject to restrictions as provided herein regarding confidentiality and data protection, grant a license to another entity for the purpose of providing ancillary services related to verification and authentication of entries within the register. Such licenses shall be non-exclusive unless otherwise stipulated in writing by the original authorizing party. Assignment of rights pertaining to the register, including but not limited to the right to collect fees associated with licensing activities, is permitted only with prior written consent from the designated authority as defined under this Act and subject to a prescribed transfer fee. The data contained within the register shall remain the exclusive property of the Government, notwithstanding any licenses or assignments granted.

Where a gratuity is withheld from an eligible employee, or the amount determined is disputed by either the employer or the employee, the burden of proof shall lie upon the party asserting such withholding or disputing the calculated sum. The employer shall be deemed to have discharged this burden if they produce documentary evidence establishing compliance with the provisions relating to eligibility and calculation under this Act; provided that such evidence must include records of employment, salary details, and any relevant deductions. An employee challenging a gratuity determination may present evidence demonstrating errors in the assessment or highlighting factors impacting their continuous service. The adjudicating officer shall consider all presented documentation and oral testimony before rendering a decision, affording both parties an opportunity to be heard. Any finding of fact made by the officer is final unless challenged through appeal as provided herein.

Every food business operator engaged in manufacturing or processing of milk and milk products shall ensure that all premises are constructed and maintained in a manner that prevents contamination of the product, subject to compliance with hygiene requirements specified under this Act. The competent officer, upon inspection, may require submission of detailed plans illustrating water supply arrangements, drainage systems, and waste disposal protocols. Any food business operator failing to provide these plans within thirty days of such requisition shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. Further, the competent officer shall verify that all employees handling milk products have undergone requisite training in hygienic practices and possess valid health certificates. Non-compliance with these conditions renders the food business operator subject to suspension of license until remedial measures are implemented and approved by the competent officer.

Where any employee alleges that the inspection report submitted by the employer regarding gratuity liability is inaccurate or does not reflect the true terms of their employment, they may file an objection with the Controlling Authority within thirty days from the date such report was communicated to them. The employer shall be afforded a period of fifteen days following receipt of the objection to submit a written response and any supporting documentation deemed relevant by the Controlling Authority. Failure on the part of either party to comply with these timelines shall render their submissions inadmissible, subject to an exception where demonstrable prejudice arises from such delay. The Controlling Authority may, after considering all materials presented, order rectification of the inspection report or direct further investigation as it deems necessary under this Act.

Every occupier of an industrial unit generating hazardous waste, as defined under this Act, shall maintain records detailing the quantity, nature, and mode of handling of such waste. These records must contain prescribed particulars including but not limited to consignment manifests, treatment methods employed, and final disposal locations. Failure to accurately record these details or providing false information will attract a penalty of fifty thousand rupees, recoverable through prosecution under relevant sections. Further, any person found obstructing an officer authorized under this Act from inspecting such records shall be liable for imprisonment up to six months, or with a fine not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees, or both. The Central Pollution Control Board may issue guidelines regarding the format and content of these prescribed particulars.

Where a party alleges that an industrial unit is causing environmental pollution exceeding permissible limits under this Act, the burden of proof shall lie upon such alleging party to demonstrate, through documented evidence and expert testimony, the causal link between the unit’s operations and the alleged degradation. Provided that, the Central Pollution Control Board may, at its discretion, conduct independent assessments to verify claims; findings from these assessments shall be admissible as evidence subject to cross-examination of the board's personnel involved. Further, if the industrial unit presents evidence demonstrating compliance with prescribed emission standards and effluent treatment protocols, the alleging party must then provide corroborative data refuting this compliance. Failure to satisfy this burden shall render the allegation unsustainable under this Act.

Every agreement for the supply of goods exceeding a value of fifty thousand rupees shall require prior authorization from the Central Procurement Authority. Such authorization will only be granted if the supplier demonstrates compliance with all applicable quality standards, including but not limited to adherence to relevant Indian Standards and possession of requisite certifications. The Central Procurement Authority may delegate its powers relating to such authorizations to a competent officer appointed specifically for this purpose. A competent officer so designated shall possess at least ten years’ experience in procurement management or related fields, as determined by the Authority. Any supplier failing to meet these conditions shall be deemed ineligible to participate in government tenders under this Act.

Where a party to an arbitration agreement fails to disclose material facts relevant to the subject matter of the dispute at the commencement of arbitral proceedings, and such failure demonstrably prejudices the opposing party’s ability to present its case effectively, the arbitral tribunal may, upon application by the aggrieved party, order the defaulting party to provide the withheld information. Such an order shall be accompanied by a direction regarding costs incurred as a direct consequence of the delayed disclosure. The tribunal shall record its reasons for exercising this power and the determination of prejudice. An appeal lies against any such order under this Act, limited solely to questions of law pertaining to the duty of disclosure and whether demonstrable prejudice has been established.

Where an application is filed seeking payment of gratuity under this Act, the Presiding Officer of the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal shall admit such application without requiring any formal notice of admission, provided that the applicant demonstrates satisfactory compliance with all procedural requirements pertaining to the submission of documentation and verification thereof. The adjudication process shall proceed expeditiously, with a view to ensuring timely resolution of disputes concerning gratuity entitlements. It is stipulated that any challenge raised regarding the admissibility of an application on grounds other than substantive merit shall be entertained only if such challenge is made within sixty days from the date of its initial presentation. Failure to adhere to this timeframe will result in deemed waiver of the right to contest admissibility, and the matter shall proceed towards final determination under this Act. The period of limitation for filing appeals against orders passed by the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal remains confined to forty-five days.

Where any individual or entity is accused of contravening provisions relating to contractual obligations under this Act, and proceedings have been initiated before a judicial forum, the accused party may apply for permission to approach the arbitral tribunal established pursuant to an arbitration agreement connected with the subject matter of the dispute. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit demonstrating a genuine intention towards compounding of offences, including proposals for restitution or compensation as deemed appropriate by the court. The court may grant such permission if satisfied that the proposed arbitration would facilitate expeditious resolution and prevent unnecessary burden on judicial resources, provided that all affected parties consent to the referral. Any order granting or denying this application is subject to appeal under established procedures.

Where any suit or claim is brought before a Civil Court alleging breach of contract relating to the transfer of immovable property, the court shall consider whether the plaintiff has diligently pursued their remedies within the prescribed period of limitation. It shall be presumed, subject to rebuttal by evidence adduced by the defendant, that the plaintiff commenced action within the applicable time frame as provided herein unless demonstrable proof to the contrary is presented. The defendant may challenge this presumption by presenting evidence establishing a reasonable excuse for delay in initiating legal proceedings, and such excuse must directly relate to circumstances beyond the plaintiff's control. Any appeal against an order determining the applicability of the period of limitation shall lie to the High Court within ninety days from the date of that order.

Where any dispute arises concerning the enforceability of a contract entered into under this Act, and either party seeks immediate relief without prejudice to subsequent proceedings, the Court may, at its discretion, direct a summary procedure for preliminary determination of specific issues relating to the validity or performance of such contract. Such direction shall be given only upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating urgency and potential irreparable harm. The findings made under this summary procedure shall not bind the Court in any subsequent suit or appeal concerning the same contract, provided that the other party demonstrates a reasonable belief that natural justice was denied during the summary proceedings. Any order passed pursuant to this provision is subject to review on appeal as if it were an interlocutory decree.

For the purposes of this Act, a “competent officer” means an individual appointed by the Central Government or designated by State Governments, possessing qualifications specified in Schedule A annexed hereto and notified through gazette notification. Such officers shall exercise powers delegated to them under this Act relating to enforcement, investigation, and adjudication concerning breaches of contract. A competent officer may, subject to any rules framed thereunder, issue notices, conduct inquiries, and pass orders as provided herein. The designation of a competent officer does not preclude the jurisdiction of civil courts; however, decisions made by a competent officer shall be binding pending judicial review, provided that such review is sought within sixty days.

Every registered undertaking engaged in the manufacture or supply of goods exceeding a prescribed value threshold shall maintain a register of undertakings detailing all transactions pertaining to raw materials procured, finished products dispatched, and inter-company transfers. This register shall be maintained in a manner readily accessible for inspection by authorised officers under this Act. The entries within the register must include, but are not limited to, dates of transaction, quantities involved, supplier or recipient details, and relevant pricing information. Failure to maintain such a register as provided herein constitutes an offence punishable with monetary fines and potential suspension of registration privileges. Any alteration or erasure made in the register shall be conspicuously noted with the date and signature of the responsible officer. The prescribed value threshold is determined by notification issued by the Central Government from time to time.

Where a contract is entered into concerning immovable property, and a certificate of registration has been issued by the registering officer pursuant to the prescribed procedures, such certificate shall constitute prima facie evidence of the execution of the agreement and the title conveyed thereby. Any party claiming rights or interests under an unregistered agreement affecting such property shall be deemed to have acquiesced in the validity of the registered document, subject to a demonstration that the registration was obtained through fraud or coercion. The right to challenge the certificate’s accuracy rests solely with parties demonstrably prejudiced by its issuance and who can establish material misstatements within the application for registration. Failure to bring such a challenge within six months from the date of publication of notice of the certificate shall preclude any subsequent claim against the holder, provided that the holder acted in good faith.

Every insurer undertaking liability arising under this Act shall, upon written application by the Claims Tribunal, furnish particulars of all recoveries made from policyholders in respect of claims settled pursuant to awards passed by the Tribunal. Failure to provide these details within thirty days of the request will render the insurer liable to a penalty of twenty thousand rupees for each default. The State Government may, through designated officers, audit the records of insurers to verify compliance with this provision. Any person found obstructing such an audit shall be deemed guilty of an offence and subject to imprisonment extending to six months. Recovery of dues owed to the Tribunal shall take precedence over other claims against the insurer's assets.

Registration of Proprietary Food Products – Particulars Required Every proprietor intending to register a food product under this Act shall submit an application in Form A to the designated registering officer. The application shall contain prescribed particulars relating to the composition, ingredients, and manufacturing process employed for the production of the said food product. Such particulars must accurately reflect the formulation as utilized during commercial manufacture, subject to minor variations necessitated by seasonal availability of raw materials. Further details regarding packaging material specifications, including dimensions, weight, and labeling information, shall also be included. The registering officer may request additional documentation or clarification concerning any aspect of the prescribed particulars deemed insufficient or ambiguous. Provided that all submitted information is verified as compliant with applicable standards, registration will proceed accordingly.

Where a contract involves the sale or exchange of immovable property, the agreement shall specify the names of the parties to the contract and contain the prescribed particulars relating to the property involved. These particulars shall include, but are not limited to, the full postal address of the property, its survey number as recorded in relevant government land records, and a concise description sufficient for unambiguous identification under this Act. Failure to include such prescribed particulars shall render the agreement voidable at the option of the party who was not a party to the decision to omit them. The Registrar of Properties may, upon receiving complaint from an aggrieved party, issue notice requiring rectification of any deficiency in these particulars within thirty days. Any appeal against an order issued by the Registrar shall lie before the District Magistrate.

For the purposes of this Act, a statutory declaration is defined as a written statement made before an authorized officer, affirming facts believed to be true, and serving as evidence in lieu of presenting original documents. An authorized officer shall include any person holding office as Notary Public or Magistrate, or such other designation as may be notified by the Central Government under this Act. A statutory declaration presented under this Act shall conform to the format specified in Schedule B; provided that minor deviations are permissible at the discretion of the receiving authority. The validity of a statutory declaration is subject to verification and challenge based on reasonable grounds.

Registration of Demand Notices relating to Public Sector Undertakings Where a public sector undertaking is required to provide information under this Act, and that information relates to contracts exceeding ten crore rupees, the Central Information Officer shall serve upon the requesting party a notice of demand specifying the estimated cost of retrieval, transcription, or reproduction of such information. This notice of demand shall be registered with the designated postal service, ensuring proof of delivery is obtained. The requesting party shall have fourteen days from receipt of the registered notice to indicate acceptance of the demanded sum or to formally request a review of the assessment. Failure to respond within this period shall constitute abandonment of the original request and preclude subsequent re-submission without fresh application and associated fees. All registration details pertaining to notices of demand are subject to audit under this Act.

Where an arbitral award has been enforced under this Act, and proceedings are initiated to challenge its validity or enforceability, the court shall only entertain such proceedings if they are filed within a period of ninety days from the date on which the judgment enforcing the award became final. Provided that, in cases where the award is challenged based on allegations of fraud or misrepresentation relating to the arbitration agreement itself, this limitation period may be extended by thirty days to allow for discovery and production of relevant documents. Failure to comply with this prescribed period of limitation shall render the proceedings manifestly time-barred and without merit, entitling the respondent party to immediate dismissal of the challenge with costs. The court may impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees on any applicant failing to adhere to these timelines.

The Gratuity Inspection Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all inspection reports conducted pursuant to this Act, detailing observations regarding compliance with gratuity payment obligations. Such inspection reports are deemed proprietary assets of the Authority and may not be reproduced or disseminated without express written authorization. Any third party desiring access to an inspection report for purposes of auditing, verification, or due diligence shall apply in writing to the Authority, specifying the intended use and providing a security deposit as determined by regulations framed under this Act. The Authority may grant such access subject to conditions safeguarding confidentiality and preventing unauthorized commercial exploitation. Assignment of rights derived from an inspection report is permissible only with prior consent of the Authority, ensuring continued adherence to statutory guidelines.

Where a public servant possesses information relating to a matter affecting public interest acquired by virtue of their office, they shall exercise due diligence to ensure its accurate recording and preservation. Failure to do so constitutes a breach of the duty of disclosure under this Act. A public servant shall disclose such information promptly upon recognizing its relevance to an ongoing inquiry or investigation initiated by a competent authority. Provided that, if the public servant reasonably believes that disclosing the information would compromise national security or prejudice ongoing criminal proceedings, they may withhold it pending authorization from a designated judicial officer. Such withholding shall be accompanied by a detailed justification submitted in writing and subject to review as provided herein.

Every Public Information Officer failing to provide information within the time specified under this Act, without adequate cause recorded in writing, shall be liable to pay a compensatory amount of twenty-five rupees for each day of delay, up to a maximum of two hundred and fifty rupees. Such amounts shall be paid by the officer to the petitioner as damages. Any aggrieved person may file an appeal with the appellate tribunal established under this Act, seeking recovery of such compensation and further penalties. The appellate tribunal may, after due inquiry and affording opportunity for hearing, impose additional penalties not exceeding five thousand rupees where it finds that the failure was willful or negligent. Recovery of any penalty imposed shall be effected as if it were an arrear of land revenue.

Every licensee engaged in food manufacturing or processing activities shall furnish a security deposit prior to commencement of operations, the amount thereof determined by the Licensing Officer based on factors including but not limited to the scale of operation and potential environmental impact. This security deposit shall be refundable after a period of three years from the date of initial registration, subject to satisfactory compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act and regulations made thereunder. The Licensing Authority may forfeit any portion of the security deposit in instances of non-compliance relating to hygiene standards, adulteration, or misbranding of food products, providing for prior written notice and an opportunity for a hearing. Any dispute concerning the forfeiture or refund of such security deposit shall be resolved through arbitration as provided herein.

The Central Authority may, subject to regulations framed thereunder, grant licenses to individuals possessing requisite qualifications for appointment as a competent officer under this Act. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area within which the licensed individual is authorized to exercise powers and discharge duties pertaining to investigation, adjudication, and enforcement of consumer rights. A license granted under this provision may be assigned by the licensee to another qualified individual with prior written consent from the Central Authority, provided that such assignment does not create a conflict of interest as determined by the Authority. The Central Authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all licenses and assignments. Any alteration to the scope or terms of a license requires express approval from the Central Authority. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated in the license may result in suspension or revocation thereof, as deemed appropriate by the Central Authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a suit for damages arising from defamation shall be deemed to accrue on the date when the defamatory matter was first published or communicated to any person; and where such publication or communication occurs repeatedly, each repetition shall constitute a separate cause of action. The period of limitation applicable to such suits shall be two years from the date of accrual as determined above. Provided that, if the defamation is committed by means of an electronic record, the period of limitation shall run from the date on which the aggrieved party first became aware of the publication or communication. Subject to any order passed under this Act, a suit barred by the provisions herein shall not be entertained by any court.

Applications for licences pertaining to industrial effluent discharge shall be submitted to the State Pollution Control Board in Form Alpha, duly certified by a chartered accountant registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Such applications must detail the proposed treatment technology, anticipated pollutant load, and compliance mechanisms with prescribed standards. The Board may require submission of detailed project reports including environmental impact assessments where applicable. Grant of licence is subject to adherence to conditions of licence stipulated by the Board, which shall include periodic monitoring requirements and reporting obligations. Any alteration to the process or discharge parameters necessitates prior written approval from the State Pollution Control Board under this Act. Failure to comply with these conditions may render the licence liable for revocation as provided herein.

Any party failing to comply with the specific obligations delineated within a terms of settlement executed under this Act shall be deemed in breach and subject to penalties as determined by the Arbitral Tribunal. Such penalties may include, but are not limited to, monetary compensation equivalent to quantifiable losses suffered by the aggrieved party, injunctive relief compelling performance of contractual duties, and recovery of costs incurred in enforcing the agreement. The Arbitral Tribunal shall have the power to issue warrants for attachment of assets belonging to the defaulting party where compliance remains elusive. Further, any wilful disregard of a terms of settlement shall constitute contempt of the Tribunal and render the defaulter liable for such sanctions as are appropriate under law.

Registration of Eco-Sensitive Areas and Revocation thereof The Central Government may register any area as an Eco-Sensitive Area under this Act if it is ecologically significant, including areas rich in biodiversity, crucial for water conservation or vital for maintaining ecological balance. Applications for registration shall be accompanied by a detailed environmental impact assessment report prepared by accredited institutions, outlining potential impacts and mitigation strategies. Any registered Eco-Sensitive Area may be subject to review at intervals not exceeding five years, and the Central Government shall provide opportunity for public feedback during such reviews. The grounds of revocation of registration include demonstrable evidence that the area no longer possesses the ecological significance upon which it was initially registered, or where activities undertaken within the area demonstrably contravene regulations established under this Act.

The Central Licensing Authority, acting under this Act, may, through notification published in the Official Gazette, delegate to designated State Food Safety Officers specific powers relating to the issuance, renewal, and suspension of licenses for food processing units engaged in the manufacture or distribution of packaged foods. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a detailed schedule outlining the scope and limitations of authority conferred upon each Officer, including permissible fee structures and conditions precedent to license assignment. Any existing license granted prior to this notification remains valid until its expiry date; however, subsequent assignments of such licenses require explicit approval from the Central Licensing Authority and registration with the designated State Food Safety Officer. The Authority reserves the right to revoke any delegation of powers if it determines that the delegated functions are not being exercised in accordance with principles of fairness and transparency as provided herein.

Any consumer demonstrably prejudiced by an unauthorized interruption of electricity supply, or subjected to excessive billing due to faulty metering, may file a complaint with the appropriate distribution licensee. The licensee shall investigate such complaints within thirty days and provide reasoned findings to the complainant. Failure to address a substantiated grievance within this timeframe constitutes a breach of contract under this Act. Any consumer seeking redress for such breaches may appeal to a competent officer appointed by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. A competent officer shall, after affording the licensee an opportunity to be heard, determine appropriate compensation, which may include adjusted billing and damages. The determination of a competent officer is final, subject to further appeal before the State Appellate Tribunal within sixty days.

Registration of agreements relating to agricultural produce shall be mandatory for all transactions exceeding a value of ten thousand rupees. Every party entering into such an agreement shall submit a memorandum detailing the nature of the produce, quantity involved, agreed price, and duration of the contract to the designated registering office within thirty days of execution. The Registering Officer, being a competent officer appointed by the State Government, shall verify the identities of the parties and ensure that they possess the legal capacity to enter into such agreements under this Act. Failure to register as provided herein renders the agreement unenforceable in any court. Any dispute arising from unregistered agreements may be referred to arbitration as per rules framed by the government.

The assignment of contractual obligations relating to the supply of agricultural produce processing licenses shall be permissible only with the express written consent of the Licensing Authority, provided that such consent shall not be withheld without due cause which shall be recorded in writing and made available to the assignor and assignee. Any attempt to delegate powers or responsibilities associated with the performance of licensed activities without prior authorization from the Licensing Authority will constitute a material breach of the license agreement. The licensee may, subject to these provisions, assign any right to receive payments arising under this Act relating to processing fees and royalties; however, liability for non-compliance with licensing conditions shall remain solely with the original licensee unless explicitly transferred as part of a formally approved assignment. Further, the Licensing Authority may require an assignee to demonstrate sufficient technical competence before approving the delegation of powers.

Where an arbitration agreement is silent regarding the appointment of an arbitrator, or where the appointed arbitrator refuses to act or is unable to do so, the High Court or other designated judicial authority shall, upon application by a party to the dispute, proceed to appoint an arbitrator in accordance with the provisions herein. The judicial authority may, for the purpose of facilitating such appointment, direct any party making the application to furnish security deposits as deemed appropriate. Any officer appointed by the judicial authority under this Act to assist in the arbitration process shall be considered a competent officer for all intents and purposes. Such competent officer shall perform duties as directed by the judicial authority or the arbitrator, including but not limited to serving notices, maintaining records, and facilitating communication between parties. The appointment of a competent officer may be revoked by the judicial authority at any time, provided that reasons are recorded in writing.

Any person found to have discharged untreated industrial effluent in violation of prescribed standards, subject to appeal under this Act, shall be liable to pay an environmental compensation as determined by the competent authority, considering factors including the scale of operation and duration of the offence. The said compensation may be recovered as a civil debt or through attachment of property. Further, where such discharge results in demonstrable harm to human health or ecological integrity, the offender shall also face prosecution under relevant provisions relating to criminal negligence. Appeals against orders imposing environmental compensation or initiating prosecution shall lie before the appellate tribunal established for this purpose, and its decision shall be final.

The Central Information Commission may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to qualified entities for the processing and dissemination of information received under Section 6, provided that such entities demonstrate adherence to standards of data security as determined by the Commission. Any license granted hereunder shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, with prior written consent from the Central Information Commission, which may impose conditions on any subsequent assignee relating to confidentiality and accuracy of reported information. Furthermore, an appellate tribunal established under this Act shall have jurisdiction to hear disputes arising from such assignments, including challenges to the validity of licenses or the permissibility of assignment itself. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe fees for license applications and assignment approvals.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to provide information within the time specified under this Act, or provides incomplete or inaccurate information, an aggrieved person may file a complaint before the designated Grievance Redressal Officer. Such complaints shall specify the details of the request made, the date of such request, and the nature of the deficiency in the response received. The complainant shall also state the relief sought, which may include compensation for loss or detriment suffered due to the delay or inadequacy of information. For the purpose of determining appropriate compensation, the Grievance Redressal Officer shall consider the prescribed particulars of the request, including the sensitivity of the information and the potential impact on the public interest. The officer may award monetary relief up to a sum not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees.

Where a Public Information Officer fails to provide information within the time specified under this Act, or provides incomplete or inaccurate information, an aggrieved citizen may file a complaint before the designated Grievance Redressal Authority. Such complaints shall be accompanied by a copy of the original request for information and any correspondence relating thereto. The Authority shall afford both the complainant and the Public Information Officer an opportunity to present their case, subject to principles of natural justice. In determining fees payable under this Act, the Central Government may prescribe a schedule of fees which shall take into account the cost of photocopying, printing, and other expenses incurred by the public authority in providing information. Provided that no fee shall be charged for the first ten pages of documents provided.

The gratuity payable to any employee upon termination of their employment, whether due to retirement, resignation, death, or disability, may be assigned by the employee to any financial institution or other entity engaged in providing credit facilities, subject to prior written consent from the employer. Such assignment shall create a readily enforceable claim against the employer for the full amount of gratuity accrued under this Act. The terms and conditions governing such assignments are deemed contractual and binding on all parties involved. Any dispute arising from an assignment may be resolved through a summary procedure as prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government, ensuring expeditious adjudication without undue delay or procedural complexities. Further, the employer shall provide a certificate of gratuity entitlement to the employee at the time of assignment, detailing the amount assigned and relevant terms.

Where any claim for compensation arising from injury to or damage to property sustained by reason of the use of a motor vehicle is disputed, the claimant may submit a statutory declaration affirming the particulars of the loss and asserting the reasonableness of the amount claimed under this Act. Such declaration shall be sworn before an oath commissioner or notary public and shall accompany the claim form presented to the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. The Tribunal may, subject to its discretion, consider such declarations as prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein. Any party disputing the veracity of a statutory declaration may apply to the Tribunal for directions regarding cross-examination of the declarant, provided that reasonable cause is demonstrated. Failure to comply with these provisions shall not automatically invalidate the claim but may be considered during assessment of liability and quantum.

Information deemed to be confidential under this Act shall not be disclosed except where a public authority demonstrates that disclosure would demonstrably benefit the public interest, and satisfies the Central Information Commission that reasonable endeavours have been made to ascertain the views of the concerned third party. Where a request for information relates to data licensed by a public authority to a private entity, the burden of proof regarding any restriction on disclosure shall lie upon the licensee, who must provide evidence substantiating their claim of proprietary interest or contractual obligation preventing release. Assignment of rights pertaining to data management and processing undertaken pursuant to licensing agreements with public authorities is permitted, subject to conditions approved by the Information Commission. Any sub-assignment requires prior written consent from both the original licensor and the assigning party, as provided herein.

Where a document is tendered as evidence containing information relating to immovable property, the Court shall require that the document specify the prescribed particulars necessary for identification of the property. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the district in which the property is situated, the village or local area where it is located, and any unique survey numbers assigned under applicable revenue regulations. Failure to provide these prescribed particulars may result in the Court refusing to admit the document as evidence unless the party offering the document demonstrates that such particulars were inadvertently omitted and can be readily supplied without undue prejudice to any other party. The Registrar of Assurances shall maintain a register detailing standard forms for compliance with this requirement, available for inspection by all interested parties. Any officer authorised under this Act may certify copies of entries in the Register of Assurances.

Every officer authorized under this Act to take or receive evidence shall ensure that all recordings of testimony, whether audio-visual or otherwise, are preserved securely for a period not less than seven years from the date of conclusion of proceedings in which they were adduced. Such preservation shall include maintaining appropriate environmental controls to prevent degradation and ensuring accessibility to designated personnel only. The officer shall be responsible for creating and maintaining an index detailing each recording’s content and associated case file number, accessible through a digital repository as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these requirements regarding the maintenance of records will render the officer liable to disciplinary action under applicable service rules. Any request for access to such recordings by authorized parties must be processed within thirty days.

For the purposes of this Act, an inspection report means a written document prepared by an authorized officer following an inspection conducted at any premises or facility where activities are undertaken that may impact the environment. The inspection report shall detail observations pertaining to compliance with applicable environmental standards and conditions stipulated in consents granted under this Act. It must include particulars of deficiencies identified, photographs documenting non-compliance, and recommendations for remedial action. Every inspection report shall be signed by the authorized officer and submitted to the State Pollution Control Board within thirty days of the completion of the inspection, as provided herein.

Where a claim is made alleging violation of environmental standards prescribed under this Act, the burden of proof shall rest upon the claimant to establish, by affirmative evidence, that such violation has occurred and resulted in demonstrable harm to the environment or public health. The Central Pollution Control Board may, at its discretion, require the claimant to submit detailed technical reports, including but not limited to water samples, air quality assessments, and soil analysis data, as a prerequisite for further consideration of the claim. Provided that, the Board may waive this requirement where preliminary investigation suggests an obvious and substantial breach of prescribed limits. The evidentiary standards applied shall be those generally recognized in judicial proceedings. Any party contesting the claimant’s assertions may present counter-evidence to rebut the findings presented. Decisions regarding the sufficiency of evidence will be made by the adjudicating authority as provided herein.

Any Public Information Officer designated under this Act who fails to exercise the powers delegated to them by the Central or State Government, including but not limited to processing requests within the stipulated timeframes and providing information as required, shall be liable to a monetary penalty of five hundred rupees for each instance of non-compliance. Such penalties may be imposed by the Designated Grievance Redressal Officer upon finding evidence of dereliction of duty. Repeated failure to comply with delegated powers, exceeding three instances within a calendar year, will result in suspension without pay for a period not less than thirty days and may lead to further disciplinary action as deemed appropriate by the relevant Government authority. The Central or State Government may, through notification, specify additional penalties for specific failures related to delegation of powers.

The Central Information Commission may, in its discretion, review any determination made by a Public Authority regarding the appropriate fees to be charged under this Act; provided that such review shall only occur upon written application demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the fee structure. The schedule of fees prescribed by the Public Authority shall be published prominently on its website and disseminated through other accessible means. Any citizen disputing the reasonableness or legality of a fee levied may file an appeal with the Commission, outlining specific grounds for challenge. The Commission’s determination regarding the validity of the schedule of fees shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions relating to appeals before tribunals.

Any person who procures registration of an agreement under this Act by means of false statements or fraudulent misrepresentation relating to the nature or terms of the contract shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the form of application for obtaining a certificate of registration and specify the fees payable therefor. Failure to submit all required documents as stipulated under this Act shall render the application invalid and subject the applicant to penalties as determined by the Registrar. Any officer found to have knowingly issued a certificate of registration based on false information is liable to disciplinary action, including dismissal from service.

Where any public authority fails to remit dues payable to the Central Government or State Government under this Act within a period of thirty days from the date on which such dues became due, the designated recovery officer shall initiate proceedings for the recovery of those dues as arrears of land revenue. The recovery officer may serve a notice upon the defaulting public authority detailing the amount outstanding and providing a further fifteen-day window for remittance. Failure to comply with this notice will empower the recovery officer to attach moveable property belonging to the public authority, subject to judicial review under established principles. Any funds recovered shall be credited directly into the designated account maintained by the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission as applicable. The process of recovery of dues is governed by rules framed in accordance with this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an appellate tribunal is defined as a body established or empowered by statute to hear appeals from orders passed by subordinate tribunals or authorities; it includes any authority designated for the purpose of receiving and processing appeals relating to matters governed by legislation concerning civil procedure, criminal law, or commercial disputes. An appellate tribunal shall possess such powers as are expressly conferred upon it under this Act or other applicable laws, including but not limited to the power to review findings of fact and legal conclusions made by the original adjudicating authority. The jurisdiction of an appellate tribunal is subject to limitations prescribed in the statute creating or empowering it.

For the purposes of this Act, “adulteration” with respect to any food includes the addition of extraneous matter which deteriorates or diminishes the quality of the food, or substitution of one ingredient for another without authorization, or abstraction of valuable constituents from the food; and where an act of adulteration has been committed, a suit may be brought under this Act within two years from the date on which the cause of action arises. The period of limitation as provided herein shall not apply to proceedings initiated by the Food Safety and Standards Authority based on information received or detected during inspection, sampling, or analysis undertaken after the expiry of said period, subject to prior approval of the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, “material information” with regard to goods or services means particulars relating to the quantity, purity, quality, standard, grade, price and place of origin which are likely to affect the decision of a consumer in making a purchase; and includes any other information that may be prescribed. A seller shall have a duty of disclosure regarding material information pertaining to the offered product or service. This duty extends to providing clear and unambiguous details about warranties, guarantees, and potential risks associated with usage. Failure to comply with this duty of disclosure constitutes an unfair trade practice under this Act and renders the seller liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any person desiring to execute a deed for the transfer of immovable property or any other instrument requiring attestation under this Act may, in lieu thereof, make a statutory declaration in Form A annexed hereto, verified before an oath commissioner or notary public authorized under the Notaries Act, 1957. Such declaration shall contain all material facts and circumstances relevant to the transaction intended to be recorded therein, and shall be deemed sufficient evidence of those facts subject to any order passed by a competent court. The registering officer shall maintain a register for recording these declarations, noting the date of verification and particulars of the declarant. Any alteration made to a statutory declaration after its verification shall render it void, as provided herein. Further, the execution of a false statutory declaration shall be deemed an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code.

Where a gratuity becomes due to an employee upon termination of their employment or retirement, and the employer fails to disburse such gratuity within thirty days from the date it became payable, the aggrieved employee shall be entitled to approach the Controlling Authority established under this Act. The Authority shall adopt a summary procedure for expeditious resolution of disputes concerning unpaid gratuities, prioritizing prompt redressal of grievances. Evidence presented before the Authority may include pay slips, appointment letters, and termination notices; however, strict adherence to formal rules of evidence is not required in order to ensure swift adjudication. The employer shall be afforded an opportunity to present its defence, but any unreasonable delay or obfuscation tactics employed by the employer may be considered detrimental to their case. Where the Authority finds that a gratuity remains unpaid, it shall direct the employer to pay interest at such rate as is prescribed under this Act.

Where a consumer intends to file a complaint relating to goods or services procured by him, he shall do so within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose. Provided that the Central Authority may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, entertain complaints received after the expiry of the said period of limitation if it is satisfied that the delay was unintentional and due to circumstances beyond the control of the complainant. The District Commission shall have the same power to condone such delays. Any order passed by the Central Authority or the District Commission under this provision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal before the State Commission as provided herein. For the purposes of determining the period of limitation, the date of receipt of the complaint by the concerned authority shall be deemed relevant.

Where a Public Information Officer denies access to information or provides incomplete information, citing concerns regarding the protection of commercial confidence, an aggrieved party may file a complaint before the Central Information Commission. The Commission shall examine any accompanying inspection report submitted by the Public Information Officer detailing the rationale for withholding such information. This examination is subject to the condition that the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe the inspection report contains material misrepresentations or omits pertinent facts relevant to determining whether the exemption applies under this Act. Failure of the Public Information Officer to submit an inspection report, as provided herein, shall be deemed a denial of access and may trigger further action by the Commission.

Where an occupier of land is found to be contravening any provision relating to discharge of effluents or emissions under this Act, a summary procedure shall be followed for determining the extent of non-compliance. The Central Pollution Control Board may, upon receiving a complaint or conducting its own inspection, direct the occupier to cease operations pending assessment. Such direction shall remain in effect until compliance is demonstrated through remedial action as prescribed by the Board. Provided that the occupier shall have the right to submit representations within seven days of the directive. Failure to comply with the remedial action plan within the stipulated timeframe will result in further penalties, including but not limited to financial sanctions and suspension of consent to operate, subject to appeal before an appellate authority established under this Act.

Where a complainant alleges deficiency in service or unfair trade practice on the part of a service provider, the burden of proof regarding such allegation shall initially rest upon the complainant to establish a prima facie case. However, provided that the respondent service provider denies the claim and presents evidence rebutting the complainant's assertions, the onus may shift, subject to judicial discretion, requiring the respondent to demonstrate compliance with applicable standards or regulations. Any determination concerning the shifting of this burden shall be recorded in writing by the adjudicating officer, along with reasons for such decision. Appeals against orders relating to the allocation of the burden of proof are permissible under this Act and will be entertained upon demonstration of substantial prejudice arising from any error committed therein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appointed authority” means an individual designated by the State Government, through notification in the Official Gazette, to exercise specific powers and discharge duties relating to the enforcement of contracts and resolution of disputes arising thereunder. The appointed authority shall possess qualifications as may be prescribed, including, but not limited to, experience in legal practice or a degree in law from a recognized institution. An appointed authority may issue notices, conduct hearings, and pass orders binding on parties subject to appeal under provisions outlined herein. The State Government may remove an appointed authority for cause, following due process as provided herein.

Registration of Generating Sets and Associated Meters: Every person owning or operating a generating set with an installed capacity exceeding one hundred kilowatts shall register the same with the appropriate State Electricity Regulatory Commission within thirty days of commencement of operation. Upon registration, the Commission shall assign a unique identification number to each generating set and associated meters. Any objection to the accuracy of meter readings submitted during the registration process must be made in writing within fifteen days of receipt thereof. The burden of proof regarding the correctness of such meter readings shall lie upon the applicant for registration or the owner of the generating set, as applicable, supported by documentary evidence. Failure to register a generating set as provided herein will render the operator liable to penalty under this Act.

Where a notice or other document is required to be served under this Act, the manner of service shall conform strictly to the provisions hereinafter laid down. Service by ordinary post shall be deemed sufficient provided that proof of posting, in the form of a postal receipt bearing the address and date of dispatch, is retained by the sender. Where registered post is prescribed as the sole method of service, such service shall only be valid if confirmation of delivery is obtained and recorded. If personal service is mandated, it must be effected either by delivering the document to the addressee or by leaving it at their usual place of abode. The serving officer shall prepare a memo of service detailing the date, time, location, and identity of the person served, which memo shall be signed by both parties and retained as evidence.

Any person failing to pay dues owed to the Food Safety and Standards Authority within thirty days of issuance of notice under this Act shall be liable to pay simple interest at the rate of twelve per centum per annum on the outstanding amount until payment is made. The Authority may, subject to due process, initiate recovery proceedings against such defaulting persons as arrears of land revenue, including attachment and sale of movable and immovable property. Provided that where a default continues for more than ninety days, the Authority shall have the power to issue an order directing suspension of license or registration until full payment is received. Any officer authorised by the Central Government may serve notices and enforce orders relating to recovery of dues.

Where a project proponent undertakes an activity involving potential environmental impact, including but not limited to construction or operation of industrial units, mining activities, or infrastructure development, they shall furnish a security deposit to the State Pollution Control Board. The amount of this security deposit shall be determined based on the scale and nature of the proposed activity, as detailed in guidelines issued by the Central Government. This deposit is intended to ensure compliance with environmental conditions stipulated under this Act and subsequent regulations. The State Pollution Control Board may utilise the security deposit for remediation measures necessitated by non-compliance or failure to adhere to prescribed standards. Any portion of the security deposit remaining after satisfactory completion of the project, subject to verification by a committee constituted as provided herein, shall be refundable to the project proponent within six months of final project closure. The board may also impose penalties and recover costs associated with environmental damage from the security deposit, provided that due process is followed under this Act.

Where an arbitral award has been made, a party seeking its revocation may apply to the designated judicial authority demonstrating that the composition of the arbitral tribunal was improperly influenced by bias or conflict of interest on the part of one or more arbitrators; or that the subject matter of the dispute did not fall within the terms of the arbitration agreement. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date the party became aware of the grounds for revocation, and failure to do so shall preclude such challenge.
