The judicial authority may, after affording an opportunity of hearing to all parties concerned, determine whether the award is vitiated by any of the specified grounds of revocation. If the award is revoked under this Act, the arbitration proceedings shall be deemed null and void ab initio, entitling each party to seek restitution for costs incurred in pursuing the challenged award.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, grant licenses to qualified entities for the purpose of facilitating the compounding of offences relating to unfair trade practices and deceptive advertising. Such licenses shall permit the licensee to act as an intermediary between the complainant, the alleged wrongdoer, and the Authority, assisting in negotiations towards a mutually agreeable resolution. A license granted hereunder is assignable only with prior written consent from the Central Consumer Protection Authority, provided that such assignment does not compromise the confidentiality of information received during the compounding process. Any licensee found to be acting contrary to the terms of their license or engaging in practices detrimental to consumer interests shall have their license suspended or revoked. The Authority may also prescribe fees for licenses and assignments, as deemed necessary to cover administrative costs.

For the purposes of this Act, “notice of demand” with respect to an obligation created in pursuance of a contract, means communication to the obligor indicating that the time for performance of the obligation has arrived and requiring its fulfillment within a specified period. Such notice shall be deemed sufficient if delivered by registered post or through electronic mail to an address maintained by the obligor under this Act. The specification of the period shall be reasonable considering the nature of the obligation, prevailing market conditions, and any prior dealings between the parties. Failure to provide such notice does not invalidate subsequent enforcement proceedings provided that the obligor demonstrates prejudice resulting from the lack thereof.

Subject to the provisions of section fifteen, any Environmental Clearance granted under this Act may be revoked if, following its issuance, it is established that the applicant misrepresented material facts or withheld relevant information pertaining to the likely environmental impacts of the project for which clearance was obtained. Such revocation shall not be absolute but may be stayed pending judicial review by a High Court, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the immediate cessation of operations. The authority responsible for granting the Environmental Clearance shall provide written reasons for its decision regarding grounds of revocation and such reasons are open to challenge under established appellate procedures as provided herein.

Any person found to have engaged in fraudulent misrepresentation concerning the subject matter of an arbitration agreement, or who has wilfully obstructed the proceedings under this Act, shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Arbitral Tribunal, not exceeding five per centum of the claimed amount. The Arbitral Tribunal may, at its discretion, order recovery of costs incurred by any party due to such obstruction. Further, where an offence is committed involving a breach of confidentiality obligations relating to arbitration proceedings, compounding of offences shall be permitted only after prior approval from the High Court. Provided that this power to compound does not preclude prosecution under any other law for the time being in force.

Where a Gratuity Authority deems it necessary to ascertain whether an employer has complied with the requirements of this Act or to investigate allegations of non-payment or delayed payment of gratuity, such Authority shall possess the power of entry into any premises occupied by the employer, subject to giving reasonable notice to the employer and recording the reasons for such entry in a formal memorandum. Provided that where the circumstances indicate an imminent threat of destruction of evidence relevant to determining gratuity liability, the Gratuity Authority may exercise its power of entry without prior notice. Any person obstructing or attempting to obstruct the lawful exercise of this power of entry shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act and liable for appropriate penalties as determined by a competent court. The employer shall provide all necessary assistance to facilitate such investigations.

The Central Government, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 26 under this Act, hereby specifies the schedule of fees for various activities relating to environmental clearances and post-clearance monitoring. These fees shall be applicable to all projects requiring prior environmental clearance, subject to exemptions as may be notified from time to time. The amount specified within the schedule of fees is indicative and may be revised periodically based on prevailing costs and inflation indices; however, such revisions shall not apply retrospectively to applications already submitted. Any dispute arising concerning the applicability or calculation of these fees may be referred to a Grievance Redressal Committee constituted by the Ministry, whose decision shall be final, provided that an appeal against such decision lies with the appellate tribunal within sixty days.

Where a food business operator has suffered loss or injury due to an act or omission by another person relating to food safety standards, such operator may institute legal proceedings within three years from the date on which the cause of action arose. This period of limitation shall apply irrespective of whether the loss is quantifiable in monetary terms or involves damage to reputation. Provided that, where the violation constitutes a criminal offence under this Act, the relevant authorities shall have the power to investigate and prosecute without prejudice to the rights of any aggrieved party to pursue civil remedies. The Central Food Safety Authority may, upon receiving representations from affected food business operators, extend the period of limitation in exceptional circumstances involving complex investigations or discovery of concealed violations; such extensions shall be subject to reasoned orders recorded in writing.

Where an arbitral award has been set aside under this Act, the party seeking enforcement of the award shall bear all costs incurred by the other party in opposing the application for setting aside, including but not limited to legal fees and disbursements reasonably substantiated. Any party alleging grounds of revocation of an arbitral award may file a petition with the designated judicial authority within ninety days from the date the award was communicated; failure to do so shall preclude such challenge. The judicial authority may, upon review of the petition and supporting documentation, order inspection of the original arbitration agreement and related records. If found to lack merit, the petition for revocation shall be dismissed with costs awarded against the petitioner.

For the purposes of this Act, an adjudicating officer means a person appointed by the Central Government or State Government, as applicable, to discharge functions relating to the determination of disputes concerning intellectual property rights, subject to any qualifications specified in the appointment order. Such appointments shall be made on the basis of demonstrated expertise in relevant fields including, but not limited to, law, engineering, and scientific disciplines. The adjudicating officer shall exercise powers and perform duties as provided herein, including the authority to issue orders binding upon the parties involved under this Act. An adjudicating officer is deemed to possess such jurisdiction as may be necessary for just adjudication.

Where an establishment employs fifty or more employees, the employer shall, at least once in each financial year, provide to each employee a statement containing particulars of their gratuity entitlement under this Act, calculated as per prevailing rules and regulations. This statement must clearly indicate the amount of gratuity payable upon retirement, resignation, disablement, or death, along with the date on which such payment becomes due. The employer shall ensure that this duty of disclosure is fulfilled through a readily accessible medium, either physical or electronic, as determined by internal policy. Provided that, if an employee fails to acknowledge receipt of the statement within thirty days, the employer may assume compliance with this provision. Further, any alteration in gratuity calculations must be accompanied by a revised statement issued promptly to all affected employees.

Every individual seeking registration of a commercial vehicle under this Act shall submit a statutory declaration verifying compliance with all applicable safety standards stipulated by the Central Motor Vehicle Rules. This declaration must explicitly state that the vehicle’s chassis identification number matches the documentation presented, and that it conforms to emissions regulations as currently enforced. The Regional Transport Authority may require additional supporting documents, including but not limited to, manufacturer's certificates and inspection reports. Failure to provide a true and accurate statutory declaration shall render the application for registration liable to rejection, subject to an opportunity being afforded to the applicant to rectify any discrepancies identified. Further, any subsequent violation of conditions declared herein will be deemed a material misrepresentation under this Act.

Where a distribution licensee fails to supply electricity in accordance with the terms of the agreement or applicable regulations, any consumer affected may serve upon the licensee a written notice of demand specifying the nature and extent of the deficiency in supply and the compensation claimed for consequential damages suffered. The licensee shall, within fourteen days from the receipt of such notice of demand, either rectify the deficient supply or submit a detailed response outlining the reasons for the failure and proposing an alternative remedy, including payment of compensation. Failure to provide this response within the stipulated period shall be deemed conclusive evidence against the licensee regarding their diligence in addressing consumer grievances. Any dispute arising from the contents of the licensee’s response may be referred to adjudication under procedures as provided herein.

Appellate tribunals established under this Act shall adhere strictly to the procedural requirements outlined herein regarding the filing of appeals and counter-claims. Notice of appeal must be served upon all respondents within thirty days from the date of the order appealed against, failing which such appeal shall stand dismissed. The tribunal may, at its discretion, entertain applications for condonation of delay in filing appeals, provided that satisfactory reasons are adduced to justify the delay. Evidence presented before the appellate tribunal shall be subject to the rules governing admissibility under this Act and relevant case law. Parties appearing before the tribunal shall be deemed to have full knowledge of these provisions. The tribunal’s decisions on procedural matters are final and binding, subject only to review by a superior court on grounds of jurisdictional error. Any application for intervention in proceedings before an appellate tribunal must be made within fifteen days of the initial notice.

Where a Central Information Commission has issued an order requiring the disclosure of information, and subsequently determines that such order was erroneous or based on a misinterpretation of fact, it may, acting upon its own motion or following a representation from a public authority, review said order. Such review shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, affording all affected parties an opportunity to present their case. The Commission may, after due consideration and subject to the reasons recorded in writing, modify or substitute the original order. However, the grounds of revocation of any disclosure order shall be limited to demonstrable errors of law or fact; it shall not extend to a reassessment of policy considerations that initially informed the decision. Any person aggrieved by an action taken under this provision may seek redressal before a judicial forum as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a competent officer is defined as an individual holding a position within a government department or public body, designated in writing by the head of that department or body and possessing qualifications deemed sufficient for the accurate collection and preservation of documentary evidence relating to matters falling under the purview of such department or body. Such designation shall specify the scope of authority granted to the competent officer regarding the production of documents and the verification of their authenticity. A person appointed as a competent officer may be revoked from that status by written order of the same official who initially conferred it, subject to due process considerations as provided herein.

Where an action is brought before an adjudicating authority constituted under this Act seeking redressal for environmental damage or harm, the action shall ordinarily be deemed barred if the complaint is instituted more than three years from the date on which the cause of action arose. This period of limitation may be extended by the Central Government in cases involving continuing violations or where investigation necessitates a longer duration. Provided that, discovery of material facts relevant to the claim after the expiry of the initial three-year period shall not preclude an action if it is demonstrated that such non-discovery was due to fraudulent concealment by the defendant. As provided herein, this limitation applies irrespective of whether the damage is immediately ascertainable.

For the purposes of this Act, an “appointed authority” means a person designated by the Central Government, or where so specified in the arbitration agreement, by the State Government, to perform functions as provided herein relating to the appointment of arbitrators. The appointed authority shall possess such qualifications and experience as may be prescribed. An appointed authority is deemed to have been duly notified under this Act if their designation has been published in the Official Gazette. Any challenge to the impartiality or independence of an appointed authority shall be determined according to procedures established by rules made under this Act, subject to judicial review.

Where a contract for the performance of services relating to the management of intellectual property rights arises under this Act, the parties may, by written agreement, designate one party as the holder of exclusive assignment authority pertaining to all deliverables produced pursuant to such contract. Such designation shall not preclude the original creator from retaining moral rights in respect of their creations. Any assignment of rights made pursuant to a designated authority requires notification to be filed with the relevant registry within thirty days of execution. Failure to provide such notification renders the assignment voidable at the option of any aggrieved party, subject to demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the lack of public record. The procedure for determining such claims shall follow a summary procedure as provided herein, prioritizing expeditious resolution and minimizing costs to all stakeholders.

Every establishment required to provide gratuity under this Act shall, upon receiving a request from an employee or their authorized representative, permit inspection of relevant records pertaining to gratuity eligibility and calculation. Such inspection shall occur during working hours and in the presence of an officer designated by the employer. The employer may require prior written notice for the inspection, not exceeding five business days, to ensure proper record retrieval. Any discrepancies identified during the inspection report process must be documented clearly within the report itself, noting specific clauses under this Act potentially implicated. The employee shall have a reasonable opportunity to respond to any findings in the inspection report before its finalization. Failure to provide access or obstructing the inspection process constitutes an offense and is subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any consumer disputes the determination of tariff or charges levied by a distribution licensee, or challenges the correctness of any assessment made under this Act relating to electricity consumption, such dispute may be referred to the appointed authority for adjudication. The appointed authority shall provide both parties with an opportunity to present evidence and arguments in writing and orally. Any order passed by the appointed authority is subject to appeal within sixty days from the date of communication thereof to the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. Provided that the Commission may, after hearing all concerned parties, confirm, vary or set aside the order of the appointed authority. The aggrieved party shall bear the costs as determined by the Commission.

Where evidence is produced relating to any matter in issue, and that evidence pertains to documents or electronic records held by a party to the proceedings, such party shall be deemed to have a duty of disclosure towards the opposing party concerning the existence, nature, and custody of those materials. Provided that this duty does not extend to privileged communications between legal professionals and their clients, as defined under this Act. Failure to comply with this duty may render the non-compliant party liable for costs incurred by the other side in undertaking further discovery or investigation; however, such liability is subject to review on appeal. The court may, upon application by either party, order a determination of whether a failure to disclose has occurred and assess appropriate remedies.

Where any amount is due from a food vendor or importer under this Act, the State Food Safety Authority shall issue a notice specifying the amount payable, the reasons for its determination, and providing a period not less than thirty days for payment. The notice shall be served by registered post with acknowledgment due to the vendor or importer at their principal place of business as recorded in their registration documents. Failure to comply with the notice within the stipulated time may result in further action under this Act. Recovery of dues determined pursuant to such notices, including interest accrued at a rate not exceeding eighteen percent per annum from the date the amount became due, shall be recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. The Authority may also initiate proceedings for attachment and sale of property belonging to the defaulting vendor or importer.

Where a party claims performance of an agreement is excused due to impossibility, the burden of proof shall lie entirely upon that party to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that the event rendering performance impossible was not anticipated by either party at the time of contracting. Such demonstration must include detailed documentation establishing the nature of the unforeseen circumstance and its direct causal link to the inability to perform contractual obligations as originally stipulated. Provided that a force majeure clause exists within the agreement, the interpretation and application thereof shall be governed by principles of fairness and equity; however, even with such a clause, the claimant retains the burden of proof regarding impossibility. Failure to satisfy this evidentiary standard will result in dismissal of the claim under this Act.

Any entity seeking a licence under this Act to provide arbitration services shall submit an application detailing its proposed operational procedures, including but not limited to mechanisms for conflict resolution and data security protocols. The Central Authority may, at any time, require the submission of revised documentation demonstrating continued compliance with these stipulations. A licence shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates adequate financial stability and possesses requisite professional indemnity insurance coverage as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Further, the conditions of licence are subject to periodic review; failure to maintain standards prescribed may result in suspension or revocation. The Authority shall publish a list of licensed entities on its website, updated quarterly.

Any person found to have manufactured, sold, distributed, imported, or exported any misbranded food product, in violation of the standards laid down under this Act, shall be liable to pay a monetary penalty not exceeding two lakh rupees for the first offence and one lakh rupees for subsequent offences. Where such violation results in demonstrable harm to public health, the adjudicating officer may impose an additional penalty up to five times the value of the goods involved. Appeals against orders passed by the adjudicating officer shall lie before the appellate tribunal established under this Act. The tribunal’s decision is final subject to further appeal to the High Court within sixty days. Failure to comply with a remedial order issued by the appellate tribunal will attract daily penalties as determined by the authority.

For the purposes of this Act, an inspection report relating to a public authority shall mean a document prepared by an officer or employee of the public authority, designated for that purpose by the competent authority, recording observations and findings resulting from a physical examination of premises, equipment, records, or processes under the control of the public authority. Such reports may include photographs, diagrams, or other visual representations documenting conditions observed during the inspection. An inspection report shall be considered a record as defined herein and is subject to disclosure under this Act, provided that any information contained therein exempted under Section 8 shall not be disclosed.

Where an inquiry is undertaken concerning the validity of a will, the Court may, subject to provisions under this Act relating to testamentary capacity, direct that evidence pertaining thereto be taken before an appointed authority possessing expertise in handwriting analysis and estate administration. The appointed authority shall record all such evidence presented, including expert opinions regarding the genuineness of the testator’s signature and any alterations made to the will. Evidence so recorded shall be submitted to the Court within thirty days of its collection, provided that a written request for extension may be filed with the Court, which may grant such extension if reasonable cause is demonstrated. The appointed authority shall not determine the ultimate validity of the will but shall solely provide factual findings regarding the evidence presented before them.

Registration officers shall maintain a register for recording details pertaining to agreements entered into concerning the transfer or mortgage of agricultural land, irrespective of whether stamp duty has been affixed prior to registration. Any party contesting the validity of an entry in this register may petition the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, presenting evidence supporting their claim. The burden of proof regarding the authenticity of documents submitted for registration shall rest upon the applicant seeking such registration. Provided that, if the registration officer possesses reasonable grounds to suspect forgery or fraudulent misrepresentation, they may direct any party to produce original documentation for verification. Such direction does not relieve the initial applicant from fulfilling their obligation under this Act to demonstrate genuineness.

In cases where a motor vehicle is involved in an accident resulting in injury or death, the owner or operator shall furnish particulars relating to the vehicle to the investigating officer promptly upon request. These prescribed particulars include, but are not limited to, the registration number, chassis number, engine number, insurance policy details and the name and address of the registered owner. Failure to provide these prescribed particulars without reasonable cause constitutes an offence under this Act and renders the defaulting party liable for penalties as determined by the competent authority. The investigating officer may require further documentation if deemed necessary for a complete investigation. Any person claiming compensation arising from such accidents is entitled to access these records, subject to due process and privacy considerations as provided herein.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a scheme for the assignment of permits granted under this Act to operate commercial passenger vehicles, subject to conditions as deemed necessary. Such assignment shall require a statutory declaration from both the assignor and assignee, verifying their compliance with all applicable provisions relating to vehicle fitness, insurance coverage, and driver qualifications. The declaration must also explicitly state that the assignee accepts full responsibility for adherence to route permits and fare structures stipulated under this Act. Further, any transfer of ownership in a commercial vehicle operating under such a permit shall be accompanied by an updated statutory declaration confirming the new owner’s awareness of their obligations as detailed herein. Failure to provide accurate information within these declarations will render both parties liable to penalties as provided for under this Act.

Where any arbitration tribunal is required under this Act to maintain records relating to arbitral proceedings, including but not limited to transcripts, correspondence, and documents presented during hearings, failure to do so diligently shall be grounds for challenge to the award. Such a challenge may be brought before the judicial authority specified herein within ninety days of the date the party aggrieved becomes aware of the deficiency in record-keeping. The judicial authority shall consider whether the omission materially prejudiced the position of the challenging party; provided that, mere inconvenience or minor discrepancies shall not constitute prejudice warranting annulment. An order directing the maintenance of records may be appealed to a higher court within sixty days, subject to satisfaction of conditions regarding costs as determined by the appellate forum.

Registration of Demand Notices pertaining to Micro-generation Systems Every person intending to establish a micro-generation system for self-consumption or feeding into the grid shall submit a notice of demand to the concerned distribution licensee at least thirty days prior to commencement of installation. Such notice shall contain details including, but not limited to, the proposed capacity of the system, anticipated energy generation, and intended point of connection to the distribution network. The distribution licensee may require additional information for assessment purposes and shall communicate its decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of the notice of demand within fifteen days of receipt. Failure to adhere to this process constitutes a violation under this Act. Any dispute arising from the rejection of a notice of demand may be referred to an appellate authority as provided herein.

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a schedule of fees for various activities undertaken under this Act relating to the licensing of transmission and distribution undertakings. Such fees shall include, but not be limited to, charges for initial grant of license, annual license fee renewals, and processing applications for amendment or modification of existing licenses. Further, any assignment or transfer of a license granted under this Act, whether partial or complete, shall require prior approval from the Commission and attract an additional assignment fee as determined within the schedule of fees. The Commission may review and revise the schedule of fees periodically, not less than once every three years, to account for inflation and evolving operational costs. Provided that any licensee seeking to sub-license distribution activities must also pay a prescribed fee under this Act.

Where a service provider undertakes to provide services relating to goods sold or agreed to be sold, and fails to do so within the stipulated period or within any time as may be mutually agreed upon, the consumer shall be entitled to receive a notice of demand for compensation reflecting the quantifiable loss incurred by reason of such delay. Such notice of demand may be served electronically or through registered post, and shall clearly specify the nature of the deficiency in service, the amount claimed as damages, and the basis thereof. The right to serve a notice of demand under this Act is assignable, subject to prior written consent from the relevant consumer forum, allowing for the transfer of claims relating to delayed services to third parties engaged in debt recovery or similar activities. Provided that any assignment shall not affect the consumer’s rights as provided herein.

Every distribution licensee shall maintain records of all inspection reports conducted pursuant to this Act relating to its infrastructure, including but not limited to substations, transmission lines, and consumer meters. Failure to preserve these inspection reports for the period specified under regulations framed by the Central Commission shall be deemed a violation subject to penalties as determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. Any person found obstructing an authorised officer from accessing or reviewing an inspection report shall face imprisonment of up to six months, or a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees, or both, as may be appropriate. The State Government may, through notification, prescribe procedures for challenging findings within an inspection report and timelines for redressal.

Where a gratuity becomes payable to an employee or nominee, any claim made by such employee or nominee relating to the amount of gratuity due shall be instituted within three years from the date on which the gratuity became payable. This period of limitation applies irrespective of whether the employer has acknowledged the liability for gratuity or not. Provided that where there is evidence of fraud or misrepresentation by either the employer or the employee, the Central Government may, in its discretion, entertain claims presented after the expiry of the said three years. The determination of whether such fraud or misrepresentation occurred shall be subject to judicial review under this Act. Failure to initiate proceedings within the prescribed time does not automatically preclude recovery; however, it will be a relevant factor considered by adjudicating authorities when assessing fairness and equity in individual cases as provided herein.

Where a generating station or transmission licensee fails to maintain adequate security measures at its installations, resulting in disruption of electricity supply affecting distribution licensees or consumers, the appropriate authority may, after due inquiry, issue directions requiring remedial action within a specified timeframe. Failure by the licensee to comply with such directions shall render it liable for compensation payable to affected parties, as determined by the State Commission under this Act. The amount of compensation shall be commensurate with the duration and severity of the disruption, considering factors such as economic loss and public inconvenience. Any distribution licensee aggrieved by a direction issued under this provision may appeal to the State Appellate Tribunal. These conditions of licence are subject to periodic review by the State Government, ensuring continued relevance and effectiveness in safeguarding consumer interests.

The Central Information Commission may, upon application from a Public Authority, authorize the assignment of outstanding dues owed to that Public Authority under this Act to a licensed Recovery Agent. Such authorization shall only be granted where the Public Authority demonstrates diligent attempts at recovery and provides evidence satisfactory to the Commission regarding the financial stability and operational capacity of the proposed Recovery Agent. The Recovery Agent, upon assignment, shall be vested with all rights pertaining to the recovery of dues, including but not limited to the right to initiate legal proceedings against defaulting parties. Any agreement between a Public Authority and a Recovery Agent relating to such assignment shall specify the commission payable to the Agent and shall be subject to review by the Commission. The Central Information Commission may issue guidelines regarding the terms and conditions for licensing Recovery Agents under this provision, provided that these guidelines do not unduly restrict access to information.

For the purposes of this Act, a “register of undertakings” means a publicly accessible electronic record maintained by the Regional Transport Authority in each State, containing particulars of every entity engaged in providing motor transport services, whether for hire or reward, and including details such as the nature of services offered, registered office address, authorized signatories, and vehicles operated. The register shall be updated periodically, not less than once every six months, to reflect any changes in the aforementioned particulars. Access to the register is open to all citizens subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Authority to protect privacy or prevent misuse as provided herein.

Registration of Food Product Establishments – Detailed Procedure Every person operating a food product establishment intending to register under this Act shall submit an online application through the designated portal, accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documents including site plans and flow diagrams detailing production processes. The application must also specify the intended range of food products to be manufactured or processed at the establishment. Upon receipt of the application, the State Food Safety Authority shall assign it a unique registration number and forward it to the appropriate *competent officer* for inspection. The *competent officer*, after conducting a thorough on-site assessment verifying adherence to hygiene standards and good manufacturing practices as provided herein, shall submit a report recommending either approval or rejection of the registration. Any objection raised by an interested party may be considered by the State Food Safety Authority before making a final determination.

For the purposes of this Act, “summary procedure” means an inquiry conducted in a manner expedited for the purpose of achieving prompt resolution, subject to certain limitations on the scope of evidence admissible and the procedures followed. Such summary procedure shall only apply where the presiding officer is satisfied that the matter does not involve substantial questions of law or fact requiring extensive examination. The application of summary procedure may be declined if any party demonstrates prejudice would result from its operation. Evidence presented under a summary procedure shall be deemed admitted for the purposes of establishing relevant facts, provided that all parties have been afforded reasonable opportunity to present their case.

Where a creditor seeks recovery of dues from a debtor under this Act, the production of a duly stamped and registered agreement outlining the terms of the debt shall be admissible as evidence, provided that the agreement clearly specifies the principal amount, rate of interest applicable, and repayment schedule. Such an agreement is not conclusive proof of the debt if the debtor demonstrates, through corroborating documentation such as bank statements or postal receipts, that the agreed-upon sum was less than what is stated in the document. The creditor shall be obligated to present this corroborating evidence upon challenge by the debtor. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to recovery of dues must be executed in writing and attested by two witnesses; failure to comply renders such assignments voidable at the option of the debtor.

Any employer failing to remit gratuity amounts due to an eligible employee within thirty days of becoming liable therefor shall be deemed to have committed a default under this Act. Such default shall attract interest at the rate of twelve percent per annum from the date the gratuity became payable until actual remittance is made. The Controlling Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding non-remittance, issue notice requiring the employer to show cause why penalty should not be imposed. Failure to comply with such notice or demonstrating insufficient funds shall render the employer liable for a pecuniary penalty not exceeding fifteen percent of the gratuity amount due. Further recovery of dues can be initiated through civil court proceedings as provided herein.

Every business engaged in selling goods or providing services shall maintain comprehensive records pertaining to consumer transactions, including details of purchase, service agreements, warranties, complaints received, and resolutions offered. These records must be preserved for a minimum period of five years from the date of the transaction and made accessible to consumers upon reasonable request. Failure to provide access or demonstrable evidence of diligent record keeping may attract penalties as provided herein. The Central Authority shall have the power to conduct audits to ensure compliance with these requirements, subject to due process. Consumers demonstrating prejudice arising from a business's failure in maintenance of records are entitled to compensation for losses incurred and punitive damages at the discretion of adjudicating officers under this Act.

Every distribution licensee shall, upon receiving a request from a consumer seeking disconnection of electricity supply due to outstanding charges, promptly initiate proceedings before the appointed authority. The appointed authority shall serve notice upon both the consumer and the licensee, detailing the amount claimed and providing an opportunity for each party to present their case within thirty days. If, after considering all evidence submitted, the appointed authority determines that the claim is valid, it may order the licensee to proceed with disconnection. Provided that, if the consumer disputes the charges, they shall deposit a sum equivalent to fifty percent of the claimed amount with the authority as security, pending final determination. Failure by either party to comply with orders issued by the appointed authority may result in penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Where a complaint is received by the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, such Commission shall, after giving notice to the parties concerned, afford them an opportunity of being heard. The Commission may, at its discretion, require attendance of any party or witness before it and may examine them under oath. Evidence may be adduced in support of or in opposition to the complaint, subject to rules regarding admissibility as determined by the Commission. In cases where the value of goods or services involved does not exceed two hundred thousand rupees, the District Commission shall ordinarily dispose of the complaint within thirty days from the date of its receipt. The adjudicating officer appointed by the State Commission may, for reasons recorded in writing, extend this period. Decisions of the adjudicating officer are subject to appeal under this Act.

Every consumer dispute concerning the deficiency of services rendered by a banking institution or financial service provider shall be first adjudicated under this Act before any other forum. Provided that, where a consumer has already approached a civil court for redressal, no proceedings shall be entertained by the appellate tribunal established as provided herein. The Central Authority may, subject to regulations framed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, direct banking institutions to implement specific corrective measures following findings made by the appellate tribunal. Any order passed by the appellate tribunal shall be final and binding on all parties involved, unless it is challenged under appeal within sixty days. Failure by a banking institution to comply with an order issued by the appellate tribunal will attract penalties as determined under this Act.

Every distribution licensee shall, prior to entering into a contract for the supply of electricity to any consumer, provide a clear and concise document outlining all applicable tariffs, surcharges, and associated fees. This document must also detail the procedures for lodging complaints regarding billing discrepancies and service interruptions. The licensee shall ensure that this information is readily accessible on its website and at designated customer service centres. Failure to comply with these requirements constitutes a breach of duty of disclosure under this Act. Provided that, where a consumer requests clarification concerning any aspect of the tariff structure, the licensee shall furnish a written explanation within seven working days. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines regarding the format and content of such documents as provided herein.

An undertaking intending to offer goods or services for sale, whether through retail outlets, electronic means, or any other medium, shall register itself with the Central Consumer Protection Authority in the prescribed manner. The registration shall be valid for a period of five years and may be renewed upon application, subject to compliance with prevailing regulations under this Act. Every registered undertaking shall maintain a current register of undertakings, accessible for inspection by officers authorized by the authority. This register shall include details such as the nature of goods or services offered, address of principal place of business, and contact information. Failure to accurately maintain the register of undertakings may result in penalties as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the register may appeal to the Authority.

Where any offence has been committed under this Act or regulations framed thereunder, the State Government may, subject to conditions deemed appropriate, direct that the offender be given an opportunity to make a representation and enter into a compromise with the injured party or their legal representatives. Provided that such direction shall only be issued where the offence does not involve moral turpitude or poses a significant threat to public safety. The compounding of offences under this Act shall require prior written consent from both parties, which may be challenged in an appropriate forum. Any dispute arising regarding the terms of the compromise agreement or its validity may be referred to a designated conciliatory authority for resolution; their decision is final and binding unless appealed within thirty days to the High Court.

Any distribution licensee failing to remit fees prescribed under this Act within thirty days from the date on which they become due shall be liable to pay interest at the rate of two per centum per annum on the amount outstanding until payment is made. The State Commission may, after giving opportunity for hearing to the concerned licensee, impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each instance of delayed remittance. Any consumer who has suffered financial loss directly attributable to an incorrect assessment or collection of fees by the distribution licensee shall be entitled to claim compensation from the licensee, subject to verification and validation under procedures as provided herein. The schedule of fees applicable to various services rendered by distribution licensees shall be published prominently on their websites and displayed at all customer care centres.

Where in any proceeding before a court or other judicial tribunal evidence is offered to prove or disprove a fact alleged or asserted, the party offering such evidence shall be deemed to have the burden of proving its truth unless the Court determines that, under this Act, the burden lies upon some other person; and where such determination is made, the party so burdened shall be entitled to adduce evidence in answer. However, it shall be open to any party aggrieved by a finding regarding the allocation of the burden of proof to challenge such finding on appeal, provided that such challenge demonstrates a material misdirection of law affecting the ultimate decision. The Court may, at its discretion, require a party seeking to shift the burden of proof to furnish reasons satisfactory to the Court.

The rights and obligations arising from a settlement agreement executed pursuant to arbitration proceedings undertaken under this Act are deemed proprietary in nature subject to any express limitations contained therein. Any party to an arbitration may, with the written consent of all other parties bound by the terms of settlement, assign or license their interest in such settlement agreement to another person, provided that the assignee or licensee shall be bound by and obliged to perform all obligations as if originally a party to the said settlement. Such assignment or licensing shall not prejudice any right of action available under this Act to a party against the assignor or licensor for breach of the terms of settlement prior to the date of assignment or license, respectively. The consent required for assignment or licensing may be conditioned upon such terms and conditions as are deemed appropriate by all parties involved, including but not limited to restrictions on sub-assignment or further licensing.

Where a person accused of an offence punishable under this Act has made a confession or admitted his guilt, the Court may, if satisfied that circumstances exist which render it just to do so, enter into a composition with him. Such composition shall involve the payment by the offender of such sum as the Court deems fit, and may be subject to conditions regarding community service or restitution to any injured party. The Court shall record its reasons for ordering compounding of offences in writing. Prior to entering into such a composition, the Court must provide notice to all affected parties, including the complainant, and afford them an opportunity to be heard. Any agreement reached through compounding shall be final and binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal under established procedures. The Court may refuse compounding if it deems that public interest or the severity of the offence warrants a trial.

Where a contract involves the transfer or exchange of goods, services, or property, all parties involved shall maintain accurate and complete records pertaining to the transaction, including but not limited to invoices, receipts, delivery notes, and correspondence relevant to performance obligations. Failure to do so may render a party unable to substantiate claims for breach of contract under this Act. Any dispute arising from incomplete or inaccurate record-keeping shall be resolved by assessing whether such deficiencies materially prejudiced the ability of any party to fulfill their contractual duties. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to recover damages commensurate with the demonstrable harm suffered as a direct result of deficient maintenance of records, provided that reasonable opportunity was afforded for correction prior to legal action. This obligation extends to digital and physical formats; all records must be accessible for inspection upon reasonable notice.

Every public authority, while designating a competent officer under this Act, shall ensure that the designated individual possesses at least five years of experience in personnel management or information technology administration, or both, relevant to the functions of the public authority. The designation shall be made in writing and published on the website of the public authority, clearly outlining the scope of responsibilities assigned to the competent officer. Subject to appeal under this Act, any decision by a competent officer regarding the disclosure of information is binding unless revised by an appellate authority as provided herein. Provided that, if a designated competent officer fails to respond to a request within the time stipulated, the request shall be escalated to the Public Information Officer for immediate action.

Where a gratuity liability arises pursuant to the termination of employment, whether through voluntary resignation, retrenchment, or other cause as defined under this Act, any person acquiring an establishment or undertaking by way of purchase, merger, amalgamation, lease, hire-purchase, or otherwise shall be deemed to have become the employer in relation to such gratuity liability. The previous employer shall retain the right to assign, pledge, or otherwise transfer their obligation for recovery of dues pertaining to outstanding gratuities to any financial institution or other entity approved by the Central Government. Such assignment shall not prejudice the entitlement of an employee to receive gratuity as determined under this Act. Any such assignment must be disclosed in writing to the concerned employee at least thirty days prior to its effective date, outlining the terms and conditions of the transfer.

The Central Licensing Authority may, upon application from a food processing unit holding a valid State-level license under this Act, grant a national assignment of its production rights pertaining to specified packaged foods. Such assignment shall not exceed a term of five years and is renewable subject to compliance with prevailing safety standards and periodic audits as determined by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. Any transfer or sub-assignment of such national assignment requires prior written consent from the Central Licensing Authority, and failure to obtain such consent renders the secondary assignee liable for penalties under this Act. In instances where disputes arise concerning the validity or scope of a national assignment, parties may seek resolution through terms of settlement approved by an adjudicating officer, which shall be binding on all concerned.

Every Regional Transport Authority shall maintain a comprehensive register of all vehicles registered within its jurisdiction, detailing particulars including but not limited to chassis number, engine number, registration date, owner details, and fuel type. Such registers shall be preserved in both physical and digital formats, with the latter being regularly backed up to prevent data loss. The authority is obligated to ensure that these records are accessible for inspection by authorized officers under this Act, upon due request and subject to reasonable restrictions safeguarding privacy. Furthermore, any amendment or modification to vehicle registration details must be accurately reflected within the registers immediately and a record of such changes shall also be maintained. Failure to maintain accurate and complete maintenance of records as provided herein constitutes an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees.

Where any party disputes the findings of fact recorded by the Arbitral Tribunal under this Act, or alleges material irregularities affecting the natural justice afforded to either party during arbitral proceedings, an appeal may be filed with the designated appellate forum within sixty days from the date of communication of the award. Provided that such appeal shall only be entertained if it is demonstrated that the disputed findings were demonstrably based on a misapprehension of evidence or involved a clear error of law. The appellate forum shall consider the matter expeditiously and may, subject to procedural safeguards, adopt a summary procedure for hearing appeals relating to purely factual determinations. Any order made by the appellate forum shall be final, unless further appeal is permitted under provisions concerning judicial review.

Where an application is made under this Act concerning a gratuity claim dispute, the Controlling Authority shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, proceed to investigate the matter in such manner as it deems fit. The Authority may call upon any person whose evidence appears necessary for the proper determination of the dispute. Any document or record produced before the Authority shall be deemed admissible under this Act unless objection is raised by a party within fifteen days from the date of its presentation. Decisions regarding procedural matters and interim orders shall be final, subject to appeal as provided herein. For the purpose of adjudicating disputes and performing functions related thereto, the Controlling Authority may appoint a *competent officer* who shall act in accordance with directions issued by the Authority.

The authorization to undertake environmental impact assessment studies as provided herein relating to projects involving the handling of hazardous substances may be assigned by the authorized entity to a qualified consultant, subject to prior approval from the Central Pollution Control Board. Such assignment shall not extend to the liability of the original authorizing entity under this Act for ensuring compliance with conditions stipulated in the Environmental Clearance granted. The period of limitation for initiating legal proceedings against an assignor or assignee relating to non-compliance occurring before the assignment is complete shall be three years from the date of such non-compliance. Further, any subsequent transfer of the authorization requires fresh registration and approval as detailed in Schedule III. This provision applies equally where the assignment involves a partial delegation of responsibilities.

Where any food business operator is required to submit a statutory declaration regarding adherence to hygiene practices under this Act, and disputes arise concerning the veracity or completeness of such declaration, the Food Safety Officer may initiate an inquiry. The inquiring officer shall provide all parties with notice in writing and a reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments. Any party disputing the findings of the Food Safety Officer may appeal to the State Food Safety Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The appellate authority, after hearing both sides, may confirm, vary, or reverse the order made by the Food Safety Officer; provided that the appellate authority shall not be bound by any particular finding of fact rendered during the inquiry.

Where any dispute arises concerning the interpretation or enforceability of a terms of settlement agreed upon pursuant to arbitration proceedings under this Act, either party may file an application before the designated judicial forum seeking clarification regarding the scope and effect of such agreement. The court shall entertain such applications only if it is demonstrated that the ambiguity in the terms of settlement prevents a clear determination of rights and obligations. Provided that any order passed by the court on such application shall be subject to appeal under the general rules applicable to civil procedure, and the appellate forum may consider whether the lower court exceeded its jurisdiction in interpreting the terms of settlement.

Any person failing to produce documents relevant to an inquiry conducted under summary procedure, when duly summoned by a Magistrate or other officer empowered to issue summons under this Act, shall be deemed to have wilfully disobeyed the order and is liable to imprisonment for a term that may extend to one year, or with a fine, or both. Provided that if the failure results from reasonable excuse, the Court may condone the default after hearing arguments from both parties. The officer issuing the summons shall record reasons for any such condonation. Any appeal against an order imposing penalty under this provision shall lie only to the High Court within thirty days of the order and subject to a fine not exceeding one thousand rupees.

An employee shall not be entitled to gratuity if the termination of his employment is without notice or payment in lieu thereof, unless the termination is demonstrably attributable to closure of the industrial establishment, retrenchment, or other circumstances beyond the control of the employee. Where an employee’s services are terminated for a cause deemed sufficient under this Act, including but not limited to wilful disobedience, theft, fraud, or indiscipline, the employer may initiate proceedings for revocation of gratuity entitlement. Such proceedings shall be conducted in accordance with prescribed procedures, affording the employee a reasonable opportunity for representation and submission of written explanation. The determination regarding grounds of revocation is subject to review by an appellate authority as provided herein, upon application made within thirty days from the date of communication of the revocation order. Any appeal against such determination will be finally decided by the appellate authority after considering all relevant documents and hearing both parties.

Where a party has unequivocally communicated his intention to revoke a contract to the other party, the revocation shall take effect from the time when the communication is received by the other party, or if it is sent by post, from the time when it is put into the course of posting and such transmission is ordinarily delivered in the usual course of post. The offeror may prescribe a manner for exercising the right to revoke, and any revocation not complying with that prescribed manner shall be void. Any person claiming to have suffered loss as a consequence of a purported revocation may file a complaint before the designated Grievance Redressal Forum established under this Act within ninety days from the date of receipt of such communication. The forum shall provide an opportunity for both parties to present evidence and arguments relating to the grounds of revocation.

Every vehicle registered under this Act shall bear a registration certificate issued by the registering authority, detailing the prescribed particulars relating thereto. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the make and model of the vehicle, chassis number, engine number, fuel type, colour, seating capacity, and name and address of the registered owner. The registering authority may require submission of original documents establishing ownership or right to possession prior to issuance of such certificate. Any alteration to the prescribed particulars after initial registration shall be reported to the registering authority within thirty days, accompanied by relevant documentation for verification. Failure to report alterations as provided herein renders the vehicle liable for penalties under this Act and invalidates the existing registration certificate until updated.

Where a distribution licensee proposes to enhance the capacity of its existing distribution network or establish a new distribution network for supply of electricity, it shall issue a notice of demand to all potentially affected consumers within the area proposed to be served. Such notice of demand shall clearly state the intended enhancements or establishment and provide an estimated timeline for completion as provided herein. The licensee may, after publication of the notice of demand, conduct surveys and assessments to ascertain actual consumer requirements. Any consumer desiring connection or enhancement of load following issuance of a notice of demand shall make application in the prescribed form. Failure by a consumer to respond within thirty days from the date of the notice of demand shall be deemed as non-acceptance of the proposed service conditions.

Where a consumer seeks redressal against unfair trade practices or deficiencies in services, they may file an appeal with the appellate tribunal established under this Act. The tribunal shall entertain appeals from orders passed by District Commissions, State Commissions, and National Commission within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Appeals shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed, and the consumer shall clearly state grounds for challenging the original decision. The tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned, dismiss frivolous or vexatious appeals. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the appellate tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The tribunal shall have the power to grant such remedies as are provided herein, including compensation for loss or injury suffered by the consumer.

Any driving license issued under this Act may be revoked by the Regional Transport Authority if the holder is found to have misrepresented material facts during the application process, or has subsequently been convicted of an offence involving the use of a motor vehicle that demonstrates a clear disregard for public safety. The authority shall serve notice upon the licensee detailing the specific allegations forming the basis for proposed revocation and affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit their explanation in writing and be heard personally before a duly constituted committee. Grounds of revocation also extend to instances where the license holder has been declared medically unfit by a qualified medical practitioner registered under the relevant Medical Council Act, or if it is determined that the licensee habitually operates a motor vehicle in a manner dangerous to other road users. The authority’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal before the Transport Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of notification.

Every industrial undertaking generating or handling hazardous substances, as defined under this Act, shall maintain a comprehensive register of undertakings, detailing the nature and quantity of such substances handled, waste generated, and pollution control measures implemented. This register shall be maintained in a readily accessible format and made available for inspection by authorized officers upon request. Failure to comply with this provision renders the undertaking liable to penalties as provided herein, including fines and potential closure orders. Any person claiming injury or damage due to non-compliance regarding the register of undertakings may pursue legal remedies under this Act, subject to demonstrating a causal link between the deficiency in record keeping and the resulting harm. The Central Pollution Control Board may issue guidelines concerning the format and content of the register of undertakings.

Where the Central Pollution Control Board deems it necessary to require remedial measures from an industrial unit following a finding of non-compliance with prescribed environmental standards, it shall issue a notice of demand to the concerned proprietor or occupier. Such notice shall specify the nature and extent of the remedial action required, including but not limited to installation of pollution control equipment, modification of production processes, or restoration of degraded areas. The notice of demand shall also indicate the time within which compliance is expected, taking into consideration the technical feasibility and financial implications for the industrial unit. Failure to comply with a notice of demand may result in further action under this Act, including but not limited to imposition of environmental compensation charges and directions for cessation of operations. Any aggrieved party may submit representations against a notice of demand within thirty days from its receipt, which shall be considered by the Board before final determination.

Where an arbitral tribunal determines that a party has failed to comply with a direction issued under this Act regarding the submission of documents or information, it shall, before imposing any costs pursuant to sub-section (2) of section 35, provide written notice to the defaulting party specifying the nature of the non-compliance and affording them an opportunity of being heard. The arbitral tribunal may, in its discretion, waive such costs if satisfied that the failure was unintentional or due to circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the party. Further, any fees payable under the schedule of fees shall be adjusted downwards by twenty percent where the arbitration proceedings are conducted predominantly through video conferencing technology and all parties consent thereto in writing. Provided that this adjustment does not apply where a dispute arises concerning enforcement of an arbitral award.

Every registration authority appointed under this Act shall, upon receipt of an application for transfer of ownership of a motor vehicle, verify that the applicant is the registered holder or has obtained consent from the registered holder, provided that verification shall include confirmation through the central database maintained by the competent transport department. The appointed authority may require submission of additional documents to establish identity and financial solvency if deemed necessary. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures for transfer, including timely notification to insurance companies as stipulated herein, will render the appointed authority liable for penalties under this Act. Any dispute arising from discrepancies in submitted documentation shall be resolved by the appointed authority after providing an opportunity for both parties to present their case.

Registration of Consumer Grievance Redressal Forums shall proceed upon submission of Form CG-1, duly completed and attested by the complainant or their authorized representative. The Forum shall maintain a register of all registrations, recording date of receipt, details of the grievance, and contact information for subsequent communication. Any application filed after the expiry of two years from the date on which the cause of action arose shall be deemed inadmissible, subject to exceptions as provided herein relating to cases of fraud or misrepresentation. The Central Authority may prescribe guidelines regarding electronic filing and verification of registration documents. Failure to adhere to prescribed timelines during the registration process may result in delays; however, such delay does not affect the applicable period of limitation for pursuing remedies under this Act.

Where any suit is instituted challenging the enforceability of a contract entered into prior to the amendment of Schedule A to this Act, the plaintiff shall be deemed to have acquiesced in the continued validity of said contract until the date of institution of the suit, provided that such acquiescence shall not prejudice any right of action arising under this Act. The defendant may raise as a defence the bar against suits instituted beyond the period of limitation applicable at the time of the alleged breach, and it shall be incumbent upon the plaintiff to demonstrate that circumstances existed which justified an extension of said period. Any order granting such extension is subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date thereof.

The fees payable for various services rendered under this Act relating to inspection, testing, certification, and licensing shall be governed by the schedule of fees annexed hereto. The Central Food Safety and Standards Authority may, from time to time, revise said schedule, provided that any such revision shall be published in the Official Gazette at least thirty days prior to its effective date. Any food business operator aggrieved by a determination of fee levied under this Act, or by the application of a revised schedule, may within sixty days of receipt of notification thereof file an appeal with the State Food Safety Appellate Authority. The appellate authority shall consider any evidence submitted and pass orders as it deems just; decisions made by the appellate authority are subject to further appeal to the Central Food Safety Standards Authority.

For the purposes of establishing liability in actions concerning recovery of dues, “dues” shall mean any sum of money legally owed by one party to another, whether arising from a contractual obligation or otherwise; and includes, but is not limited to, amounts due for goods sold and delivered, services rendered, or work performed. The term "creditor" signifies the person entitled to receive such dues, while “debtor” denotes the individual obligated to make payment as provided herein. Acknowledgment of a debt, whether express or implied, shall be admissible evidence under this Act. Nothing in these provisions shall affect any right available to a creditor under other legislation relating to recovery of property or enforcement of contracts.

Any dispute arising between a food vendor and a consumer regarding quality, quantity or price of edible oils, processed foods, or packaged drinking water may be resolved through mediation facilitated by the Food Safety Officer designated under this Act; provided that both parties consent to participate in said mediation. Should mediation fail to yield resolution within sixty days from initiation, either party shall have recourse to civil remedies as available under other laws. Any agreement reached pursuant to such mediation and formalized into terms of settlement shall be binding on both vendor and consumer, subject to the provisions relating to consumer protection enshrined herein. The Food Safety Officer shall maintain a record of all mediations undertaken and may issue guidelines for ensuring fairness in the process.

Every food business operator seeking a licence under this Act shall comply with all stipulated conditions of licence pertaining to premises, equipment, personnel hygiene, and operational procedures. The licensing authority may conduct inspections at any time to ascertain adherence to these conditions, providing the licensee reasonable notice except in cases where immediate verification is deemed necessary. Any deviation from prescribed standards relating to water quality or pest control will constitute a violation, subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, all records pertaining to raw material procurement and finished product distribution must be maintained accurately and made available for inspection upon request. The licensing authority shall issue written communication regarding any non-compliance observed, affording the licensee an opportunity to rectify deficiencies within a specified timeframe.

Information relating to contracts entered into by a Public Authority for the provision of services, including but not limited to data processing, analysis, or storage, may be released under this Act subject to the provisions regarding commercial confidence. Any third party possessing such information, obtained pursuant to a contract with a Public Authority, shall be deemed to hold it in trust for the benefit of the public and may grant licenses permitting access thereto, provided that such licensing agreements explicitly acknowledge the right of any citizen to extract and utilize data released under this Act. The assignment of these rights is permitted through written agreement, subject to review by the Central Information Commission using a summary procedure to ensure compliance with the principles of transparency and accountability as provided herein. Any Public Authority may delegate authority for processing requests pertaining to licensed information.

Where a party to legal proceedings possesses information relevant to a claim or defence, that party shall have a duty of disclosure towards the opposing party, extending to all documents and electronic records which would, if presented at trial, be directly admissible as evidence or materially influence the determination of any issue arising in those proceedings. This duty is not discharged by merely providing a list of such materials; rather, it requires their production unless privilege applies under this Act. Failure to comply with this duty shall constitute a breach and render the defaulting party liable for costs incurred by the opposing party as a consequence of the non-disclosure, including reasonable expenses of investigation and discovery. Provided that a party acted in good faith and could not reasonably have known of the existence of relevant information, such party may be relieved from liability; however, the court shall retain discretion to impose penalties where appropriate.

Every Public Authority shall designate a Central Information Officer who shall receive requests and provide information as required under this Act. The designation shall be made within thirty days from the date of commencement of this Act. Where a Public Authority comprises several offices located at different places, each office may designate one or more Central Information Officers to deal with requests received by that office. Any grievance regarding the functioning or decision of a Central Information Officer may be addressed to an appointed authority designated by the Public Authority. The appointed authority shall examine such grievances and pass orders as it deems fit, providing reasons for its decision in writing within forty-five days. Appeals against orders passed by the appointed authority are subject to review under the provisions detailed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “gratuity records” means all documents pertaining to the employment history of an employee, including but not limited to attendance registers, salary slips, appointment letters, resignation notices, and any correspondence relating to termination or retirement. The employer shall maintain these gratuity records in a safe and accessible manner, ensuring their preservation for a period of five years from the date of cessation of employment of each employee. Failure to properly maintain such records constitutes an offence under this Act. The maintenance of records shall be deemed satisfactory if they are readily available for inspection by designated officers authorized under this Act.

Where a contract involves the supply of goods which are to be inspected prior to delivery or acceptance, the seller shall afford the buyer reasonable opportunity for examination of the goods at any mutually agreed place. The inspection report prepared by the buyer’s designated representative following such examination shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the condition of the goods at the time of inspection, subject to demonstrable proof of fraud or misrepresentation on the part of the seller. Any dispute concerning the contents of an inspection report may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. The seller shall maintain a record of all inspections undertaken and associated documentation for a period not less than seven years from the date of delivery. Failure by the seller to provide access for inspection, or interference with the buyer’s examination process, shall constitute a breach of contract under this Act. The authority may issue guidelines regarding standard formats for inspection reports.

Where information is supplied in electronic form under this Act, the Public Information Officer shall provide the same through email or other commonly used digital platforms, provided that the requestor consents to such manner of service and possesses the requisite technological access. If the requestor disputes the chosen method of delivery, citing demonstrable inability to access the electronic format, the Public Information Officer shall revert to supplying the information in a physical form as per sub-section (1) of section 6. Any appeal arising from a dispute concerning the manner of service shall be entertained by the Appellate Authority only if it is demonstrated that the prescribed method prejudiced the requestor’s ability to reasonably access the sought information, subject to the provisions regarding costs outlined elsewhere under this Act.

The Registrar shall maintain a register for recording details pertaining to security deposits furnished by tenants under agreements for residential premises within areas governed by urban local bodies. Such register shall include, but not be limited to, the name and address of both tenant and landlord, the amount of the security deposit paid, the date of payment, and particulars of any deductions made therefrom upon termination of the tenancy. The Registrar may require landlords to submit prescribed forms detailing these deposits at intervals as determined by notification in the Official Gazette. Failure to comply with such requirements shall render the landlord liable for a penalty under this Act. Any dispute regarding deductions from the security deposit, if not resolved amicably, may be referred to the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission as provided herein.

An employee who has ceased employment due to dismissal for gross misconduct shall nevertheless be eligible for gratuity payment if such dismissal was obtained through a legally sanctioned process, evidenced by a judgment or order from an Industrial Tribunal or Labour Court affirming the fairness of the termination. The employer shall furnish proof of this adjudication alongside the gratuity claim form. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence will result in denial of gratuity and render the employer liable for compensatory damages equivalent to twice the amount of gratuity payable, recoverable through civil suit. Any dispute concerning the conditions of licence relating to gratuity payments under this Act may be referred to a Grievance Redressal Committee established by the State Government, whose decisions shall be binding on both parties.

Any person who knowingly presents as genuine a document purporting to be a certificate of registration issued under this Act, but which is false or has been altered without due authorization, shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be subject to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe procedures for verifying the authenticity of certificates of registration. Failure to comply with such prescribed procedures when challenging the validity of a document presented as evidence shall render the party liable to costs in the suit or proceeding.
