Any officer failing to report suspected forgery of a certificate of registration as provided herein shall be subject to disciplinary action under applicable service rules.

For the purposes of this Act, an adjudicating officer means an individual appointed by the appropriate authority, possessing qualifications as specified in the notification issued under this Act, and whose duty it is to determine disputes relating to gratuity claims. The appropriate authority shall notify the names and jurisdictions of all such adjudicating officers in the Official Gazette. An adjudicating officer shall exercise such powers as are conferred upon him or her by this Act and rules made thereunder, including but not limited to the power to summon witnesses, examine evidence, and issue orders binding on both employers and employees subject to appeal under provisions herein.

Where a distribution licensee fails to provide electricity service in accordance with the standards prescribed under this Act, or deviates from the procedures established for connection, metering, or billing, any consumer affected may lodge a complaint before the Grievance Redressal Forum constituted by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. The Forum shall investigate such complaints and determine whether the manner of service rendered was deficient or otherwise in violation of regulations. Any order made by the Grievance Redressal Forum concerning compensation or remedial action is subject to appeal within sixty days to the State Appellate Tribunal, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the original decision.

For the purposes of this Act, “employer” includes any establishment employing twenty or more persons, and where an employee leaves service, the gratuity payable shall be determined based on factors including length of service and last drawn salary. An employer’s duty of disclosure regarding gratuity eligibility extends to providing each employee with a written statement outlining the conditions for gratuity payment, detailing the amount accrued, and specifying any deductions applicable under this Act. This duty of disclosure is triggered upon commencement of employment and renewed annually thereafter. Failure to provide such statements constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein.

The Central Transmission Utility shall grant permission for entry upon any land lawfully held by a generating station, transmission licensee, distribution licensee, or any person acting on their behalf, for the purpose of inspecting, testing, repairing, or maintaining electrical lines, equipment, and installations necessary for the secure operation of the grid. Such permission shall be subject to payment of compensation as determined by the appropriate authority under this Act. A licensee intending to assign rights related to a transmission license granted pursuant to this Act may, prior to such assignment, seek authorization from the Central Government regarding access to infrastructure required for continued operational compliance. The power of entry conferred herein is not absolute and requires prior notification unless an emergency situation necessitates immediate action, provided that subsequent reporting shall be undertaken expeditiously.

For the purposes of this Act, “notice of demand” with respect to any document or thing includes written communication addressed to the person obligated to produce it, specifying the document’s nature and purpose for which production is sought. Such notice shall clearly indicate a reasonable timeframe within which compliance is expected. A verbal request, however insistent, does not constitute notice of demand under this Act. Where a document is held by an agent acting on behalf of another, notice of demand may be served upon the agent, provided that the principal’s identity and connection to the agent are reasonably ascertainable from the communication.

Every Public Information Officer appointed under this Act shall, upon receipt of an application requesting information, furnish to the applicant a certificate specifying the prescribed particulars relating to the records held by the public authority concerned. Failure to provide such a certificate within thirty days from the date of receipt of the application shall be deemed a violation subject to penalty as provided herein. The Central Information Commission may, after affording the Public Information Officer an opportunity of being heard, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees for each instance of default. Any person aggrieved by such imposition may appeal to the appellate authority under this Act within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, a “competent officer” means an officer designated by the Central Government or State Government, as the case may be, for adjudicating disputes relating to gratuity payments and conducting inquiries under this Act. The designation shall be published in the Official Gazette. A competent officer shall possess at least a bachelor's degree and have experience of not less than five years in personnel management or industrial relations. Subject to any rules made by the Government, a competent officer may exercise such powers as are conferred upon him under this Act and shall follow principles of natural justice while conducting proceedings.

Where any dispute arises concerning the validity of a certificate of registration issued under this Act, or regarding the particulars recorded therein, either party may file an appeal with the Regional Transport Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision sought to be challenged. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the order is contested. The Appellate Authority shall consider evidence submitted by both parties and may direct any further inquiry deemed necessary for proper adjudication. Provided that, if the dispute involves allegations of fraud or misrepresentation in obtaining the certificate of registration, the Appellate Authority may require additional documentation and testimony as it deems appropriate before rendering its decision.

Where a person possesses documentary evidence relating to a transaction involving intellectual property rights, that person shall have a duty of disclosure to any prospective assignee or licensee should they represent themselves as acting on behalf of the original proprietor. This duty extends to providing all material information reasonably ascertainable regarding potential encumbrances upon such rights, including but not limited to prior assignments, licenses, or security interests. Failure to comply with this duty shall render the assignor or licensor liable for damages sustained by the assignee or licensee as a direct consequence of the non-disclosure. This liability is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act or at law. The scope of information required to be disclosed may be clarified through guidelines issued by the Central Government, provided that such guidelines do not contradict provisions herein.

Where a consumer has suffered loss or injury due to deficiency in goods or services, they may file a complaint with the District Commission, State Commission, or National Commission as applicable. Upon receiving such a complaint, the concerned Commission shall afford the party against whom the complaint is made an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence under this Act. The Commissions are empowered to order remedies including but not limited to refunds, replacements of goods, repairs of services, and compensation for loss suffered. In determining appropriate relief, the Commissions shall consider the nature of the deficiency and the circumstances of the case. Each Commission shall be assisted by an adjudicating officer who will conduct hearings and record findings. The adjudicating officer's decisions are subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any individual or community demonstrably suffering harm from environmental degradation attributable to industrial activity is hereby empowered to petition a jurisdictional authority seeking redress. Such petitions must specify the nature and extent of the damage, along with proposed remedial measures. The jurisdictional authority shall, upon receiving such a petition, promptly designate a competent officer to investigate the matter and submit a report within sixty days. This report shall detail findings regarding the industrial activity’s contribution to the harm and recommend appropriate compensation or restorative action. Compensation may include monetary relief for loss of livelihood, property damage, or health impacts. The competent officer's recommendations are binding on the jurisdictional authority subject to judicial review under this Act. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the responsible party liable to penalties as provided herein.

Every distribution licensee shall, prior to commencement of electricity supply to a consumer under a contract involving anticipated peak demand exceeding five hundred kilowatts, recover from such consumer a security deposit equivalent to three months’ average billed amount for the preceding year, or such higher amount as may be determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission. Provided that, if the consumer is a government entity or a public utility undertaking, the commission may waive the requirement of furnishing a security deposit subject to conditions regarding timely payment of electricity bills and adherence to distribution licensee’s operational protocols. The security deposit shall be refunded to the consumer upon termination of the contract, less any amounts due to the licensee under this Act for outstanding charges or damages caused by negligence in operation or maintenance of electrical installations.

For the purposes of this Act, “material document” means any record, irrespective of its form or medium, which contains information directly relevant to a fact in issue or a matter under investigation; and includes documents generated electronically or stored in digital format. The duty of disclosure shall apply where a party possesses a material document pertaining to a claim or defence, whether that party is a witness or not. A person failing to comply with the duty of disclosure may be deemed to have withheld evidence as provided herein. This obligation extends to all persons who, by virtue of their profession or employment, handle or possess such documents.

Where a party to an agreement fails to perform their contractual obligations as provided under this Act, and such failure results in demonstrable financial loss to the other contracting party, that aggrieved party shall be entitled to initiate proceedings for recovery of dues. This right to recovery is subject to the condition that the non-performing party was not relieved from their obligations due to force majeure events or acts of government. Provided that any claim for recovery must be substantiated by detailed accounts and expert testimony demonstrating a direct causal link between the breach and the financial loss incurred. Further, such claims shall be barred if legal proceedings are not commenced within three years from the date of default. The court may award interest at prevailing rates where applicable.

Where a sole arbitrator or arbitral tribunal is appointed pursuant to this Act, it shall maintain complete and accurate records of all proceedings undertaken during the arbitration process, including but not limited to pleadings, evidence presented by parties, awards rendered, and any interim orders issued. The record shall be preserved for a period of three years from the date on which the final arbitral award is communicated to the parties. Any party demonstrating that the maintenance of such records was deficient or deliberately manipulated in a manner prejudicial to their interests may petition the judicial authority for appropriate redress, including but not limited to setting aside the award or ordering rectification of the record. The judicial authority shall consider any evidence presented and may grant such relief as it deems just, provided that the party seeking redress establishes demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the deficient maintenance of records.

An employee who has rendered continuous service of five years or more is entitled to gratuity at a rate not exceeding fifteen days’ wages for each completed year of service, or twenty-four months' wages whichever is higher. Where the termination of employment occurs due to dismissal for cause as defined under this Act, such employee shall be deemed ineligible for gratuity; however, if an appeal against such dismissal is pending and ultimately succeeds, entitlement shall arise retrospectively from the date of original termination. The manner of service, including but not limited to transfers, promotions, and changes in job designation, does not affect the determination of continuous service unless it results in a significant alteration of duties rendering the employee incapable of performing their assigned tasks. An employer shall provide written notification of gratuity eligibility and calculation details to each eligible employee at least thirty days prior to any event triggering payment.

Where an offence has been committed involving a violation of procedural guidelines prescribed under this Act, the Central Information Commission shall have the power to entertain applications for compounding of offences, provided that the Public Authority concerned initiates the process within ninety days from the date the alleged infraction comes to its notice. The application shall be accompanied by a detailed report outlining the nature of the offence and any remedial measures undertaken. Upon receipt of such an application, the Commission may direct the offender to pay a sum not exceeding five thousand rupees as compensation to the complainant or deposit it with the Government for disbursement to victims of maladministration. This direction is subject to the condition that the offender admits guilt and undertakes to rectify the procedural deficiency which led to the offence. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the matter liable for further adjudication under this Act.

The State Commission shall, upon receiving a request from an appropriate distribution licensee, delegate certain functions relating to tariff determination and enforcement to a committee constituted for that purpose. Such delegation shall be accompanied by a formal instrument detailing the specific powers transferred, the duration of the delegated authority, and any reporting requirements applicable to the committee. The Commission may, at any time, revoke or modify such delegation if it deems it necessary in the public interest or due to operational inefficiencies. Any action taken by the committee acting under delegated power shall be reported to the State Commission within thirty days of its completion. This delegation of powers does not extend to matters concerning license renewals or major policy decisions relating to electricity generation, and remains firmly within the purview of the State Commission itself. The licensee requesting such delegation must demonstrate adequate staffing and expertise within the proposed committee.

For the purposes of this Act, a statutory declaration relating to food safety practices shall mean a written statement made before an authorised officer, affirming the truthfulness of facts pertaining to the handling, processing, packaging, and storage of food products. Such declarations shall be in the form specified by regulations framed under this Act and shall include particulars regarding the premises where food is manufactured or handled, details of personnel involved in such activities, and adherence to prescribed hygiene standards. A person making a statutory declaration shall be deemed to have declared that the information contained therein is true and correct to the best of their knowledge.

Where an employee dies or ceases to be employed otherwise than by way of voluntary resignation or termination for cause, a person nominated by the deceased employee or, if no such nomination has been made, any legal heir of the employee shall be entitled to claim gratuity under this Act. The employer shall, within thirty days from the date of death or cessation of employment, serve upon such nominee or legal heir a notice of demand specifying the amount of gratuity payable and requiring him to submit proof of identity and relationship to the deceased employee. Failure to comply with the provisions of this notice may render the employer liable for penalties as provided herein. The claimant shall be required to produce documents establishing entitlement, including but not limited to death certificate or succession certificate. An appeal against any determination made by the employer regarding eligibility or amount payable may be filed before the Controlling Authority within sixty days from the date of communication of such determination.

The State Electricity Regulatory Commission shall determine the schedule of fees payable by distribution licensees for various services rendered under this Act, including but not limited to applications for license renewal, deviation from standards specified therein, and appeals against orders issued by the Commission itself. The initial schedule of fees shall be published in the Official Gazette and may be revised periodically, subject to a public consultation process as provided herein. Any licensee disputing any fee levied under this schedule may file an objection with the Commission within thirty days of the date of demand, accompanied by reasons for such dispute. The Commission shall consider such objections and pass reasoned orders; appeals against these orders are permissible before the appellate tribunal, subject to the limitations period specified elsewhere under this Act.

Any person engaged in industrial activity involving the release of hazardous substances into the environment shall have a duty of disclosure regarding the nature, quantity, and potential impact of such releases. Failure to provide complete and accurate information as required under this Act, or providing false information with intent to mislead, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with a fine which may extend to one hundred thousand rupees, or both. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the form and manner of disclosure required under this Act. Any officer failing to diligently investigate complaints regarding non-compliance with these disclosure requirements shall be liable for penalty as provided herein.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a scheme for the assignment of claims arising from accidents involving motor vehicles, including but not limited to claims relating to compensation payable under this Act. Such scheme shall provide that any insurance company holding a valid license to conduct general insurance business may assign its rights and obligations concerning recovery of dues owed to it by policyholders or third parties involved in vehicular incidents. Assignment under the prescribed scheme shall be deemed a valid transfer, subject to conditions regarding disclosure of material facts to the assignee. The Central Government may also specify procedures for verifying the validity of assignments and resolving disputes arising therefrom. No assignment shall prejudice the rights of claimants seeking compensation as provided herein; however, any subsequent recovery from an assigned debt shall be shared according to terms stipulated in the assignment agreement.

Where a party desires to initiate arbitration proceedings pursuant to an agreement, they shall serve upon the other party a written notice of demand specifying the nature of the dispute, the relief sought, and the number of arbitrators proposed under this Act. Such notice of demand must be served by registered post with acknowledgment due or through electronic means as prescribed by regulations framed thereunder. The recipient of the notice of demand shall, within thirty days from the date of its receipt, acknowledge the receipt of the same and indicate their acceptance or rejection of the proposed arbitrators. Failure to respond within that period shall be deemed an acceptance of the arbitration agreement and the nominated arbitrator(s). Any subsequent communication regarding appointment of arbitrators must adhere to procedures as provided herein.

Registration of food premises involving a security deposit shall be conducted according to the procedures outlined herein. Any person intending to operate a food business requiring registration under this Act must submit an application in Form A to the designated Food Safety Officer. Along with the application, a security deposit, calculated as per Schedule D, shall be remitted. This security deposit is intended to cover potential costs associated with rectifying deficiencies identified during inspections or ensuring compliance with hygiene standards. The amount of the security deposit may be adjusted periodically by notification in the Official Gazette. Upon successful completion of registration and subsequent satisfactory adherence to regulations, the security deposit shall be refundable, subject to deductions for any penalties levied under this Act.

An employee who has suffered a loss due to an incorrect or delayed gratuity payment is hereby empowered to file a written complaint with the appropriate appellate authority, detailing the nature of the grievance and providing supporting documentation as evidence. The appointed authority shall, upon receiving such a complaint, conduct an inquiry within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of receipt. During this inquiry, both the employee and the employer shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case and cross-examine witnesses. Any order passed by the appointed authority may direct the employer to pay the outstanding gratuity amount along with interest at such rate as may be determined under this Act. Failure to comply with an order of the appointed authority is deemed a civil offence, subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where a Central Information Commission determines that an information-holding public authority has failed to provide access to information within the prescribed time limit, or otherwise obstructs the exercise of the right to information guaranteed under this Act, it may direct such authority to permit entry upon its premises for the purpose of examining records and documents relevant to the request. Such power of entry shall be exercised only with due regard to the operational requirements of the public authority and after providing reasonable notice, unless the Commission deems immediate access necessary in the interests of fairness or transparency. The person exercising this power shall be accompanied by such officers as the Commission may direct. Any individual preventing or obstructing a duly authorized entrant shall be liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where any dispute arises concerning the validity or enforceability of an agreement entered into pursuant to a tender process conducted by a public body, either party may file a petition before the appointed authority for determination thereof. The appointed authority shall provide both parties with written notice of the hearing and an opportunity to present evidence and arguments relevant to the matter under consideration. Any order made by the appointed authority concerning such disputes is subject to review upon appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the appellant demonstrates a substantial legal error occurred in the proceedings before the appointed authority. The public body shall furnish all documents pertaining to the tender process to the appointed authority and the High Court as required.

Where a service provider fails to render services with due care and attention, or deviates substantially from established standards of practice within their industry, the consumer is entitled to redress as provided herein. This includes situations where the manner of service falls below a reasonable expectation based on prior representations made by the service provider, whether in advertising materials, promotional offers, or through employee conduct. The Central Authority may investigate complaints regarding deficient services and issue directions requiring the service provider to rectify their practices and compensate affected consumers. Further, a consumer seeking redress for unsatisfactory service shall be entitled to claim damages including consequential losses directly attributable to the failure in the manner of service. Nothing in this section shall prevent a consumer from pursuing alternative remedies available under other laws.

Where an offence has been committed under this Act or regulations made thereunder, the State Electricity Regulatory Commission may, if satisfied that it is expedient so to do, enter into a compromise with the offender. Such compromise shall involve the payment by the offender of such sum of money as the Commission deems fit, representing compensation for any loss suffered by the injured party and reflecting the seriousness of the offence committed. The Commission shall provide written notice to all affected parties prior to initiating proceedings regarding compounding of offences. Any agreement reached through this process must be recorded in writing and signed by the offender and an authorised representative of the Commission. Failure to comply with the terms of such a compromise will render it void, and the offender shall be liable for prosecution as if no such agreement had been made. The prescribed procedure for conducting hearings related to compounding shall be followed diligently.

Where a licence is granted under this Act, the conditions of licence shall be recorded in a register maintained for that purpose at the office of the Licensing Authority. Every licensee shall, within thirty days of the grant of the licence, present to the Sub-Registrar a certified copy of the recorded conditions. The Sub-Registrar shall endorse such copy on the application for registration and retain it as part of the official record pertaining to the contract. Any modification or alteration to the conditions of licence subsequent to the initial grant must also be registered with the Sub-Registrar in like manner, ensuring a complete and accurate reflection of the contractual obligations. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the licence liable to cancellation by the Licensing Authority, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a consumer files a complaint alleging deficiency in service or unfair trade practice, the District Commission shall adopt a summary procedure for expeditious disposal. The Commission may direct the parties to appear before it on dates fixed by notice, provided that failure of either party to attend without just cause shall be deemed sufficient grounds for ex parte proceedings. Evidence shall be adduced orally or in documentary form as the Commission deems appropriate, and witnesses may be examined under oath. The Commission shall record its findings and pass orders within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of the last hearing. Any order passed by the District Commission is subject to appeal before the State Commission within sixty days. The Central Authority may issue guidelines regarding the conduct of proceedings and timelines for adherence, as deemed necessary to ensure uniformity in application of this summary procedure across all Commissions.

The licensing authority shall grant a license for the manufacture, processing, and distribution of packaged drinking water only after verification that the applicant possesses requisite infrastructure and adheres to hygiene protocols as provided herein. A licensee may assign their license to another entity subject to prior approval from the competent authority and payment of a transfer fee not exceeding two percent of the initial licensing cost. Any assignment shall be deemed invalid unless registered with the Food Safety and Standards appellate tribunal within thirty days, along with a detailed justification for the proposed transfer. The tribunal may reject an assignment if it determines that the assignee lacks the necessary qualifications or poses a risk to public health. Further, any change in ownership structure of a licensed entity requires notification to the licensing authority and potential review by the appellate tribunal.

Where a principal contractor undertakes an agreement involving multiple subcontractors, the delegation of powers necessary for efficient project execution shall be governed by these provisions. The Principal Contractor shall furnish a detailed schedule outlining all delegated authorities to the Subcontractor, specifying the scope and limits of such delegation in writing. This schedule must be approved by the designated Project Oversight Committee prior to commencement of work under the subcontract agreement. Any subsequent alteration or expansion of delegated powers requires a revised schedule submitted for re-approval. The Principal Contractor shall maintain meticulous records pertaining to all delegations, including dates of approval, officer designations receiving authority, and specific tasks authorized. Subcontractors may not further delegate any power granted by the Principal Contractor without express written consent obtained in advance. Failure to adhere to these procedures constitutes a breach of contract and renders the Subcontractor liable for damages as provided herein.

The Central Information Commission may, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate its powers relating to the hearing of complaints under Section 18, provided that such delegation is made only to an officer specifically designated in writing for that purpose. Any such delegated power shall be exercised solely within the geographical jurisdiction assigned by the Commission and only concerning matters pertaining to public authorities located therein. The Commission shall ensure that any officer to whom powers are delegated possesses appropriate experience in adjudicating administrative disputes, as determined by a review conducted annually. Further, no delegation of powers shall absolve the Central Information Commission from ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with this Act; all decisions rendered by delegated officers remain subject to review and revision by the Commission itself.

Environmental clearances granted under this Act relating to industrial projects involving processing of hazardous substances shall be assignable subject to conditions specified by the Central Government. Any entity seeking assignment of such clearance must provide a detailed plan outlining continued compliance with stipulated environmental safeguards and mitigation measures, as determined satisfactory by the State Pollution Control Board. The original holder of the clearance remains jointly liable for any breaches occurring after assignment until expiry of a period of two years from the date of transfer. Assignment shall require prior approval in writing from the Central Government, processed through a summary procedure designed to expedite decisions while ensuring adequate scrutiny. This summary procedure allows for expedited review and decision-making based on documented evidence and without extensive oral hearings.

Every distribution licensee shall provide electricity supply in the manner of service prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, ensuring adherence to standards of voltage, frequency, and reliability as notified by the appropriate authority. Failure to comply with these prescribed standards, or any deviation from the approved manner of service without prior authorization, constitutes a violation subject to penalties as determined by the State Commission. Any consumer aggrieved by a perceived deficiency in the licensee’s manner of service may lodge a complaint before the concerned Grievance Redressal Forum established under this Act. The forum shall investigate and, if warranted, impose financial penalties upon the licensee for non-compliance; provided that such penalties are proportionate to the extent of disruption caused.

Every food business operator involved in the manufacture, processing, packaging, storage, distribution, sale, or import of any article of food shall have a duty of disclosure regarding all ingredients used, additives employed, and processes undertaken to produce said food product. Failure to provide this information accurately and completely, as required under this Act, constitutes an offence punishable with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees for the first instance and one hundred thousand rupees for subsequent offences. Any officer authorized by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India may seize any food article where there is reasonable suspicion that the duty of disclosure has been violated. Repeated non-compliance shall render the business operator liable to suspension of license, provided that a hearing opportunity is afforded.

Where a distribution licensee fails to provide electricity service within the timeframe stipulated under this Act or as agreed upon with a consumer, the aggrieved consumer shall have recourse to remedies provided herein. A consumer seeking connection or restoration of supply may serve a written notice of demand on the licensee specifying the nature of the deficiency and requiring rectification within thirty days. The licensee shall acknowledge receipt of such notice of demand and respond outlining steps taken or proposed to address the grievance. Failure by the licensee to rectify the deficiency within the stipulated period, or to provide a satisfactory response, constitutes a breach of contract subject to adjudication under this Act. Compensation for losses incurred due to the delay in providing electricity service may be awarded as determined by an appropriate forum, provided that such claims are substantiated with documentary evidence.

Any individual seeking to establish the authenticity of a transaction or fact before a registering authority shall have the option of submitting a statutory declaration in lieu of presenting witnesses or producing documentary evidence ordinarily required under this Act. Such declaration must be made before an oath commissioner or notary public duly authorised under the Notaries Act, 1951. The declaration shall clearly state the full name, address, and occupation of the declarant, along with a precise description of the fact or transaction being affirmed. It is provided that the registering authority may, at its discretion, require supplementary documentation to verify the contents of the statutory declaration. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements renders the declaration invalid for purposes of establishing legal certainty as provided herein. The registering authority shall maintain a record of all statutory declarations received and processed, accessible for inspection by authorised personnel only.

Where any gratuity is paid in installments, the employer shall furnish to the employee, along with each installment, prescribed particulars relating to the amount paid, the total gratuity due, and the balance remaining unpaid. Failure to provide these particulars as required under this Act shall be deemed a material irregularity rendering the payment liable for review by the Controlling Authority. An appeal lies to the appellate authority within thirty days from the date of notification of such review order. It is provided that an employee may challenge the adequacy of the prescribed particulars, alleging insufficient detail regarding calculation methodology, and such challenge constitutes grounds for an appeal under this Act. The appellate authority shall consider evidence presented by both parties before issuing a determination.

Any arbitration agreement lawfully entered into by a corporate body shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent delegation of powers undertaken by that body, provided that the delegated authority did not explicitly revoke or modify the original arbitration clause. Failure to honour an arbitration agreement due to purported lack of authorization from the delegating officer shall constitute a breach subject to penalties as prescribed under this Act. The adjudicating authority may impose a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of such non-compliance, and further order specific performance compelling adherence to the agreed arbitral process. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from an unauthorized delegation shall be entitled to claim compensatory damages, recoverable through enforcement proceedings as provided herein.

Applications for registration of gratuity-paying establishments shall be submitted to the Controlling Authority within whose local jurisdiction the establishment is situated. Each application must contain certified copies of the Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association, or equivalent founding documents where applicable, alongside a detailed list of employees as on the date of application. The authority may require further documentation demonstrating compliance with provisions under this Act relating to employee eligibility and gratuity calculation. Any objection to the registration shall be communicated in writing within thirty days from the date of receipt of the application by the Controlling Authority. Failure to address such objections within a period of limitation of ninety days, or where applicable, as extended by the authority for justifiable cause, will preclude further challenge to the proposed registration.

The Central Government may, through notification published in the Official Gazette, authorize any person to act as a Licensing Agent for the assignment of environmental clearances pertaining to industrial projects requiring assessment under this Act. Such authorization shall specify the scope of activities permitted to be assigned by the Licensing Agent, including but not limited to, transfer of responsibility for compliance with conditions stipulated in the clearance order. A Licensing Agent may assign rights and obligations arising from an environmental clearance only after obtaining prior written consent from the project proponent and the recipient entity. The adjudicating officer shall review any assignment undertaken without proper authorization or exceeding the scope granted under the license, and may impose penalties as provided herein. Further, the Central Government may revoke a Licensing Agent’s authority if they fail to adhere to guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

The gratuity payable under this Act to any employee who has rendered service for not less than five years shall vest in his legal heirs or nominees upon his death, subject to the provisions regarding assignment as detailed herein. Where an employee intends to assign their right to receive gratuity, such assignment must be executed by a deed registered with the Sub-Registrar of Assigments and explicitly identify the assignee and the specific gratuity entitlement being transferred. Assignment shall not extend to any portion of gratuity accrued prior to the date of the assignment deed. Further, the employer may withhold payment pending verification of the authenticity of the assignment and confirmation from the concerned Gratuity Authority. Grounds of revocation of such assignments include demonstrable fraud in the execution or material misrepresentation concerning the employee’s entitlement under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “employer” means any person who employs twenty or more persons in his establishment; an establishment includes not only factories but also offices, workshops, stores, and other places where work is performed under a contract of employment. "Gratuity" shall mean a sum of money granted to or paid to an employee on the termination of his service or on his retirement or resignation. An offence under this Act which is compoundable shall be so specified herein; such offences are those relating primarily to procedural defaults in payment, and not those involving deliberate non-compliance with obligations regarding eligibility or calculation. The power to order compounding of offences vests solely with a Labour Court as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “gratuity” means the payment in cash of a sum calculated according to provisions herein, granted to an eligible employee by his employer upon such employee’s retirement or termination of service. An action to recover gratuity shall not be maintainable unless it is instituted within three years from the date on which the gratuity became payable; however, this period of limitation may be extended in cases where the delay is attributable to circumstances beyond the control of the claimant. The employer shall provide all necessary documentation pertaining to eligibility and calculation as required under this Act.

Where a party seeks to initiate arbitration or conciliation proceedings, a written notice of demand shall be served upon the other party specifying the nature of the dispute, the relief sought, and the number of arbitrators proposed under this Act. Such notice must clearly identify the contract or agreement giving rise to the claim. The service of such notice shall be deemed valid if delivered personally, sent by registered post with acknowledgment due, or transmitted electronically through a secure digital signature as prescribed in the rules made thereunder. Failure to provide adequate particulars within the notice of demand may result in objections being raised regarding the scope and validity of subsequent arbitral proceedings. A party receiving a notice of demand shall acknowledge receipt thereof within seven days, failing which it shall be presumed that the notice has been duly received. The time for responding to a notice of demand is governed by regulations made under this Act.

Any document purporting to be a certificate of registration issued by the Registrar of Societies shall be admissible as evidence in any court or proceeding relating to the constitution, governance, or activities of a registered society, provided that the certificate is accompanied by a written declaration from the issuing officer verifying its authenticity and compliance with applicable regulations. The party producing such certificate shall be deemed to have discharged an initial burden of establishing the genuineness of the registration unless credible evidence is presented demonstrating forgery or material alteration. Any person alleging fraud or misrepresentation relating to the contents of a certificate of registration may challenge its admissibility, subject to the provisions under this Act regarding cross-examination and production of relevant records. The Registrar shall be liable for damages if it is proven that a false certificate of registration was knowingly issued.

Where a consumer alleges that an electricity distribution licensee has failed to provide adequate voltage or frequency, or has otherwise acted in violation of its obligations as specified under this Act, such consumer may file a complaint with the appropriate appellate authority established under these regulations. The appointed authority shall, upon receiving such a complaint, serve notice on the licensee and afford both parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard. If, after due inquiry, the appointed authority finds that the licensee has indeed failed to meet its obligations, it may direct the licensee to rectify the deficiency within a specified timeframe and award compensation to the consumer for any losses suffered as a consequence of the default. This compensation shall be determined based on the extent of disruption and the prevailing tariff structure, provided that the total liability of the licensee shall not exceed an amount as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where any industrial unit engaged in activities listed under Schedule I is required to undertake environmental impact assessment, the unit holder shall furnish a comprehensive report detailing all potential hazards associated with the proposed project, including but not limited to effluent discharge, air emissions, and noise pollution. This duty of disclosure extends to providing readily accessible data on mitigation measures planned for such hazards. Failure to provide this information truthfully or omitting material facts shall be deemed an offence punishable under this Act. Any party claiming prejudice due to non-disclosure or misrepresentation may appeal the assessment’s validity before a designated appellate tribunal, subject to demonstrating demonstrable harm; provided that the appeal must be filed within ninety days of the order being passed.
